Rust for Experienced Developers

A course from first principles to a REST microservice with PostgreSQL, written for people who already know Kotlin, JavaScript, Python, C, operating systems and design patterns. Every topic maps Rust back to what you know, then shows where Rust is different. Comparisons use Kotlin for high-level features, and C for the low-level ones that the JVM hides.

  • Rust 1.100.0
  • Edition 2024
  • std only, plus serde, Tokio, axum, reqwest, tracing & SQLx in Ch. 20–27
  • Ubuntu 26.04 · WSL 2
  • macOS notes included
  • 27 chapters + 6 appendices
  • 106 tested examples

How to use it. Alongside the short examples, you build one project, shoes, chapter by chapter: a catalog of shoes with variants and versions. Each Project step extends it and shows the files it changes, from one printed product in Chapter 1 to the web service that Chapters 22–27 build: a REST API with axum, an HTTP client with reqwest, logging with tracing, PostgreSQL with migrations, and bearer-token authentication. Every example is a complete program. The output shown under it was captured by compiling and running it with Rust 1.100.0 on Ubuntu 26.04 in WSL 2, and examples marked does not compile show the real compiler error. Chapters 20–27 use crates (serde, chrono, Tokio, axum, reqwest, tracing, SQLx). Every project step was checked with cargo fmt, Clippy and its tests, and its output, HTTP sessions and logs were captured from real runs, Chapters 25–27 against PostgreSQL 18 in Podman. Run in Playground opens the code in the official Rust Playground so you can edit and run it. You don't need anything installed to begin: Chapter 1 starts from a Linux machine with no Rust at all and installs the toolchain and the editor you'll use throughout, VS Code with the rust-analyzer extension. On a Mac, Chapter 1 has a macOS setup section, and later chapters flag the few commands that differ. Each chapter ends with practice tasks. Topics a typical web service rarely needs (Rc and RefCell, scoped threads and std channels, async internals, unsafe and FFI, a hand-built thread pool, design patterns) are in the appendices at the end.

Part IFoundations
Chapter 01

Getting Started

Installing Rust 1.100 from scratch in Ubuntu 26.04 on WSL, setting up VS Code with rust-analyzer, the mental model, the toolchain, and a map from the languages you know to Rust.

Start here: install Rust from scratch

This course assumes you already have WSL 2 with Ubuntu 26.04 on Windows, and no Rust installed. Open the Ubuntu terminal (Start menu → Ubuntu 26.04, or wsl -d Ubuntu-26.04 in PowerShell). You need three things, all free:

  1. a C linker (build-essential): rustc uses it to produce executables;
  2. the Rust toolchain (rustc, cargo, rustfmt, clippy), installed with rustup, the official installer;
  3. VS Code with the rust-analyzer extension, the editor setup this course uses: code completion, inline types, errors as you type, and Run/Debug buttons above main and every test.

In the Ubuntu terminal, these commands install the first two:

Rustup installs into your home directory (~/.cargo, ~/.rustup), needs no root, and rustup update later moves you to each new release.

Then install VS Code and the rust-analyzer extension:

rust-analyzer ships its own language server, so there's nothing else to install with rustup. To check the setup, run cargo new hello && code hello, open src/main.rs, and click ▶ Run above fn main: Hello, world! appears in the terminal panel.

Tip

No Linux machine yet, or just want to try something quickly? Every example in this course also has a Run in Playground button that runs it in the browser, with nothing installed.

On macOS

Using a Mac instead of WSL? Follow On macOS below instead of these commands; everything after the setup is the same.

The rest of this section explains each part of that setup in more detail, plus a few WSL habits worth adopting from day one.

Step by step, in Ubuntu 26.04 on WSL

Everything in this course targets Linux: commands are bash, paths are POSIX, and every example was compiled and run on x86-64 Linux, the same x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu target that Ubuntu uses inside WSL 2. All commands below run in the Ubuntu terminal unless marked as PowerShell.

1. Install the C toolchain. rustc uses the system linker cc; without build-essential your first build fails with linker cc not found.

2. Install Rust with rustup. Ubuntu 26.04's apt install rustc cargo gives Rust 1.93.1, which is too old for this course. Use the official installer, which puts the toolchain in ~/.cargo and ~/.rustup and keeps it current with rustup update.

Watch out

Don't mix the apt packages and rustup. If you installed rustc/cargo with apt earlier, remove them first (sudo apt remove rustc cargo), otherwise whichever comes first on your PATH wins and versions get confusing.

3. VS Code with rust-analyzer (required). Install VS Code on Windows with the WSL extension, then run code . from a project folder in Ubuntu. VS Code runs its server inside Linux, so the rust-analyzer extension must be installed there: run code --install-extension rust-lang.rust-analyzer in VS Code's terminal, or click "Install in WSL: Ubuntu-26.04" on the extension's page. The status bar shows rust-analyzer once it has indexed the project. (Terminal editors such as vim, Helix or Emacs can use rust-analyzer too, but the course's instructions assume VS Code.)

4. Keep your code in the Linux filesystem. Create projects under ~/code, not under /mnt/c/.... Cargo touches thousands of small files per build, and crossing the Windows filesystem boundary from WSL 2 makes that dramatically slower. To open your Linux files from Windows, run explorer.exe . in a project folder.

On macOS

The course also works on a current macOS, on Apple silicon or Intel. The toolchain, the editor and the Rust code are the same; only the setup commands and a few system tools differ, and the chapters that use them have On macOS notes. (Unlike the Linux instructions, these macOS notes weren't run on a Mac when this page was built.) Open Terminal; its default shell is zsh.

  • Don't install Rust from Homebrew (brew install rust) as well as rustup: as with apt, two toolchains on the PATH get confusing.
  • Put the rr helper below in ~/.zshrc instead of ~/.bashrc; it works unchanged in zsh.
  • rustup show lists aarch64-apple-darwin on Apple silicon (x86_64-apple-darwin on Intel Macs). Programs are Mach-O executables rather than ELF.
  • Skip the WSL-only advice (keeping code out of /mnt/c, reaching servers from Windows): on a Mac, localhost is simply your machine.

Running the examples in this course

Each example is a complete single-file program. Paste it into src/main.rs of a scratch Cargo project and cargo run, or add this helper to ~/.bashrc to compile and run any .rs file directly:

The examples are laid out compactly for reading (one-line functions, aligned trailing comments), so rustfmt would reformat many of them; in your own projects, run cargo fmt to apply the standard style and cargo clippy to catch unidiomatic code. Every example compiles without warnings under default Clippy lints, with one deliberate exception in Chapter 9.

Examples marked tests compile with rustc --edition 2024 --test file.rs -o /tmp/t && /tmp/t.

OS view

Your new system is partly written in Rust. In Ubuntu 26.04, sudo is sudo-rs and the core utilities (ls, cat, tr, ...) are the uutils Rust reimplementation, with cp, mv and rm still GNU for this release. Run sudo --version to see it. (On macOS the command-line tools are the BSD versions.)

The mental model in one paragraph

Rust compiles ahead of time to native code through LLVM, like C. It has no garbage collector and no runtime beyond a thin standard library, yet it is memory safe: the compiler tracks who owns each value and who is borrowing it, and rejects programs that could dangle, double-free or race. Abstractions (generics, iterators, closures) are monomorphized and inlined, so they cost what the equivalent hand-written C would. There are no classes and no inheritance: data lives in structs and enums, behaviour is attached with impl blocks, and polymorphism comes from traits. Errors are values (Result), absence is a value (Option), and almost everything is an expression.

The toolchain

Tool Role Everyday commands
rustup Installs and switches toolchains rustup update stable (gets 1.100), rustup component add clippy
rustc The compiler rustc --edition 2024 main.rs (rarely used directly)
cargo Build system, test runner, package manager cargo new app, cargo run, cargo check, cargo test, cargo build --release
clippy Linter with ~800 lints cargo clippy
rustfmt Formatter cargo fmt
rust-analyzer Language server for your editor install the editor extension

cargo check type-checks without generating code and is the fastest feedback loop. Debug builds (cargo run) keep overflow checks and debug assertions; --release turns on optimizations. Build output goes to target/debug/ or target/release/ as ordinary ELF executables you can run, strace or debug with rust-gdb like any C program.

Note

Versions vs editions. The compiler version (1.100) moves every six weeks and never breaks stable code. An edition (2015, 2018, 2021, 2024) is an opt-in set of syntax and lint changes chosen per crate in Cargo.toml (edition = "2024"). Crates on different editions link together freely. This course uses edition 2024 throughout.

Hello, formatting

println! is a macro (the ! gives it away). Macros can take a variable number of arguments, and the format string is checked at compile time: a missing argument is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.

{} uses the Display trait (user-facing), {:?} uses Debug (developer-facing, derivable), {:#?} pretty-prints. Width, alignment, precision and radix work like C's printf, but type-safe.

This step

The domain is a shoe shop's catalog:

  1. Install Rust with rustup and VS Code with rust-analyzer as above, then confirm rustc --version reports 1.100.0 and rustup show lists x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu (aarch64-apple-darwin on a Mac with Apple silicon).
    Solution

    After the install commands from this chapter, open a new terminal and check the toolchain:

    The lines to look for are rustc 1.100.0 and the target x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu under installed targets. A fresh install lists only the stable toolchain; the nightly line appears here because this machine also has it.   2. Create a project under ~/code with cargo new, print a table of the first ten squares right-aligned in a 6-character column, run cargo clippy on it, and compare ls -lh of the debug and --release binaries.
    Solution

    Clippy has nothing to say, so it prints only the Checking and Finished lines. The debug binary is about ten times larger because it carries debug info (for rust-gdb and readable backtraces) and unoptimized code, while the release build is optimized and ships without debug info.

Next · Chapter 2Variables, Types & Functions
Chapter 02

Variables, Types & Functions

Immutability by default, explicit numeric conversions, the text and collection types you'll meet everywhere, and why blocks are expressions.

Bindings, mutability and shadowing

Bindings are immutable unless declared mut. Shadowing (let x = ... again) creates a new binding that may have a different type; the old value is simply no longer reachable by that name. It is commonly used for transformations like parsing, where the raw and parsed values would otherwise need two names.

Coming from Kotlin

let is Kotlin's val and let mut is var, with one important difference: val only freezes the reference, so val list = mutableListOf(1) can still be modified. Rust's immutability is deep: through a non-mut binding you can't push to a Vec or change a struct's fields either.

Scalar types

Kind Types Notes
Signed integers i8 i16 i32 i64 i128 isize i32 is the default for integer literals
Unsigned integers u8 u16 u32 u64 u128 usize usize is pointer-sized and used for indexing and lengths
Floats f32 f64 IEEE 754; f64 is the default
Boolean bool No truthiness: if 1 {} does not compile
Character char A Unicode scalar value, always 4 bytes

Literals accept separators and suffixes: 1_000_000, 0xff, 0o77, 0b1010, b'A' (a u8), 42u8, 2.5f32.

Overflow and conversions

Integer overflow panics in debug builds and wraps in release builds. When wrap-around is intended, say so with an explicit method. There are no implicit numeric conversions, not even widening ones: use as for raw casts, From/Into for lossless conversions, and TryFrom when the value might not fit.

Coming from C

Out-of-range float-to-int casts are well defined (they saturate), signed overflow is never undefined behavior, and there is no integer promotion. u8 + u8 is a u8.

Tuples, arrays and the unit type

A tuple groups values of different types; an array [T; N] holds N values of one type, with the length as part of the type. Both live on the stack. Indexing is bounds-checked: out of range is a panic, never a silent read. The empty tuple () ("unit") is the type of expressions that produce no value, like void, but it is a real type you can store and compare.

Text: one idea, several types

Most languages have one string type. Rust has several, because it separates two questions that other languages answer for you: who owns the memory, and what the bytes are guaranteed to be. You'll use two of them every day:

  • String owns its text on the heap and can grow.
  • &str (a "string slice") borrows text owned by something else, like a String or the program binary.

Both are always valid UTF-8. The other types exist for text that isn't: raw bytes, OS paths and strings for C.

Type Ownership Guarantees Where you meet it
char a value one Unicode scalar value (4 bytes) iterating with .chars()
&str borrows valid UTF-8 string literals, function parameters
String owns, growable valid UTF-8 text you build, store or return
Box<str>, Arc<str> owns, fixed size valid UTF-8 text that never changes after creation (Chapters 15–16)
Cow<'_, str> borrows or owns valid UTF-8 text that is usually passed through unchanged (Chapter 15)
&[u8], Vec<u8> borrows / owns any bytes binary data, network and file buffers
&Path, PathBuf borrows / owns an OS path, maybe not UTF-8 the file system (Chapter 19)
&OsStr, OsString borrows / owns an OS string, maybe not UTF-8 command-line arguments, environment variables
&CStr, CString borrows / owns nul-terminated, no interior nul calling C (Appendix D)

Ownership and borrowing are the subject of Chapters 4–5, so for now a rule of thumb is enough. Take &str as a function parameter, and return or store String. Chapter 14 covers String in depth.

Three things in this example surprise people:

  • len() is the length in bytes: é and ö take two bytes each in UTF-8.
  • owned[0] doesn't compile, because a byte offset isn't a character. A slice like &owned[0..6] takes a byte range, and panics if the range would cut a character in half.
  • String::from_utf8 returns a Result, because arbitrary bytes may not be valid text. Result is covered in Chapter 9.
Coming from Kotlin

A Kotlin String is immutable UTF-16, and you build text with a StringBuilder. Rust's String is both: a mutable, growable UTF-8 buffer. The closest thing to Kotlin's immutable String is &str, but that borrows its text rather than sharing it through the garbage collector. When you need an immutable string that several owners share, Rust uses Arc<str> (Chapter 16).

Collection types

The standard library has fewer collections than the JVM, and the defaults are clear. Use Vec for sequences and HashMap for lookups. Reach for the others when their one strength matters: sorted keys, a queue or a priority queue. Arrays and slices are built into the language; everything else is in std::collections, except Vec, which is always in scope.

Rust Kotlin Use for
[T; N] Array, IntArray (fixed length) a fixed number of items, known at compile time
&[T] a view, like List.subList a borrowed view of any contiguous run: array, Vec or part of one
Vec<T> ArrayList (mutableListOf()) the default sequence
VecDeque<T> ArrayDeque a queue: push and pop at both ends
HashMap<K, V> HashMap (hashMapOf()) lookups by key when order doesn't matter
BTreeMap<K, V> TreeMap (sortedMapOf()) keys kept sorted; range queries
HashSet<T> HashSet (hashSetOf()) membership tests, removing duplicates
BTreeSet<T> TreeSet (sortedSetOf()) unique values in sorted order
BinaryHeap<T> PriorityQueue (but largest first) a priority queue
LinkedList<T> LinkedList rarely the right choice: Vec or VecDeque is almost always faster

This chapter only introduces the names. Chapter 13 shows how to process collections with iterators, and Chapter 14 covers each collection, its costs, and how to choose. get returns an Option, Rust's type for "maybe a value", which Chapter 8 covers.

Coming from Kotlin

mutableMapOf() returns a LinkedHashMap, which remembers insertion order. Rust's HashMap is like hashMapOf(): its iteration order is unspecified and, because the hash function is randomly seeded, changes from run to run. Use a BTreeMap (like sortedMapOf()) when you need sorted keys. For insertion order there's the indexmap crate.

Functions and expressions

Parameter and return types are always written out: signatures are contracts, so inference stops at function boundaries. Inside a body, blocks are expressions. The last expression without a semicolon is the block's value, which is why return is mostly reserved for early exits. Adding a ; turns an expression into a statement whose value is ().

Coming from Kotlin

A Rust function body works like a Kotlin expression body (fun area(w: Int, h: Int) = w * h): the final expression is the value, and return is for early exits. () plays the role of Unit, so an extra ; after the last line turns it into a statement of type (), and a function declared -> i32 fails with expected i32, found (). As in Kotlin, there's no truthiness.

Project step 2: prices, text and bytes

This step

Store prices as whole cents in an i64, format them with a function, keep the variants in an array of tuples, and meet the type an uploaded image will have: Vec<u8>.

  • Money is integer cents. 129.99 as an f64 is not exactly 129.99, and sums drift. 12999 cents is exact. It's an i64 because that's what PostgreSQL's BIGINT becomes in Chapter 25, so the type never has to change.
  • Text types. The name is a String, owned text that can grow. The brand is a string literal, a &'static str baked into the binary.
  • Bytes are not text. An image file is a Vec<u8>: any byte values, not necessarily valid UTF-8. A String must always be valid UTF-8, so it can't hold an image.
  • A tuple per variant. (&str, &str, i64) groups the SKU, description and price. Chapter 7 replaces it with a struct that has named fields.

total / variants.len() as i64 needs the cast: len() is a usize, and Rust never converts between integer types implicitly.

Practice

  1. Write fn celsius_to_fahrenheit(c: f64) -> f64 and print a conversion table from -10 °C to 40 °C in steps of 10.
    Solution

    The loop counts in integers and converts each value with f64::from, a lossless conversion. There's no implicit i32 to f64 widening, so passing c directly wouldn't compile.

  2. Compute the 50th Fibonacci number with u32, checked_add and a loop, and print where it first overflows (F(48) no longer fits). Repeat with u64: F(50) now fits, so keep going and find where u64 overflows.
    Solution

    checked_add returns None instead of panicking (debug) or wrapping (release), so the loop can report the overflow and stop.

    u32::MAX is 4,294,967,295, and F(48) = 4,807,526,976 is the first Fibonacci number above it. u64 holds everything up to F(93); F(94) = 19,740,274,219,868,223,167 is past u64::MAX = 18,446,744,073,709,551,615.

Next · Chapter 3Control Flow
Chapter 03

Control Flow

if and loop are expressions, for works on iterators, and let-else and let chains keep the happy path flat.

if, loop, while, for

if is an expression, so Rust has no ternary operator. loop runs forever until break, and break value makes the whole loop evaluate to that value. for iterates over anything that implements IntoIterator (ranges, arrays, collections, iterator chains). There is no C-style for (i = 0; ...).

Labeled breaks

Loops can carry a label ('name:), and break 'name or continue 'name targets an outer loop directly. No flag variables, no goto.

if let, let-else and let chains

match (Chapter 8) handles every case. Three shorter forms cover the common "one interesting pattern" situations:

  • if let PATTERN = expr { ... } runs the block only when the pattern matches.
  • let PATTERN = expr else { diverge }; binds on success and must leave the scope otherwise (return, break, continue, panic!). It's the guard-clause idiom, typed.
  • Let chains (edition 2024) combine several let patterns and boolean tests with && in one if or while.
Modern Rust

Let chains became stable in Rust 1.88 for edition 2024. Before that you had to nest if let blocks or use match with guards.

Project step 3: decisions and loops

This step

Label each price with a match on ranges, find the cheapest and most expensive variant with a for loop, and stop a search early with break and a value.

  • price_band matches on ranges. The compiler checks that the arms cover every possible i64, which is why the first arm starts at i64::MIN and the last is _.
  • for (sku, description, cents) in variants destructures each tuple in the loop header.
  • loop is an expression: break Some(...) ends the loop and makes that value the result, so found is an Option<&str> without a mutable "result" variable.

Practice

  1. Write FizzBuzz for 1..=30 where the body is a single match on the tuple (i % 3, i % 5).
    Solution

    Arms are tried top to bottom, so (0, 0) has to come before (0, _) and (_, 0). The final _ makes the match exhaustive.

  2. Using loop with break value, find the smallest n such that n! exceeds one million, and return both n and n! as a tuple.
    Solution

Part IIOwnership
Chapter 04

Ownership & Moves

The one idea that replaces the garbage collector: every value has exactly one owner, and the value dies with it.

The three rules

  1. Every value has a single owner (a variable, a field, a collection slot).
  2. Ownership can be moved to another owner; the old one becomes unusable at compile time.
  3. When the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped: its destructor runs and its memory (stack or heap) is released, deterministically.

That's the whole memory model. There's no reference counting unless you ask for it (Arc, Chapter 16; Rc, Appendix A) and no tracing collector, so there are no pauses and no finalizer surprises.

OS view

A String is three machine words on the stack (pointer, length, capacity) that own a heap buffer. Moving a String copies those three words and statically invalidates the source, so exactly one owner will ever call free on the buffer. Double frees and use-after-free become compile errors.

Moves

Assignment, passing an argument and returning a value all move non-Copy values. Using the source afterwards is rejected:

Coming from Kotlin

In Kotlin val s2 = s1 copies a reference; both names alias one object and the GC frees it later. In Rust the binding itself is transferred. Aliasing is something you opt into explicitly with borrows (&s1, Chapter 5) or shared ownership (Rc).

Coming from C

A move is a plain memcpy of the value's stack part (for a String: pointer, length and capacity), like copying a C struct that holds a malloced pointer. In C you'd now have two copies of the pointer and the risk of a double free; Rust forbids using the source after the move, so exactly one owner frees the buffer.

Copy vs Clone

  • Clone is an explicit, possibly expensive deep copy: s.clone().
  • Copy marks types whose bitwise copy is a complete copy (integers, floats, bool, char, shared references &T, and tuples or arrays of Copy types). For these, assignment copies instead of moving and the source stays valid. A type that implements Drop or owns heap memory can never be Copy.

Ownership across function calls

Passing a value moves it into the parameter; returning moves it out to the caller. Most functions don't want ownership, so they borrow instead (next chapter); taking ownership is for functions that store, transform or consume the value.

Drop and RAII

Drop is Rust's destructor. Locals are dropped in reverse declaration order when their scope ends; struct fields and collection elements are dropped in order. drop(x) (just std::mem::drop, in the prelude) ends a value's life early. Files, sockets, locks and guards all release themselves this way, so there's no finally and no close() to forget.

Coming from Kotlin

use { } closes one Closeable at the end of one block, and finalizers give no timing guarantee at all. In Rust every value behaves as if it were wrapped in use, with its owner's scope as the block: drop runs exactly when the owner goes away.

Moving out of places you don't own

You can't move a value out of a Vec slot or out from behind a reference, because that would leave a hole. Either remove it, or swap something in with std::mem::take, std::mem::replace or Option::take.

Project step 4: owned variants

This step

Make the variants own their text, build them at run time, and see where values move: into a function, into a vector, and out again.

A variant is now (String, String, i64), so it can be created from any text, not only from literals. The functions show the three things a function can do with ownership:

  • new_variant borrows &str arguments and returns a value that owns copies of them.
  • add_variant takes ownership of the vector and of the variant, and gives the vector back. Writing variants = add_variant(variants, ...) each time is clumsy; Chapter 5 replaces it with a borrow.
  • print_all takes ownership and keeps it: the vector is dropped, and its memory freed, when the function returns.

clone() makes an independent copy, so changing volt_43 doesn't affect volt. The commented-out line shows what the compiler says about using a value after it has moved.

Practice

  1. Write fn longest(a: String, b: String) -> String that returns the longer string. Then explain why the caller can't use either argument afterwards, and rewrite it to take &str and return String.
    Solution

    Passing a and b moves both Strings into the function. One of them comes back as the result; the other is dropped when longest returns. Either way the caller's bindings no longer own anything, so using them is error E0382 (borrow of moved value), and the compiler's note even suggests borrowing instead. The rewrite borrows both inputs and allocates only the result:

    Taking &str also accepts string literals and slices, not just Strings. Returning a &str instead would avoid the copy, but that needs a lifetime annotation (Chapter 6).

  2. Give a struct Connection { id: u32 } a Drop impl that prints "closing {id}". Create three connections in nested scopes and predict the output before running it.
    Solution

    Each connection is closed at the closing brace of the scope that owns it, so they close innermost first: 3, then 2, and 1 only after main ends is printed. The bindings are named _c1 rather than _ on purpose: let _ = Connection { id: 1 }; binds nothing, so that connection would be closed immediately.

Next · Chapter 5Borrowing & Slices
Chapter 05

Borrowing & Slices

References that the compiler proves are valid, and the aliasing rule that eliminates data races and iterator invalidation.

Shared and exclusive references

A borrow lets code use a value without owning it:

  • &T is a shared reference: read-only, any number at once.
  • &mut T is an exclusive reference: read-write, and while it's alive no other reference to that value may be used.

This is the aliasing XOR mutability rule. It's checked at compile time and has no runtime cost. A borrow lasts until its last use, not to the end of the block (non-lexical lifetimes), so code that looks sequential usually just works.

Method calls auto-reference and auto-dereference (s.len() works whether s is a String, &String or &mut String), so you write * mostly when assigning through a reference.

What the rule prevents

Mutating a collection while iterating over it is a classic bug: in Kotlin on the JVM, adding to a MutableList inside a for loop over it throws ConcurrentModificationException at run time, and in C, using a pointer into an array that has since been realloced is undefined behavior. In Rust it doesn't compile:

The same rule rules out dangling references. A reference can never outlive the value it points to:

OS view

Aliasing XOR mutability is a readers-writer lock enforced by the type system at zero cost. Because &mut T is guaranteed unique, the compiler can also give LLVM noalias information that C only gets from restrict.

Slices: borrowed views

A slice is a reference to a contiguous run of elements: a fat pointer holding an address and a length.

  • &[T] views part of an array, Vec<T> or another slice.
  • &str is a slice of UTF-8 bytes. String literals are &'static str, baked into the binary.
  • String and Vec<T> are the owning counterparts.

Write function parameters as &str and &[T] rather than &String and &Vec<T>: thanks to deref coercion (&String → &str, &Vec<T> → &[T]) and unsized coercion (&[T; N] → &[T]), callers can pass a &String, a &Vec, an array or a literal (which is already a &str).

Watch out

String slicing uses byte offsets. Slicing in the middle of a multi-byte character (&"héllo"[0..2]) panics. Use char_indices() or chars() when you need character positions (Chapter 14).

Borrowing guidelines

Parameter type Use when the function...
&T / &str / &[T] only reads (the default choice)
&mut T modifies the caller's value in place
T (by value) stores it, consumes it, or returns a transformed version

Project step 5: borrowing instead of moving

This step

Pass the variants by reference: shared borrows to read, exclusive borrows to change, and slices to work on part of the list.

  • add_variant(&mut variants, ...) borrows the vector exclusively for the call, so there's no round trip of ownership.
  • print_variants and total_cents take &[Variant], a slice. A &Vec<Variant> converts to it automatically, and so does part of one: &variants[..2].
  • discount(&mut variants[2..], 10) changes only the variants from index 2 on, in place, through an exclusive slice.

Practice

  1. Write fn trim_all(words: &mut Vec<String>) that trims every string in place, and fn longest_index(words: &[String]) -> Option<usize> that returns the position of the longest word.
    Solution

    Looping over a &mut Vec<String> yields &mut String, so *word = ... replaces each element in place. word.trim() borrows from the old string, and to_string() copies it out before the assignment, so the borrow checker is satisfied. longest_index only reads, so it takes a shared slice, which also accepts arrays and parts of vectors. len() counts bytes; use chars().count() if the words can contain non-ASCII text.

  2. Implement fn middle(xs: &[i32]) -> &[i32] that returns the slice without its first and last element (empty if there are fewer than three). Call it on an array, a Vec and a sub-slice.
    Solution

    The result is a view into the caller's data: no copy, just a pointer and a length. &[] is a borrow of an empty array that lives for the whole program, so it can be returned too. &array, &vec and &array[2..] all coerce to &[i32], which is why one function covers all three.

Next · Chapter 6Lifetimes
Chapter 06

Lifetimes

Lifetime annotations don't change how long anything lives. They describe how references relate, so each function can be checked on its own.

What an annotation means

A lifetime is the region of code in which a reference must stay valid. Most are inferred. You write one when a function returns a reference and the compiler can't tell which input it borrows from:

'a is a generic parameter, like T. At each call site the compiler picks the overlap of the arguments' lifetimes, so using the result after b is dropped is rejected at the caller, without looking inside longest:

Elision rules

You rarely write lifetimes because three rules fill them in:

  1. Each reference parameter gets its own lifetime.
  2. If there's exactly one input lifetime, it's assigned to every output reference.
  3. If there's a &self or &mut self, its lifetime is assigned to every output reference.

If the rules don't determine the output, you must annotate.

Structs that hold references

A struct may store references if it declares a lifetime parameter. Lexer<'src> reads "a lexer that can't outlive the source text it points into". This is how Rust does zero-copy parsing: tokens are slices of the original input, with no allocation and no risk of dangling.

Design note

When a struct with a lifetime starts infecting every type around it, that's a signal to own the data instead (String rather than &str). Borrowing structs suit short-lived views such as parsers, iterators and guards.

'static and the T: 'static bound

&'static T is a reference valid for the entire program: string literals, constants, or deliberately leaked memory. The bound T: 'static means something weaker: T contains no non-static references. Every owned type (String, Vec<u8>, i32) satisfies it, even a value that's about to be dropped. That's why thread::spawn requires 'static: the closure must own everything it uses.

Note

Two more forms you'll meet: '_ asks the compiler to infer a lifetime in a type (Formatter<'_>, impl Iterator + '_), and for<'a> Fn(&'a str) -> &'a str (a higher-ranked bound) means "works for every lifetime", which is what a closure that accepts any borrowed string needs.

Project step 6: returning references

This step

Write lookups that return references into the list instead of copies, and see when lifetimes must be written out.

  • cheapest(variants: &[Variant]) -> Option<&Variant> has one reference parameter, so the elision rules tie the result to it. No annotation is needed.
  • find_variant has two: the list and the SKU. The compiler can't guess which one the result borrows from, so 'a says it: from variants, never from sku. That's why the caller may drop the String it searched for while still using the result.
  • colour returns a slice of its input, the text up to the first comma, without copying.

The loops in find_variant are what Chapter 13 replaces with Iterator::find; until then, an #[allow] silences Clippy's suggestion to do exactly that.

Practice

  1. Add a fn peek(&self) -> Option<Token<'src>> to the lexer that returns the next token without consuming it. (Hint: copy the lexer.)
    Solution

    Changes to the chapter's lexer: #[derive(Clone)] on Lexer, the new peek method, and a main that prints each token with the one after it. next_token is unchanged apart from rustfmt layout.

    peek only has &self, so it can't move pos. It advances a temporary copy instead, and the copy is dropped at the end of the statement. Returning a token from that temporary is fine because the token's lifetime is 'src, the input's, not the copy's. Had next_token returned Token<'_> tied to &mut self, this would fail to compile.

  2. Write fn split_pair<'a>(s: &'a str, sep: &str) -> Option<(&'a str, &'a str)> without using split_once, then remove the annotations and read the compiler's explanation (E0106). Then change sep to a char and explain why the unannotated version now compiles (elision rule 2).
    Solution

    The annotation says both halves borrow from s only, so the caller may drop sep while still using the result. Without the annotations:

    Rule 1 gives s and sep a lifetime each. There are two input lifetimes, so rule 2 doesn't apply, and there's no self for rule 3, so the outputs get none. The compiler's suggested fix ties sep to 'a as well, which compiles for the function but makes the block in main fail with E0597 (sep does not live long enough). Only you know the result never points into sep.

    With a char separator there's nothing to annotate:

    char is a value, not a reference, so s is now the only reference parameter. Rule 1 gives it one lifetime, and rule 2 (exactly one input lifetime) assigns it to every output reference: the compiler reads the signature as fn split_pair<'a>(s: &'a str, sep: char) -> Option<(&'a str, &'a str)>. Skipping the separator needs sep.len_utf8(), since a char can be up to 4 bytes in UTF-8.

Next · Chapter 7Structs & Methods
Part IIIModeling Data
Chapter 07

Structs & Methods

Data in structs, behaviour in impl blocks, encapsulation at the module boundary, and no inheritance.

Three kinds of struct

  • Named-field structs: struct Point { x: f64, y: f64 }
  • Tuple structs: struct Meters(f64);, ideal for newtypes (Appendix F)
  • Unit structs: struct Marker;, zero-sized, used as type-level tags

Methods live in impl blocks (a type may have several). The receiver decides what a method may do with the value:

Receiver Meaning Kotlin analogy
&self read-only borrow a member function that only reads
&mut self mutable borrow a member function that changes properties
self takes ownership (consumes the value) no equivalent
(none) associated function, called as Type::f() a companion object function

There are no constructors. By convention an associated function named new (or with_capacity, from_parts...) returns Self.

#[derive(...)] generates trait implementations: Debug for {:?}, Clone/Copy for duplication, PartialEq for ==. Chapter 11 covers the full set.

Coming from Kotlin

#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)] gives you roughly what a data class generates (toString, copy, equals, hashCode), and struct update syntax Point { y: 10.0, ..p } plays the role of p.copy(y = 10.0). Rust has no properties with custom getters/setters: fields are plain data, and accessors are ordinary methods.

Encapsulation lives at the module boundary

Fields and methods are private to their module by default. pub exposes them. Because a struct literal must name every field, a type with any private field can only be built through its public functions, which is how you enforce invariants.

Coming from Kotlin

Two differences from Kotlin: Rust is private by default (Kotlin is public by default), and privacy is per module, not per class. Code in the same module can see the private fields of every type in it, and pub(crate) corresponds to Kotlin's internal. There's no protected because there's no inheritance, and so no open/final either.

Composition instead of inheritance

Rust has no extends. You reuse code by embedding one struct in another and delegating, and you get polymorphism through traits (Chapter 11). This removes the fragile-base-class problem and keeps every type's layout explicit.

Project step 7: structs, versions and a catalog

This step

Replace the tuples with structs, add versions (the many-to-many part of the model), and put the products in a Catalog whose private fields only its methods can change.

The model now has the shape it keeps until the end:

  • Product has many Variants and many Versions: two one-to-many relations.
  • A Version lists the SKUs of the variants it offers. A variant can appear in several versions, and a version offers several variants: a many-to-many relation. In Chapter 25 it becomes a table of its own.
  • NewProduct, NewVariant and NewVersion are what a caller provides: everything except the ids. In Chapter 22 they're the JSON body of a request.

The catalog module makes the data types' fields public but keeps Catalog's fields private. Code outside the module can't push a product or change a counter directly. It has to call create, which hands out ids, one sequence per kind of record, as each table will have in PostgreSQL.

Product::find_variant returns a reference without a lifetime annotation, although the free function in step 6 needed one. With &self among the parameters, elision ties the result to self.

Practice

  1. Build a Rectangle { width: u32, height: u32 } with area, can_hold(&self, other: &Rectangle) and an associated square(size) constructor.
    Solution

    square has no self parameter, so it's an associated function called as Rectangle::square(20), like a function on a Kotlin companion object. can_hold only reads the other rectangle, so it borrows it, and the caller can keep using small afterwards.

  2. Make a Temperature type whose only constructor rejects values below absolute zero, so an invalid temperature can't exist anywhere in the program.
    Solution

    The field is private to the temperature module, so outside it a struct literal doesn't compile and new is the only way to get a Temperature. There's no setter, so a valid value stays valid. Any method added later that changes celsius has to live inside the module, which keeps the check in one place. Code holding a Temperature never has to re-validate it.

Next · Chapter 8Enums & Pattern Matching
Chapter 08

Enums & Pattern Matching

Sum types that carry data, Option instead of null, and a match that the compiler checks for completeness.

Enums are tagged unions

Each variant of a Rust enum can carry its own data, with named fields, a tuple, or nothing. The compiler stores a tag plus enough space for the largest variant, and match must handle every variant: add a variant later and every non-exhaustive match in the codebase becomes a compile error that points you to the code needing an update.

Coming from Kotlin

The closest Kotlin equivalent is a sealed interface with data class subtypes and an exhaustive when. Rust's enum is a single value type with no heap allocation or virtual dispatch, and its patterns destructure fields directly (Shape::Rect { w, h }), where when smart-casts the subject and you read its properties afterwards.

Option: absence as a type

There is no null. A value that may be missing has type Option<T>, which is either Some(value) or None, and you can't use the T inside without handling None. Combinators like map, and_then and unwrap_or keep this concise. The compiler also uses invalid bit patterns (a null pointer, for example) as the None tag, so Option<&T> and Option<Box<T>> are the same size as a raw pointer.

Coming from Kotlin

Kotlin's null safety (T?) is the same idea built into the type system, so this will feel familiar. Roughly: ?. and ?.let { } become map / and_then, the Elvis operator ?: becomes unwrap_or / unwrap_or_else, and !! becomes unwrap() / expect(). The difference is that Option is an ordinary enum: it nests (Option<Option<T>> is not the same as Option<T>, while T?? collapses to T?), and it comes with dozens of combinator methods instead of special operators.

The pattern language

Patterns appear in match, if let, while let, let, and function parameters. They can:

  • match literals, ranges (1..=9) and alternatives (A | B)
  • destructure structs, tuples, enums, arrays and slices ([first, .., last])
  • bind with @ while also testing (n @ 1..=99)
  • add a guard: pattern if condition, including if let guards
  • ignore parts with _ and ..
Tip

Matching on a reference (match self where self: &Shape) binds the fields as references automatically ("default binding modes"), so you rarely need the old ref keyword.

Enums as state machines

Enums with data are a natural way to model protocols. Matching on (state, event) tuples makes every transition explicit, and invalid states simply have no representation.

Project step 8: image types and optional images

This step

Model the accepted image formats as an enum, recognize them from a file's first bytes, and give products and variants an optional image.

  • ImageType::detect matches on a byte slice with slice patterns. Every PNG file starts with the same 8 bytes, every JPEG with FF D8 FF, and every WebP file with RIFF, four size bytes (any value, hence _), then WEBP. The service will trust these bytes, not the type a client claims.
  • Image pairs the bytes with their type. Image::from_bytes returns None for anything else, using ? on an Option.
  • Products and variants have image: Option<Image>: absence is a value the compiler makes you handle, as describe_image does with match.
  • Catalog::get returns Option<&Product>. set_variant_image uses let ... else to leave early when the product or the variant doesn't exist.

Practice

  1. Model a vending machine with enum State { Idle, HasMoney(u32), Dispensing(String) } and a step function for the events Insert(u32), Select(String, u32) and Cancel.
    Solution

    As in the chapter's connection example, step matches on the (state, event) pair and takes both by value, so the item name moves from the event into Dispensing without a clone. The two Select arms on HasMoney differ only by the guard; the first that matches wins. There's no catch-all arm, so adding a state or an event makes the compiler point at every transition you haven't decided yet.

  2. Write fn summarize(xs: &[i32]) -> String that uses slice patterns to return "empty", "one: x", "two: x, y" or "many: first..last".
    Solution

    The four patterns cover every length, so the match is exhaustive without a _ arm. [first, .., last] needs at least two elements, but the arms above already handle lengths 0 to 2, so it only sees three or more.

Next · Chapter 9Error Handling
Chapter 09

Error Handling

Bugs panic; expected failures are values. The ? operator makes propagation as short as an exception, but visible in every signature.

Two kinds of failure

  • Unrecoverable: a bug or a broken invariant (index out of bounds, unwrap on None). panic! unwinds the current thread, running destructors, and prints a message. It's never undefined behavior.
  • Recoverable: file not found, bad input, network down. These are returned as Result<T, E>, an enum of Ok(T) and Err(E), and the caller must deal with them.
Coming from Kotlin

Kotlin has only unchecked exceptions, so nothing in a signature tells you what can fail. Rust puts failure in the return type, and callers can't silently ignore it (Result is #[must_use]). Kotlin's Result<T> with runCatching comes closest, but it wraps any Throwable; Rust's Result<T, E> names the error type, and ? propagates it in one character.

Result and the ? operator

expr? means: if expr is Err(e), return Err(From::from(e)) from the current function right away; otherwise unwrap the Ok value. It works in any function that returns Result (or Option, for None).

unwrap() and expect("why this can't fail") turn an Err into a panic. Use them in tests, prototypes and where failure would truly be a bug; prefer ? everywhere else.

Defining your own error type

Library errors are usually an enum with one variant per failure mode. Implement Display for the message and std::error::Error to plug into the ecosystem, and override source() to expose the underlying cause so callers can walk the chain.

Automatic conversion with From

? calls From::from on the error, so implementing From<LowLevelError> for MyError lets ? convert errors as they propagate. For applications, Box<dyn Error> accepts any error type (and even a plain string), and main itself can return a Result.

? on Option

The same operator short-circuits on None in functions returning Option. Convert between the two with ok_or / ok_or_else (Option → Result) and .ok() (Result → Option).

Note

Popular crates (thiserror for deriving error enums, anyhow for application errors) automate the boilerplate above. Everything they do is built on the std traits shown here.

Project step 9: rules and errors

This step

Check the catalog's rules before storing anything, report each broken rule as its own error variant, and add update and delete.

Two error types split the work:

  • ValidationError is what's wrong with one product on its own: an empty name or brand, an empty or repeated SKU, a price that isn't positive, a version number below 1 or repeated, or a version that lists a SKU the product doesn't have.
  • CatalogError is everything the catalog can refuse. Invalid wraps a ValidationError, and source() exposes it. The others need the whole catalog to decide: a product that doesn't exist, or a name or SKU another product already uses.

From<ValidationError> for CatalogError lets create write validate(&new)?. report in main.rs prints an error followed by its chain of causes.

update replaces a product's fields, variants and versions. A variant whose SKU was there before keeps its id and its image; the others are new. std::mem::take moves the old variants out of the product, leaving an empty vector, so their images can be moved into the new variants without cloning.

Practice

  1. Write fn read_point(s: &str) -> Result<(i32, i32), PointError> parsing "3,4", with variants for a missing comma and a bad number, wrapping ParseIntError as the source.
    Solution

    ok_or turns the missing comma into an error, and From<ParseIntError> lets ? wrap a failed parse in BadNumber. The Display message describes this layer only and leaves the detail to source(), so a caller that walks the chain doesn't print the cause twice.

  2. Change run in the last-but-one example to return Result<(), AppError> and see which line stops compiling, and why. (Hint: what does .into() on a &str need now?) Then explain why changing main the same way compiles fine.
    Solution

    The example is from_conversions.rs, with run now returning Result<(), AppError>:

    Only the last line fails. price_total(...)? still compiles: its error is already an AppError, and std implements From<T> for T for every type, so ? converts it to itself. .into() on a &str needs From<&str> for the target type. Box<dyn Error> has that impl (std wraps the text in an error type of its own), but AppError converts only from ParseIntError and ParseFloatError. To make it compile, add a variant such as Other(String) with a From<&str> impl, or keep Box<dyn Error> at the application level.

    Changing main instead, with run left as it was:

    This compiles because main's only ? is on "-12".parse::<i32>(), whose ParseIntError converts into AppError through the existing From impl. The error from run() is handled by if let, not propagated with ?, so its type doesn't have to match main's. main may return Result<(), E> for any E that implements Debug, which AppError derives. On Err it prints the Debug form and exits with status 1.

Next · Chapter 10Modules & Project Structure
Chapter 10

Modules & Project Structure

Crates are compilation units, modules are namespaces with privacy, and pub use lets you shape a public API independently of your file layout.

Vocabulary

Term Meaning
Crate One compilation unit: a binary (has main) or a library. Rust compiles a crate as a whole, which is why generics and inlining work across files.
Package A Cargo.toml with one library crate and/or any number of binary crates.
Module A namespace inside a crate, declared with mod. Forms a tree rooted at main.rs or lib.rs.
Workspace Several packages sharing one Cargo.lock and build directory.

Visibility

Items are private to the module that declares them and its descendants. You widen access explicitly:

Modifier Visible to
(nothing) the current module and its children
pub(super) the parent module
pub(crate) the whole crate, but not other crates
pub everyone who can reach the enclosing module
Coming from Kotlin

Watch the vocabulary: a Rust crate is closest to a Kotlin (Gradle) module, and a Rust module to a Kotlin package, so pub(crate) is Kotlin's internal. The default is reversed: Kotlin declarations are public unless marked otherwise, Rust items are private. Kotlin also has no re-exports. pub use lets you organize files however suits the implementation while exposing a flat, stable API, the facade pattern applied at the module level.

Files on disk

mod net; tells the compiler to load the module from net.rs (or the older net/mod.rs). Submodules of net live in a net/ directory next to it. The file tree mirrors the module tree; there is no separate import path configuration.

Conditional compilation

#[cfg(...)] includes or removes items at compile time based on target OS, architecture, C library, build profile or Cargo features. cfg!(...) evaluates the same predicates to a bool in ordinary code. Ubuntu on WSL 2 is a regular Linux target (target_os = "linux", target_env = "gnu"), so there's no WSL-specific cfg; if a program needs to know, it checks the kernel release at run time.

On macOS

The first line prints debug build for macos/aarch64 with another libc, 64-bit pointers and the second running under WSL: false: macOS is target_os = "macos", its C library is libSystem, and target_env is empty. Try adding a #[cfg(target_os = "macos")] function of your own.

Coming from C

#[cfg] replaces #ifdef, but works on parsed items rather than text, so disabled code still has to be syntactically valid and can't leave unbalanced braces.

Project step 10: a library and a binary

This step

Split the single file into a library with four modules, and keep main.rs as a thin user of it.

A package can have a library (src/lib.rs) and a binary (src/main.rs). The binary uses the library like any other crate, by its package name: use shoes::Catalog;. Only pub items are visible to it. Chapter 18's integration tests and Chapter 22's web server use the library the same way.

FileContents
model.rsthe data types, ImageType, Image, format_price
validate.rsValidationError and validate
error.rsCatalogError
store.rsCatalog, the in-memory store

The code moved without changes, except that find_variant_mut becomes pub(crate): the store, in another module, needs it, but users of the library mustn't change a variant behind the catalog's back. lib.rs re-exports Catalog and CatalogError so callers can write shoes::Catalog. The output is the same as in step 9.

Practice

  1. Split the bank example from Chapter 7 into src/bank.rs and src/main.rs in a Cargo project, then add a bank::audit submodule that can read balances but is pub(crate).
    Solution

    cargo new bank, then move the mod bank { ... } body into src/bank.rs and declare it with mod bank; in main.rs. The submodule lives in src/bank/audit.rs. Because audit is a child of bank, it can read the private balance field directly; pub(crate) lets main.rs call it while keeping it out of any public API.

  2. Add a Cargo feature verbose and use #[cfg(feature = "verbose")] to compile a logging function only when it's enabled (cargo run --features verbose).
    Solution

    Declare the feature in Cargo.toml. #[cfg] works on statements too, so each call to log carries the same attribute; otherwise the default build wouldn't compile, because the function isn't there.

    -q only hides Cargo's own Compiling lines. Features add up across the dependency graph, so use them to switch extra code on, not to switch between two incompatible versions of it.

Next · Chapter 11Traits
Part IVAbstraction
Chapter 11

Traits

Interfaces that you can implement for any type, dispatched statically by default and dynamically when you ask.

Defining and implementing

A trait is a set of method signatures, optionally with default bodies. Any type can implement it, including types you didn't write. A function then accepts "anything implementing Shape" in one of two ways:

  • Static dispatch (T: Shape or impl Shape): the compiler generates a specialized copy per concrete type, so calls can be inlined. This is the default.
  • Dynamic dispatch (&dyn Shape, Box<dyn Shape>): one copy of the code; calls go through a vtable. A dyn reference is a fat pointer (data pointer + vtable pointer). Use it for heterogeneous collections and plugin-style boundaries.
Coming from Kotlin

Traits resemble Kotlin interfaces with default methods, plus the reach of extension functions: you can implement your trait for an existing type, even i32 or str. A Kotlin extension can add methods to String but can't make it implement an interface; impl MyTrait for str does exactly that. Dispatch is static unless you write dyn, and a trait can require associated types and constants, not just methods.

Standard traits worth knowing

Trait Gives you Derivable
Debug / Display {:?} / {} formatting Debug only
Clone / Copy .clone() / implicit bitwise copies yes
PartialEq / Eq ==; Eq promises reflexivity (floats are only PartialEq) yes
PartialOrd / Ord <, max, sort yes
Hash use as HashMap/HashSet key (with Eq) yes
Default Type::default() yes
From / Into, TryFrom conversions; implement From, get Into free no
AsRef / Borrow / Deref cheap reference conversions no
Add, Mul, Neg, Index... (std::ops) operator overloading no
Iterator / IntoIterator for loops and adapters (Chapter 13) no
Drop destructor no
Send / Sync thread safety markers, implemented automatically (Chapter 16) auto

Associated types, supertraits and blanket impls

  • An associated type (type Item;) is chosen once per implementation: a Stack<char> has exactly one item type. Use a generic parameter instead (trait From<T>) when a type should implement the trait many times.
  • A supertrait (trait Labeled: Debug) requires implementors to also implement another trait.
  • A blanket impl (impl<T: Display> Labeled for T) implements a trait for every type meeting a bound. The standard library uses this to give every Display type a to_string().
  • Trait upcasting (stable since 1.86) converts &dyn Sub to &dyn Super.

The orphan rule, newtypes and extension traits

You may implement a trait for a type only if the trait or the type is local to your crate. This prevents two crates from providing conflicting implementations. To implement a foreign trait for a foreign type, wrap the type in a local newtype. To add methods to a foreign type, define a local extension trait.

Dyn compatibility

Only some traits can be used as dyn Trait. A vtable needs a fixed set of concrete function pointers, so methods may not be generic and may not return Self by value (unless marked where Self: Sized, which excludes them from the vtable). The compiler tells you exactly which method is the problem:

Implement the standard traits the types need: Display to print products, FromStr to parse a media type, Default for an empty catalog, and derived Clone, Debug and PartialEq.

  • FromStr for ImageType replaces from_content_type, so "image/png".parse::<ImageType>() works. Its error type, UnsupportedImageType, implements Display and Error like any other error. Chapter 25 uses it to read the type back from the database.

  1. Define trait Plugin { fn name(&self) -> &str; fn run(&mut self, input: &str) -> String; }, implement two plugins, store them in a Vec<Box<dyn Plugin>> and run all of them on one input.

    Each plugin is a separate type; Box<dyn Plugin> erases the type so both fit in one Vec, and calls go through the vtable. iter_mut() is needed because run takes &mut self.

Next · Chapter 12Generics & Const Generics
Chapter 12

Generics & Const Generics

Type parameters checked like Kotlin generics but compiled to specialized code for each type, plus values as type parameters and zero-sized type tags.

Generic functions, structs and impls

Type parameters go in angle brackets and are constrained with trait bounds. A where clause moves long bounds out of the signature. Inside a generic function you can only do what the bounds allow, which is why errors are reported at the definition rather than at each place the function is used.

Coming from Kotlin

Kotlin on the JVM erases generics: one ArrayList class at run time, a List<Int> holds boxed Integer objects, and type arguments are gone unless you use a reified type parameter in an inline function. Rust monomorphizes every generic, a bit like inline fun <reified T> applied everywhere: Vec<u8> and Vec<String> are separate types with separate machine code, elements are stored inline with no boxing, and T is known at compile time. The price is longer compile times and larger binaries.

Const generics

Values (integers, bool, char) can be type parameters too. The array type [T; N] is the built-in example. Dimensions encoded this way are checked at compile time: multiplying a 2×3 matrix by a 2×3 matrix is a type error, not a runtime exception.

Zero-sized type tags with PhantomData

PhantomData<T> is a zero-sized field that tells the compiler a type "uses" T without storing one. It lets you tag values with compile-time information such as units of measure, IDs for different tables, or states (Appendix F's typestate pattern), at zero runtime cost.

Coming from C

Compare with a typedef double meters;, which is just an alias and happily adds feet to meters. Here the unit is part of the type, and the generated code is the same plain f64 addition.

Project step 12: one generic helper

This step

Replace two hand-written duplicate checks with one generic function.

validate looked for repeated SKUs and for repeated version numbers with two nested loops that differed only in the type being compared. find_duplicate<T: PartialEq>(items: &[T]) -> Option<&T> does both: the bound says the function needs nothing from T except ==. It's called with a Vec<&str> of SKUs and a Vec<i32> of version numbers, and the compiler generates a copy for each type. The "unknown SKU" check becomes skus.contains(...). The output doesn't change.

Practice

  1. Write a generic struct Stack<T> with push, pop, peek and len, plus an impl<T: Display> Stack<T> block with a render(&self) -> String method.
    Solution

    The first impl<T> works for any T. The second adds render only for stacks whose items implement Display, so a Stack<Vec<i32>> still compiles, it just has no render.

  2. Write fn chunk_sums<const N: usize>(xs: &[u32]) -> Vec<u32> that sums consecutive groups of N elements, using xs.chunks(N).
    Solution

    chunks yields a shorter last slice when the length isn't a multiple of N, so its sum is just smaller. chunk_sums::<0> compiles but panics (chunk size must be non-zero); a first line const { assert!(N > 0) }; moves that check to compile time.

Next · Chapter 13Closures & Iterators
Chapter 13

Closures & Iterators

Closures that capture by borrow or by move, three Fn traits that say how they're called, and lazy iterator pipelines that compile to tight loops.

Closures and the Fn traits

A closure |args| body captures variables from its environment, by shared reference, by mutable reference or by value, whichever its body needs. Each closure has its own anonymous type, and implements one or more of three traits:

Trait Can be called Typical capture
Fn many times, through a shared reference reads captured state
FnMut many times, one at a time mutates captured state
FnOnce once moves captured state out

move |...| forces every capture to be by value, which you need when the closure outlives the current scope (returned, stored, sent to a thread). Accept closures generically (impl Fn(i32) -> i32, static dispatch) or as trait objects (Box<dyn Fn...>, dynamic dispatch). Plain functions and non-capturing closures also coerce to function pointers (fn(i32) -> i32).

Coming from Kotlin

Like Kotlin lambdas, closures capture variables from their scope, but the capture mode is part of the type. A Kotlin lambda can capture and mutate any var (the compiler moves it into a heap box behind the scenes). In Rust, a closure that mutates what it captured can't be called from two places at once, and one that must outlive its scope must move what it captures. That's what makes closures safe to hand to threads.

Iterators

The Iterator trait has one required method, fn next(&mut self) -> Option<Self::Item>, and about 75 provided ones. Adapters (map, filter, zip, take...) return new iterators and do nothing until consumed; consumers (collect, sum, fold, find, count...) drive the pipeline. After inlining, a chain usually compiles to the same loop you'd write by hand, often without bounds checks.

Laziness

Because adapters are lazy, elements flow through the whole chain one at a time, and infinite sources are fine as long as something stops consuming.

Coming from Kotlin

Kotlin's collection operations (list.map { }.filter { }) are eager and allocate a new list at every step; asSequence() makes them lazy. Rust iterators always behave like Sequences, and a chain compiles to a single loop that allocates nothing until collect.

iter(), iter_mut(), into_iter()

Call Yields Collection afterwards
v.iter() or for x in &v &T still usable
v.iter_mut() or for x in &mut v &mut T still usable, possibly modified
v.into_iter() or for x in v T moved, gone

Writing your own iterators

Implement next, and every adapter comes for free. To make for x in &collection work, implement IntoIterator for a reference to your type. To return an iterator without naming its (often unnameable) type, return impl Iterator<Item = ...>.

Modern Rust

Since edition 2024, -> impl Trait automatically captures all lifetimes in scope. When you need the opposite, a precise capturing clause such as impl Iterator<Item = u32> + use<> (stable since 1.82) says exactly which generic parameters the hidden type may use.

Project step 13: filters and iterators

This step

Add ProductFilter, the filter behind the service's GET /products?name=&brand=&minPrice=&maxPrice=, and replace the remaining loops with iterator chains.

ProductFilter has four optional fields. matches combines them: each Option that is None accepts everything (is_none_or), and the price range matches when any variant's price is inside it. in_range is a closure that captures the filter, so it can read self.min_price without taking it as an argument. Catalog::list(&filter) is now one line: filter, then collect.

The lookups become iter().find(...) and position(...), and price_range uses min() and max() over a mapped iterator. In check_unique, others is a closure that returns a new iterator each time it's called, so two different checks can walk "every other product" without repeating the filter. The #[allow(clippy::manual_find)] attributes are gone.

Changes since step 121 filesrc/main.rs

Practice

  1. Implement an iterator Primes that yields prime numbers forever, then print the sum of the first 100 with take and sum.
    Solution

    The iterator keeps the primes found so far and tests each candidate against them up to its square root. next always returns Some, so the iterator is infinite and take decides where to stop; adapters are lazy, so nothing past the 100th prime is computed.

  2. Given Vec<(String, u32)> of (department, salary), build a HashMap<String, (u32, u32)> of (count, total) with one fold, then print departments sorted by average salary.
    Solution

    The fold's accumulator is the map itself: the closure takes it by value (mut acc), updates one entry and hands it back. Averages are f64, which isn't Ord, so the sort uses total_cmp.

Next · Chapter 14Collections
Chapter 14

Collections

Vec, String, the map and set families, deques and heaps, and how to pick between them.

Vec<T>

A growable array: contiguous heap buffer, amortized O(1) push, O(1) indexing. It's the default collection; reach for something else only with a reason.

String and UTF-8

A String is a Vec<u8> guaranteed to hold valid UTF-8. Because characters take 1 to 4 bytes, there's no O(1) indexing by character: s[0] doesn't compile. Iterate with chars() (Unicode scalar values), bytes(), or char_indices() for byte offsets, and slice by byte ranges that land on character boundaries.

Coming from Kotlin

A Kotlin String indexes UTF-16 code units: s[i] is O(1), but an emoji takes two units, so s[i] can return half of one and length counts it twice. Rust exposes the UTF-8 bytes honestly: len() is bytes, and anything per-character is an explicit iteration.

HashMap and BTreeMap

HashMap<K, V> needs K: Eq + Hash. Its default hasher (SipHash) resists hash-flooding attacks, and iteration order is unspecified. The entry API does insert-or-update with a single lookup. BTreeMap keeps keys sorted, iterates in order and supports range queries, at O(log n) per operation.

Sets, deques and heaps

Putting them together: Dijkstra

A priority queue of Reverse((distance, node)) plus a HashMap of best-known distances is the textbook shortest-path algorithm, in about 20 lines.

Choosing a collection

Need Use Kotlin equivalent
A list, stack or buffer Vec<T> mutableListOf()
Queue or double-ended queue VecDeque<T> ArrayDeque
Key-value lookup HashMap<K, V> hashMapOf()
Sorted keys, range queries BTreeMap<K, V> sortedMapOf()
Membership, deduplication HashSet<T> / BTreeSet<T> hashSetOf() / sortedSetOf()
Priority queue BinaryHeap<T> (a max-heap) PriorityQueue on the JVM (a min-heap)
O(1) splicing of whole lists (append, split_off) LinkedList<T> (rarely the right answer; its cursor API for mid-list insertion is still nightly-only) LinkedList on the JVM
Coming from Kotlin

Kotlin's mutableMapOf() and mutableSetOf() return insertion-ordered LinkedHashMap/LinkedHashSet, so iteration order matches insertion order. Rust's HashMap and HashSet have no defined order (it can differ between runs), which is why the examples above sort before printing. Use a BTreeMap when you need a stable order.

Project step 14: the right collections

This step

Store products in a BTreeMap keyed by id, and find duplicates with a HashSet in one pass.

  • BTreeMap<i64, Product> finds a product by id in O(log n) instead of scanning a Vec, and keeps its keys sorted, so list still returns products in id order. A HashMap would be as fast but return them in an arbitrary order. index_of is gone: get, get_mut and remove take the key. update takes the product out of the map, changes it, and puts it back.
  • find_duplicate now inserts each item into a HashSet: insert returns false for a value the set already holds. That's O(n) instead of comparing every pair. It also takes any iterator (impl IntoIterator), so validate no longer collects SKUs into a Vec first. The Copy bound lets the set keep one copy of an item while find returns another; &str and i32 are both Copy.

The output is the same as in step 13.

Practice

  1. Write an LRU cache with capacity N using a HashMap<K, V> plus a VecDeque<K> for recency, with get and put.
    Solution

    The map holds the values; the deque holds the keys from least to most recently used. Keys live in both, hence K: Clone. get takes &mut self because a read changes the recency order.

    Moving a key to the back is a linear scan of the deque, so get and put are O(n). A production LRU keeps the order in a linked list whose nodes the map points to, which gets both down to O(1).

  2. Read a paragraph of text and print each distinct word with its count, sorted by count descending, then alphabetically, using a BTreeMap for the tie-breaking.
    Solution

    Count into a BTreeMap, so the entries come out alphabetically. Then a stable sort on the count alone: ties never swap, so they stay alphabetical with no second comparison.

Next · Chapter 15Smart Pointers: Box, Cow & Lazy Values
Part VMemory & Concurrency
Chapter 15

Smart Pointers: Box, Cow & Lazy Values

Box for heap ownership and trait objects, Cow to avoid copies you don't need, LazyLock for values built on first use, and how to choose a pointer.

Box<T>: one owner, on the heap

Box<T> is a pointer to a heap allocation with a single owner; dropping the box frees it. You need it for:

  • recursive types, whose size would otherwise be infinite
  • trait objects (Box<dyn Trait>) whose concrete size isn't known
  • moving large values cheaply (only the pointer moves)

Box implements Deref, so &Box<T> coerces to &T and methods are called straight through.

Lazy initialization and Cow

  • LazyLock<T> (thread-safe) and LazyCell<T> initialize a value on first access, replacing the old lazy_static! macro. OnceLock/OnceCell are their lower-level, set-once counterparts: you decide at each call site what value to initialize them with.
  • Cow<'a, T> ("clone on write") holds either a borrowed or an owned value. Functions that usually return their input unchanged can avoid allocating.

Which pointer?

Type Owners Mutation Threads Cost
Box<T> one through &mut if T allows one allocation
Arc<T> many none (add Mutex/RwLock/atomics) yes atomic refcount
Cow<'a, T> borrowed or owned clones on first write if T allows an enum tag

Arc is covered in the next chapter, together with the locks that make shared data mutable.

Note

Rc, Weak, Cell and RefCell, the single-threaded tools for shared ownership and interior mutability, are in Appendix A. A web service shares state between requests that may run on different threads, so it uses Arc with a Mutex or RwLock instead (Chapter 16).

Project step 15: errors of any type from main

This step

Let main return Result<(), Box<dyn Error>>, so ? works on every kind of error in it.

main deals with several error types: CatalogError, UnsupportedImageType, and a missing image, which is only an Option. Box<dyn Error> holds any of them: ? converts each one into the box, and ok_or("not an image")? turns a None into an error carrying that message. If an error reaches the end of main, the program prints it and exits with status 1. Expected failures in the demo are still reported with report and don't stop it.
