Practice

  1. Write fn escape_html(s: &str) -> Cow<'_, str> that replaces <, > and & with entities, and returns Cow::Borrowed when there is nothing to escape. Check both cases with matches!.
    Solution

    Building the output in one pass avoids the classic bug of chained replace calls, where escaping & last turns &lt; into &amp;lt;. Callers that only print the result never pay for an allocation when the input is clean.

  2. Define static MIME: LazyLock<HashMap<&str, &str>> mapping file extensions to MIME types, and fn mime(path: &str) -> &'static str that falls back to application/octet-stream. Print something inside the initializer to confirm that it runs once.
    Solution

    The message appears once, after before the first lookup: the closure runs on the first access to MIME, not at startup, and later lookups reuse the table. In a static, &str means &'static str, which is why mime can return the stored value; .copied() turns the map's Option<&&str> into Option<&str>.

  3. Model pricing rules as a Vec<Box<dyn Fn(u64) -> u64>> (a discount, a minimum price, rounding to 5 cents) and apply them in order to a list of prices.
    Solution

    Each closure has its own anonymous type, so they need a box to share one Vec. The move closures own copies of their settings; fold passes each price through the rules in order.

Next · Chapter 16Concurrency
Chapter 16

Concurrency

OS threads, the two marker traits that make data races a compile error, and shared state with Arc, locks that own their data, and atomics: the rules every async service runs on too.

Threads

std::thread::spawn starts an OS thread (1:1, no green threads) and returns a JoinHandle<T> whose join() yields the closure's return value, or the panic payload if the thread panicked. The closure must be 'static, so it usually moves in everything it uses.

OS view

On Linux each std::thread is a pthread, a kernel task created with clone(2), scheduled by the kernel like any other. While a threaded program runs, ps -T -p <pid> or ls /proc/<pid>/task lists its threads, and Builder::new().name("worker-1".into()) sets the name shown by top -H. The default stack for spawned threads is 2 MiB (Builder::stack_size or RUST_MIN_STACK change it).

On macOS

Threads are pthreads on top of Mach threads. There's no /proc, so list a process's threads with ps -M -p <pid> or Activity Monitor; thread names appear in lldb and Instruments. The 2 MiB default stack applies here too.

Forgetting move is caught at compile time, because the thread might outlive the data it borrows:

Send and Sync

Two auto-implemented marker traits carry thread safety in the type system:

  • T: Send: ownership of a T may move to another thread.
  • T: Sync: &T may be shared between threads (that is, &T: Send).

Rc<T>, the single-threaded reference-counted pointer from Appendix A, is neither (its counter isn't atomic), and RefCell<T> isn't Sync. thread::spawn requires Send, so passing an Rc to a thread is a compile error. A data race needs shared mutable access without synchronization; the borrow rules plus Send/Sync make that unrepresentable in safe code.

Watch out

Rust prevents data races, not every concurrency bug. Deadlocks, livelocks and logical race conditions (check-then-act across two lock acquisitions) are still possible. Keep critical sections short and acquire multiple locks in a consistent order.

Shared state: Arc, Mutex, RwLock and atomics

Arc<T> is an atomically reference-counted Rc. Mutex<T> owns the data it protects: the only way to reach the data is lock(), which returns a guard that dereferences to &mut T and unlocks when dropped. You can't forget to lock, and you can't keep a reference after unlocking. RwLock<T> allows many readers or one writer. Atomics (AtomicUsize, AtomicBool...) give lock-free counters and flags with explicit memory ordering.

Coming from Kotlin

synchronized(lock) { } and @Synchronized protect code; Mutex<T> protects data. In Kotlin nothing stops another function from touching the shared property without taking the lock, and kotlinx.coroutines' Mutex.withLock has the same gap. Here the data lives inside the mutex, so unlocked access doesn't compile. A thread that panics while holding a lock poisons it, so the next lock() returns Err and you decide whether the data is still trustworthy.

In a service

In an async service you rarely call thread::spawn yourself, but everything in this chapter still applies. tokio::spawn (Chapter 21) has the same Send + 'static requirement, shared application state is an Arc, and short critical sections use a std::sync::Mutex or RwLock exactly as here (Chapters 21–22). Scoped threads, std channels and condition variables are in Appendix B.

Project step 16: one catalog, many threads

This step

Share the catalog between threads as Arc<Mutex<Catalog>>, the type the web server will use, and see that the lock makes "check, then insert" safe.

SharedCatalog is a type alias for Arc<Mutex<Catalog>>. Arc gives every thread an owning handle to the same catalog; Mutex lets one thread at a time use it. The demo starts four threads that all try to create "City Walker". Each thread locks the catalog, then create checks that the name is free and inserts the product while the lock is held. Exactly one thread wins, and the other three get DuplicateName, whatever order they run in. Without the lock, two threads could both see the name as free.

lock() returns an error only if another thread panicked while holding the lock (the mutex is "poisoned"); expect turns that into a panic here. The guard unlocks when it's dropped, at the end of the closure.

Changes since step 151 filesrc/store.rs
Changes since step 151 filesrc/main.rs

Practice

  1. Count word frequencies of a large text in parallel: split it into N owned chunks, thread::spawn one thread per chunk that returns its own HashMap through join(), and merge the maps at the end (no Mutex needed). Appendix B shows how thread::scope avoids copying the chunks.
    Solution

    Each thread owns its String chunk (moved into the closure) and returns its own map, so nothing is shared while the threads run and no lock is needed. The only combining happens on the main thread after join.

    The join("\n") copies the whole text once. With thread::scope (Appendix B) the threads could borrow &[&str] slices of lines directly, because the scope guarantees they finish before text is dropped.

  2. Implement a "dining philosophers" simulation with five Mutex<()> forks. Make it deadlock, then fix it by ordering lock acquisition.
    Solution

    Philosopher i needs forks i and (i + 1) % 5. If each takes the left fork first, and the sleep makes sure all of them have one before reaching for the second, every philosopher waits for a neighbour in a cycle and none can continue.

    The fix is a global lock order: always take the lower-numbered fork first. Only the line choosing first and second changes. Philosopher 4 now competes with philosopher 0 for fork 0 instead of holding fork 4, so philosopher 3 gets both its forks, and the chain unwinds from there. The order of the lines varies from run to run.

    The compiler doesn't catch this: Rust prevents data races, not deadlocks. Lock ordering is the same rule you'd follow with pthread_mutex_t in C.

Next · Chapter 17Macros
Part VIMacros, Testing & I/O
Chapter 17

Macros

Hygienic code generation on token trees: declarative macros for variadic APIs and small DSLs, procedural macros for derives.

Declarative macros (macro_rules!)

A macro_rules! macro is a list of (pattern) => { expansion } rules matched against the token tree at the call site, at compile time. Patterns bind fragments with a type: $x:expr, $name:ident, $t:ty, $p:pat, $l:literal, $b:block, $tt:tt (any single token tree) and more. Repetition uses $( ... ),* (zero or more, comma-separated), + (one or more) or ? (optional).

Use a macro when a function can't do the job: variable numbers of arguments (println!, vec!), generating items (structs, impls), or syntax that isn't valid Rust expressions. Prefer functions and generics everywhere else, since they're easier to read and give better errors.

Hygiene, counting and tiny DSLs

Macros are hygienic: a variable introduced inside the expansion can't capture or clash with the caller's variables, and arguments are substituted as whole expressions, not text. The classic C preprocessor pitfalls (#define SQ(x) x*x) don't exist. Macros can also recurse over token trees to compute things at compile time, or accept syntax of your own design.

Procedural macros

Procedural macros are Rust functions that run inside the compiler, take a TokenStream and return one. There are three kinds: #[derive(MyTrait)], attribute macros (#[route(GET, "/")]) and function-like macros (sql!(...)). They must live in their own crate with proc-macro = true and use the proc_macro crate that ships with the compiler. Real-world proc macros almost always use the third-party syn and quote crates for parsing and code generation, so here is just the shape, using proc_macro alone:

Coming from Kotlin

Procedural macros fill the niche of KSP annotation processors and Kotlin compiler plugins (the way @Serializable drives kotlinx.serialization's code generation). They run inside the Rust compiler on the token stream and generate ordinary Rust code that you can inspect with the cargo expand tool.

Practice

  1. Write macro_rules! assert_approx { ($a:expr, $b:expr, $eps:expr) => ... } that panics with both values and their difference when they differ by more than eps.
    Solution

    Binding the arguments to locals first means an argument like next_sample() runs once, not three times. stringify! puts the source text of each expression into the message, as assert_eq! does. The panic location points at the call site, not the macro, because the expanded code is attributed to the invocation.

  2. Write an enum_str! macro that takes Color { Red, Green, Blue } and generates the enum plus fn as_str(&self) -> &'static str and fn all() -> [Self; N], using count! for N.
    Solution

    count! is the one from this chapter. It expands to 1usize + 1usize + 1usize + 0usize, a constant expression, so it can be an array length.

    The variant list is repeated three times in the expansion (enum body, match arms, array), which is exactly the boilerplate the macro saves. Adding a variant now updates all three.

Next · Chapter 18Testing & Documentation
Chapter 18

Testing & Documentation

Tests live next to the code, doc examples are compiled and run, and cargo test runs all of it.

Unit tests

Mark a function #[test] and cargo test builds a test binary that runs it on a thread pool and reports results. By convention unit tests sit in a #[cfg(test)] mod tests at the bottom of each file: the module is compiled only for tests, and as a child module it can call private functions.

Tool Purpose
assert!(cond, "msg {}", x) condition with a formatted message
assert_eq!(a, b) / assert_ne! shows both values on failure (needs Debug)
#[should_panic(expected = "...")] the test passes only if it panics with a message containing that text
fn t() -> Result<(), E> lets you use ? in a test
#[ignore = "reason"] skipped unless cargo test -- --ignored

Running tests

To run the single-file example above without Cargo: rustc --edition 2024 --test rpn.rs -o /tmp/rpn && /tmp/rpn.

Integration tests and doc tests

  • Files in tests/ are compiled as separate crates that use your library only through its public API, which is how your users see it.
  • Code blocks in /// comments are doc tests: cargo test compiles and runs them, so examples in documentation can't silently rot. Start a line with # to hide setup code from the rendered docs.
  • cargo doc --open renders the docs. Conventional sections are # Examples, # Errors, # Panics and # Safety.

Micro-benchmarks with std

The built-in #[bench] harness is still nightly-only. For quick measurements with stable std, time a loop with Instant and wrap inputs in std::hint::black_box so the optimizer can't constant-fold the work away. (For serious benchmarking, the criterion crate adds statistics.)

Debugging on Linux

  • Backtraces: RUST_BACKTRACE=1 cargo run prints a stack trace on panic (=full for every frame).
  • gdb: rust-gdb target/debug/app is gdb with Rust pretty-printers (it ships with rustup; gdb itself comes from sudo apt install gdb). break main.rs:42, run, bt, print my_vec all show Rust types readably. rust-lldb works too.
  • VS Code: inside WSL, the CodeLLDB extension debugs Cargo binaries and tests with breakpoints.
  • System view: strace -f for syscalls, ltrace for libc calls, valgrind for leak checks on FFI code. For profiling, perf record / perf report work on release builds with debug = true under [profile.release]; under WSL the apt linux-tools package doesn't match Microsoft's kernel, so perf has to be built from the WSL2 kernel sources.
  • Miri for undefined behavior in unsafe code (Appendix D):
On macOS

Use rust-lldb (gdb doesn't run on Apple silicon) and the CodeLLDB extension in VS Code. strace and ltrace don't exist, and dtruss is blocked by System Integrity Protection. For profiling, use Instruments (part of Xcode) or cargo install samply. Valgrind isn't available on Apple silicon, so check FFI code with AddressSanitizer instead: RUSTFLAGS=-Zsanitizer=address cargo +nightly run --target aarch64-apple-darwin. Miri works the same as on Linux.

Tip

#[expect(lint_name)] (stable since 1.81) silences a lint like #[allow], but warns if the lint stops firing, so stale suppressions don't pile up.

Move the checks out of the demo and into tests: unit tests for each module, a doc test, and integration tests that use the library from outside. main shrinks to printing the sample catalog.

Chapter 17's macros don't need a project step: the project uses macros (println!, vec!, derives) but doesn't define any.

  • Unit tests live next to the code in a #[cfg(test)] mod tests, so they can test private functions too. validate.rs checks every rule with a table of cases: each entry is a function that breaks one rule and the error it must produce. store.rs checks ids, uniqueness, that an update keeps the id and image of a kept SKU, and that a missing product is "not found" even when the new name is taken by someone else.
  • A doc test in format_price's documentation is compiled and run by cargo test, so the example can't go out of date.
  • Integration tests in tests/catalog.rs see only the public API. They start eight threads on one SharedCatalog and check that the ids are distinct and that exactly one thread wins a contested name.

The demo in main.rs was mostly checking these rules by eye, so it shrinks to building the sample catalog and printing it.

Practice

  1. Add tests for "2 +" (underflow), "1 2" (malformed) and "4 2 x" (unknown token), checking the exact error messages. Why does "4 x" report a stack underflow instead?
    Solution

    Four new tests in the tests module of the chapter's src/lib.rs (a cargo new --lib rpn project). unwrap_err() lets each test compare the message as a plain string.

    Why "4 x" underflows: eval treats every token that isn't a number as an operator and pops both operands before it matches on the token. With only 4 on the stack, the second pop fails and ? returns "stack underflow", so the other => arm is never reached. To report the unknown token instead, check that the token is one of + - * / before popping.

  2. Turn rpn into a library crate (cargo new --lib rpn), move one test to tests/, and confirm that the doc test in the # Examples section runs with cargo test --doc.
    Solution

    cargo new --lib rpn and put the chapter's code in src/lib.rs. The library is named after the package, which is why the doc test and the integration test can say rpn::eval. adds_and_multiplies moves out because it only uses the public API; private_helper_underflows has to stay, since a file in tests/ is a separate crate and can't see the private pop.

    cargo test runs three test binaries: the unit tests, one per file in tests/, and the doc tests. cargo test --doc runs only the last group; the (line 7) is the line where the code block in the # Examples section starts.

Next · Chapter 19Files, Processes & Networking
Chapter 19

Files, Processes & Networking

The std::io traits that unify files, sockets and buffers, plus fs, path, env, process, time and net.

Read, Write and BufRead

std::io is built on a few traits: Read (pull bytes), Write (push bytes), BufRead (adds line-oriented reading on a buffer) and Seek. Files, sockets, stdin/stdout, Vec<u8> and &[u8] all implement them, so a function written against impl BufRead works with every source, and tests can feed it an in-memory string.

  • BufReader/BufWriter wrap any reader or writer to batch system calls. Unbuffered File writes issue one syscall per call.
  • I/O functions return io::Result<T>; ? keeps the happy path clean.
  • Paths are Path (borrowed) and PathBuf (owned), wrapping OS strings that need not be valid UTF-8.

Environment, processes and time

  • env::args() yields command-line arguments (index 0 is the program); env::var reads environment variables.
  • process::Command builds child processes: output() waits and captures everything, spawn() returns a Child with optional piped stdin/stdout.
  • Instant is a monotonic clock for measuring durations; SystemTime is the wall clock.

The example below runs echo and tr, which on Ubuntu 26.04 are themselves Rust programs from uutils. (On macOS they're the BSD versions; the output is the same.)

TCP

TcpListener::bind plus incoming() gives you a blocking accept loop; TcpStream implements Read and Write. try_clone produces a second handle to the same socket, which is the easy way to read and write from different places. Binding to port 0 lets the OS choose a free port. One thread per connection is simple and fine for moderate loads. Appendix E adds a thread pool, and Chapter 21 replaces both with Tokio tasks.

OS view

These are thin wrappers over Linux system calls: File owns a file descriptor and calls close(2) in Drop, TcpListener::bind is socket + bind + listen, and Command::spawn uses posix_spawn or fork + exec. Watch it happen with strace -f ./target/debug/app (sudo apt install strace).

Tip

WSL networking. A server listening on 127.0.0.1:PORT inside Ubuntu is normally reachable from Windows at localhost:PORT too (WSL 2 forwards localhost), so you can test Rust servers from a Windows browser. Inside Ubuntu, nc localhost PORT (sudo apt install netcat-openbsd) is the quickest client for line-based protocols. On macOS, nc is built in and localhost is simply your Mac.

Linux-specific APIs: std::os::unix

Portable code sticks to std::fs, std::net and std::process. When you need Unix features, the std::os::unix modules add them as extension traits on the same types: PermissionsExt for mode bits, MetadataExt for inode, link count and owner, fs::symlink, UnixStream/UnixListener for Unix domain sockets, and ExitStatusExt to see which signal killed a child. /proc needs no API at all: it's just files.

On macOS

All of these std::os::unix extensions work on macOS too, because it's a Unix. The exception is /proc, which macOS doesn't have: the last line prints threads in this process: None. Use ps -M -p <pid> to see a process's threads instead.

Project step 19: configuration and files

This step

Read settings from environment variables with defaults, and load images from files on disk.

Config::from_env reads ADDR, the address the web service will listen on, defaulting to 127.0.0.1:3000. Chapters 20 and 23 add more variables, and Chapter 25 replaces this with settings files per environment, like Spring Boot's profiles. A set but unusable value is an error that names the variable. Tests don't change the real environment (env::set_var is unsafe in edition 2024, because another thread might be reading it at the same time): from_vars takes a function to look variables up, and the tests pass one backed by a HashMap.

load_image reads a file with fs::read into a Vec<u8>. An io::Error says "No such file or directory" but not which file, so the error message adds the path. Put two small PNG files and a text file in an assets/ directory next to Cargo.toml. Any images will do; the course's are 48×24-pixel drawings of a shoe, trail-runner.png (118 bytes) and volt.png (122 bytes).

Changes since step 181 filesrc/main.rs

Practice

  1. Write a grep-like tool: mygrep PATTERN FILE... that prints file:line:text for matches, reads stdin when no files are given, and exits with code 1 when nothing matched (std::process::exit).
    Solution

    One search function takes any impl BufRead, so files (through BufReader) and locked stdin share the same code. Matching is a plain substring test with str::contains. Like grep, a file that can't be opened is reported on stderr and the others are still searched.

    process::exit ends the process without running destructors of values still alive. Here that's harmless: nothing is left that needs dropping, and exit still flushes stdout.

  2. Extend the echo server so each connection gets a numbered greeting, using an AtomicUsize shared by all handler threads. Then bind it to a fixed port such as 127.0.0.1:7878 and talk to it with nc localhost 7878 from a second WSL terminal.
    Solution

    The counter is an Arc<AtomicUsize>. Each handler thread gets its own clone of the Arc and calls fetch_add, which returns the old value. Two connections arriving at the same moment therefore can't get the same number, and no Mutex is needed. Relaxed is enough because the counter doesn't guard any other data. The server now binds the fixed address 127.0.0.1:7878 and runs until you press Ctrl+C.

    An interactive nc localhost 7878 works the same way: type lines and press Ctrl+D to close the connection. The session above pipes the input in. -N makes OpenBSD nc shut down its sending side at end of input, so the server's lines() loop ends and the connection closes.

  3. Rewrite the echo server over a Unix domain socket (UnixListener::bind("/tmp/echo.sock")) and connect with nc -U /tmp/echo.sock.
    Solution

    Only the types change: UnixListener and UnixStream from std::os::unix::net have the same incoming(), try_clone(), Read and Write as their TCP counterparts. The new part is the socket file. bind creates it, and it stays behind after the process is killed, so the next bind would fail with "Address already in use". The server therefore deletes any old file first.

Part VIIBuilding the Service
Chapter 20

JSON with serde

The first chapter that leaves std: serde's derive-based serialization, serde_json's typed and untyped APIs, and the attributes that map Rust types onto real-world JSON.

Note

Beyond the standard library. Chapters 1–19 use std only. JSON is the first exception (Chapters 21–26 add more crates): the standard library has no serialization framework, and the ecosystem standard is the serde crate plus serde_json. Both are available in the Rust Playground, so Run in Playground works for every example here. Every example was built and run with serde 1.0.229 and serde_json 1.0.154 on Rust 1.100.0, and the output shown is the captured output.

Setup

From a Cargo project in your Ubuntu shell, add the two crates. cargo add edits Cargo.toml for you and picks the latest compatible versions.

How serde works

serde separates what is serialized from how:

  • serde defines a small data model (booleans, integers, floats, strings, sequences, maps, structs, enum variants...) and two pairs of traits: Serialize/Serializer and Deserialize/Deserializer.
  • Your types implement Serialize and Deserialize, almost always with #[derive].
  • Format crates implement Serializer and Deserializer: serde_json here, and the same derives work unchanged with toml, csv, MessagePack (rmp-serde), or compact binary formats such as postcard.
  • The derive macros generate the code at compile time. There is no reflection and no runtime type information; deserializing a struct compiles to a direct parser for that exact shape, and a mismatch is an ordinary Result error.
Coming from Kotlin

This is the same architecture as kotlinx.serialization: @Serializable ↔ #[derive(Serialize, Deserialize)], the Json format object ↔ serde_json's functions, a compiler plugin ↔ a procedural macro, and a format-agnostic core in both (kotlinx also has CBOR and ProtoBuf formats).

A typed round trip

to_string and to_string_pretty serialize; from_str deserializes, and the target type drives the parsing: the annotation let back: User is what tells serde_json which shape to expect.

How Rust types map to JSON by default:

Rust JSON
bool true / false
integers, floats number (non-finite floats such as NaN become null)
String, &str, char string
Option<T> null or the value
Vec<T>, arrays, tuples, HashSet<T> array
HashMap<K, V>, BTreeMap<K, V> object (integer keys are written as strings)
struct with named fields object, fields in declaration order
unit () and unit structs null
enum depends on the representation (see below)

Errors are values with a category

Deserialization never panics on bad input. You get a serde_json::Error that says what went wrong and where (the full message ends with at line 1 column N), and classify() tells syntax errors (malformed JSON) apart from data errors (valid JSON of the wrong shape) and truncated input. By default unknown keys are ignored; #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] turns them into errors, which is useful for config files where a typo should not pass silently.

Note the fourth case: 70000 is valid JSON and a valid number, but it doesn't fit in a u16, so the type system rejects it at the boundary. serde_json::Error implements std::error::Error, so ? converts it into Box<dyn Error> like any other error (Chapter 9).

Shaping the JSON with attributes

Real APIs rarely use Rust's naming conventions. Attributes adjust the mapping without changing your Rust code:

Attribute Effect
#[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")] on the type first_name ↔ "firstName" (also snake_case, kebab-case, SCREAMING_SNAKE_CASE, ...)
#[serde(rename = "e-mail")] one field's JSON name, even one that isn't a valid identifier
#[serde(default)] missing in the input → Default::default()
#[serde(default = "path")] missing → the value returned by a function
#[serde(skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none")] omit the key instead of writing null
#[serde(skip)] never read or written (the field needs a Default)
#[serde(alias = "name")] also accept an alternative key when deserializing
#[serde(flatten)] inline a nested struct's fields into the parent object
Coming from Kotlin

The rough mapping from kotlinx.serialization: @SerialName ↔ rename, @Transient ↔ skip, Kotlin default parameter values ↔ #[serde(default)]. One default is reversed: kotlinx's Json fails on unknown keys unless you set ignoreUnknownKeys = true, while serde ignores them unless you add deny_unknown_fields.

Enums: four representations

Enums are where JSON conventions vary most, so serde offers four layouts, chosen per enum:

Attribute Circle { r: 1.5 } is written as
(none): externally tagged {"Circle":{"r":1.5}}
#[serde(tag = "type")]: internally tagged {"type":"Circle","r":1.5}
#[serde(tag = "t", content = "c")]: adjacently tagged {"t":"Circle","c":{"r":1.5}}
#[serde(untagged)] {"r":1.5} (serde tries each variant in order when reading)
Coming from Kotlin

kotlinx.serialization writes sealed hierarchies with a "type" class discriminator by default, which is serde's internally tagged layout (#[serde(tag = "type")]). serde's own default is externally tagged, so add the attribute when talking to a Kotlin backend.

Watch out

Internally tagged enums support unit variants, struct variants and newtype variants that wrap a struct or map. Tuple variants are rejected at compile time (the derive reports that tag can't be used with them), and newtype variants wrapping a primitive such as Text(String) have no object to put the tag in and fail at run time when serialized, which is why Message above uses adjacent tagging. untagged gives vague errors because serde can only report that no variant matched, so prefer a tag whenever you control the format.

Untyped JSON: Value and json!

When the shape is unknown or changes often, parse into serde_json::Value, an enum of Null, Bool, Number, String, Array and Object. Reading with [] never panics (a missing key yields Null); assigning through [] inserts a missing key into an object, but panics if the value isn't an object (or, for numeric indices, an array of sufficient length). The as_* accessors return Option, and the json! macro builds values with JSON syntax.

Two details to notice. Printing a Value with {} writes JSON, so a string keeps its quotes; use as_str() for the bare text. And Value objects keep their keys sorted by default (they're backed by a BTreeMap); enable serde_json's preserve_order feature if insertion order matters.

Files and streams

to_writer/from_reader work with any io::Write/io::Read, so files, sockets and buffers all plug in (Chapter 19). For logs and append-only data, JSON Lines (one JSON value per line) is often the better format: you can append without rewriting the file, and read it line by line.

Tip

For large files, reading the whole file into a String (or Vec<u8>) and calling from_str (or from_slice) is usually faster than from_reader, which processes the input byte by byte.

Validated and custom types at the boundary

Appendix F's "parse, don't validate" applies directly. #[serde(try_from = "String")] deserializes a plain string first and then runs your TryFrom impl, so an invalid email is rejected during parsing and an Email value is always valid. #[serde(with = "module")] swaps in your own functions for one field, here to store a Duration as milliseconds instead of serde's default {"secs":…,"nanos":…} object.

Zero-copy deserialization

Lifetimes (Chapter 6) pay off here: a struct can borrow its strings straight from the input buffer instead of allocating a String per field. &str fields borrow automatically. A JSON string containing escape sequences (\", \n) can't be borrowed as-is, because its decoded text doesn't exist in the input, so use Cow<'a, str> with #[serde(borrow)]: it borrows when it can and allocates only when it must.

Choosing an approach

Situation Use
Known shape (API payloads, config) #[derive] on structs and enums
Unknown or highly dynamic shape serde_json::Value
A mostly known shape with an open-ended part a struct with a Value field, or #[serde(flatten)] extra: HashMap<String, Value>
Large inputs, high throughput from_slice on a buffer, borrowed &str/Cow fields
Append-only records, logs JSON Lines with to_writer + from_str per line
Invariants on values newtypes with #[serde(try_from = "...")]
Another format the same derives with toml, csv, rmp-serde, postcard...

Project step 20: JSON, dates and a seed file

This step

Give the model its JSON form with serde, store release dates as real dates with chrono, and load the catalog from a JSON file named by SEED_FILE.

The project gets its first dependencies:

  • Output types derive Serialize. #[serde(rename_all = "camelCase")] turns price_cents into priceCents, the usual style in JSON APIs.
  • Image serializes by hand. The JSON describes the image, {"contentType": "image/png", "size": 118}, without the bytes. A derive can't express that, so impl Serialize for Image writes the two fields with serialize_struct.
  • Input types derive Deserialize. #[serde(default)] fields may be left out. deny_unknown_fields makes a misspelled field such as brnad an error instead of being silently ignored.
  • Dates. released_on becomes a chrono::NaiveDate, a date without a time zone. It's "2026-03-01" in JSON, and an impossible date such as 2026-02-30 is rejected while parsing. chrono's default features include time-zone support the project doesn't need, hence --no-default-features.

The sample products move out of main.rs into seed.json, which main reads when SEED_FILE is set. The tests that built versions now parse their dates: "2026-01-01".parse().unwrap().

Changes since step 192 filessrc/model.rs, src/config.rs
Changes since step 192 filessrc/store.rs, src/validate.rs

serde's error messages give the line and column, and for unknown fields the list of expected ones.

Practice

  1. Add a JSON protocol to the Appendix E key-value server: requests like {"op":"set","key":"lang","value":"rust"} as an internally tagged enum Request, and responses as an internally tagged enum Response ({"status":"ok","value":"rust"} / {"status":"error","message":"..."}), one JSON object per line.
    Solution

    Add the crates with cargo add serde --features derive and cargo add serde_json. The hand-written Command parser, ParseError and FromStr are gone: #[derive(Deserialize)] on Request with #[serde(tag = "op")] does the parsing. Missing fields, unknown ops and broken JSON all become a serde_json::Error, and the server sends its message back as a Response::Error. Store::execute now returns a Response instead of a string, and serve_client writes each response with serde_json::to_string plus a newline. The thread pool, Server and Client are unchanged from Appendix E. The demo in main is shorter: the 8 concurrent INCR clients are left out.

    The two optional fields of Response::Ok use skip_serializing_if, so a set answers just {"status":"ok"}. keys becomes a real JSON array instead of the comma-joined string of the text protocol. Notice that missing field `value` has no line and column but the unknown op does. For an internally tagged enum, serde reads the whole object into a buffer while it looks for the tag, and then reads the variant's fields from that buffer, which has no positions.

  2. Write fn load_config(path: &Path) -> Result<Config, Box<dyn Error>> for a struct that rejects unknown fields and fills missing ones from impl Default for Config via #[serde(default)] on the struct.
    Solution

    Needs serde (with the derive feature) and serde_json. #[serde(default)] on the struct builds the value from Config::default() and overwrites only the fields present in the file. deny_unknown_fields turns a typo like prot into an error, so it isn't silently ignored. Both io::Error and serde_json::Error convert into Box<dyn Error> through ?.

    The I/O error has no file name in it. A real program would add it, for example with .map_err(|e| format!("{}: {e}", path.display()))?.

  3. Parse a JSON Lines access log of a few million lines twice, once into owned String fields and once into borrowed &str fields, and compare the run time with --release.
    Solution

    The program builds a 3-million-line log in memory, so the timing measures only parsing and not the disk. A real program would get the same &str from fs::read_to_string. One generic parse_all parses every line into an entry type T chosen by the caller. T: Deserialize<'a> with log: &'a str is what allows the borrowed types to point into log. A third variant uses Cow<'a, str>.

    Borrowing saves about 20%: 600 ms against 470 ms, steady over several runs. Each owned line allocates and frees four small Strings, and the borrowed version skips that. The scanning, UTF-8 checks and number parsing are the same in both and take most of the time, so the gain stays modest.

    Borrowed &str has a catch: it fails on any string that contains an escape such as \" or \n. The unescaped text doesn't exist in the input, so there is nothing to point at. Cow<'a, str> with #[serde(borrow)] borrows when it can and allocates only for escaped strings, at a cost of about 30 ms here. Use it for real logs, where you don't control the content.

Next · Chapter 21Async in Practice with Tokio
Chapter 21

Async in Practice with Tokio

The runtime under axum, SQLx and most networked Rust: tasks, timers, select!, channels, async I/O, and the rules that keep a runtime healthy.

Note

About the code in this chapter. It uses the tokio crate (1.54, with the full feature set). Every example was built and run with Cargo on Rust 1.100.0, the output shown is the captured output, and the examples pass cargo clippy -- -W clippy::pedantic and cargo fmt --check. Tokio is available in the Rust Playground, so Run in Playground works here too.

The async model in brief

  • An async fn doesn't run when called. It returns a future: a value implementing Future<Output = T>, which is a state machine the compiler generates to keep the function's local variables across .await points.
  • Nothing happens until an executor polls the future. poll returns Poll::Ready(value) or Poll::Pending.
  • A future that returns Pending keeps a waker. When the socket or timer it waits for is ready, the waker tells the executor to poll it again.
  • .await means "poll this inner future; while it's pending, pause here and let the executor run something else".

The standard library defines this protocol (Future, Poll, Waker) and the async/await syntax, but ships no executor, no async I/O and no timers. Appendix C builds a small executor by hand to show every moving part; you don't need it to use Tokio.

Coming from Kotlin

Rust's model is closest to Kotlin coroutines: async fn ≈ suspend fun, both compile to state machines, and both need a library to actually run them (kotlinx.coroutines there, a runtime crate such as Tokio here). One difference: kotlinx.coroutines' async { } builder starts running right away by default, while a Rust future does nothing until it is awaited or polled.

What Tokio provides

Tokio is the production runtime, and the de facto standard one: axum, hyper, reqwest, tonic and SQLx are all built on it. It provides:

  • a scheduler that runs many tasks on a small pool of worker threads, one per CPU core by default, and moves work between them (work stealing);
  • a reactor that waits for I/O readiness with the operating system's event queue (epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS) and keeps one timer wheel for all timers;
  • async versions of std APIs: tokio::net, tokio::fs, tokio::process, tokio::time, tokio::sync and tokio::io;
  • the everyday tools: spawn, join!, select!, timeouts and channels.
std only (built by hand in Appendix C)Tokio
block_on#[tokio::main], Runtime::block_on
one helper thread per Sleeptokio::time::{sleep, interval, timeout} on one timer wheel
join2tokio::join!, tokio::select!
(nothing)tokio::spawn: independent tasks spread over the worker threads
std::net (blocking)tokio::net (non-blocking, driven by the reactor)
std::sync::{mpsc, Mutex}tokio::sync::{mpsc, oneshot, broadcast, watch, Mutex, RwLock, Semaphore}

Setup

full turns on every part of Tokio, which is convenient while learning. Libraries and size-conscious services usually list only what they use, for example features = ["rt-multi-thread", "macros", "net", "time", "sync"].

#[tokio::main] and the runtime

main can't be async by itself, because something has to drive the future it returns. #[tokio::main] is a macro that builds a runtime and blocks on your async body, roughly like this:

#[tokio::main(flavor = "current_thread")] runs everything on the calling thread instead, which suits small tools and tests. #[tokio::test] does the same for test functions, giving each test its own runtime; Chapter 22 uses it.

Coming from Kotlin

The mapping to kotlinx.coroutines: #[tokio::main] ≈ runBlocking, tokio::spawn ≈ launch/async (its JoinHandle ≈ Deferred), join! ≈ awaitAll, select! ≈ select { }, spawn_blocking ≈ withContext(Dispatchers.IO). One big difference: Tokio tasks aren't structured. Dropping a JoinHandle detaches the task rather than cancelling it; call handle.abort(), or keep tasks in a tokio::task::JoinSet, which aborts all of them when it's dropped.

Tasks: spawn, join! and JoinHandle

Two ways to get concurrency:

  • tokio::join!(a, b) polls several futures inside the current task until all are done, exactly like Appendix C's join2.
  • tokio::spawn(fut) turns a future into an independent task that the scheduler can run on any worker thread, and returns a JoinHandle. Awaiting the handle gives Result<T, JoinError>: Err if the task panicked or was aborted.

Like thread::spawn, tokio::spawn needs a Send + 'static future, so tasks own (move) what they use. Unlike threads, tasks are cheap: a few hundred bytes each, so a server can run hundreds of thousands of them.

Both groups ran concurrently: the join! pair took 200 ms (the longer of the two) and the three spawned tasks took 300 ms, about 500 ms in total, yet no thread ever slept. Each sleep registered a timer and returned Pending, and the timer wheel woke the task when it was due.

Time, timeouts and select!

In async Rust, cancelling a future means dropping it: it simply stops at its current .await and is never polled again, and its destructors run. timeout and select! are built on that:

  • tokio::time::timeout(duration, fut) returns Err(Elapsed) and drops fut if the deadline passes first.
  • tokio::select! polls several branches, runs the first one to become ready, and drops the rest.
Watch out

Because a losing select! branch is dropped mid-way, use futures that are cancellation safe in a loop: dropping them must not lose data. recv() on a Tokio channel, tick() and accept() are cancellation safe; something like read_line, which may have read part of a line into its buffer, is not. Tokio's documentation states this for each method.

Coming from Kotlin

select! resembles select { } from kotlinx.coroutines, and join! resembles awaitAll() on several async { } results. The difference is what happens to the losers: Kotlin coroutines keep running until you cancel them or their scope ends, while the losing Rust futures are dropped on the spot, so their work stops.

Channels and the actor pattern

tokio::sync has async channels whose send and recv wait without blocking a thread:

  • mpsc: many producers, one consumer. The bounded version (mpsc::channel(n)) gives backpressure, because send(..).await waits while the buffer is full.
  • oneshot: exactly one value, typically a reply.
  • broadcast (every receiver gets every message) and watch (receivers see the latest value), useful for configuration and shutdown signals.

Together they give the actor pattern: one task owns some state, and the rest of the program sends it messages instead of sharing the state behind a lock.

Async I/O: a TCP echo server

Here is Chapter 19's echo server again, with Tokio's networking types. The shape is the same, but each connection is a task instead of a thread, and reading and writing go through the extension traits AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt and AsyncBufReadExt, the async counterparts of Read, Write and BufRead.

OS view

A task waiting for a socket doesn't hold a thread. Tokio registers the socket with epoll (through the mio crate) and parks the task; when the kernel reports the socket readable, the task is woken and scheduled again. That's how one process serves tens of thousands of mostly idle connections with a handful of threads, the limit that a thread per connection (Chapter 19) or a thread pool (Appendix E) runs into. On macOS the same happens with kqueue.

Blocking, CPU work and locks

A worker thread runs one task until it reaches an .await that returns Pending. Code that blocks without awaiting (std::thread::sleep, a blocking file or database call, a long computation) holds that worker, and every task queued behind it waits. Three rules follow:

  1. Don't block inside async code. Use the async APIs (tokio::time::sleep, tokio::fs, async database drivers), and move unavoidable blocking or CPU-heavy work to tokio::task::spawn_blocking, which runs it on a separate thread pool.
  2. Anything held across an .await in a spawned task must be Send, because the task may resume on another thread. That rules out Rc, RefCell borrows and std::sync lock guards.
  3. Pick the lock by whether it's held across .await. std::sync::Mutex is fine, and faster, when the guard is dropped before the next .await, which is what the handlers in Chapter 22 do with the in-memory catalog. If you need to hold the lock while awaiting, use tokio::sync::Mutex.

The compiler enforces rule 2:

The fixes are to end the guard's scope before the .await (put the locking in a block or a plain function), or to switch to tokio::sync::Mutex. The next example shows spawn_blocking and the Tokio mutex:

How the next chapters use Tokio

  • Chapter 22 (axum): #[tokio::main], tokio::net::TcpListener handed to axum::serve, the project's shutdown_signal for graceful shutdown, and #[tokio::test]. Every request handler is an async function that axum runs as a Tokio task.
  • Chapter 23 (reqwest): an HTTP client whose requests are futures on the same runtime, and a stand-in server spawned with tokio::spawn inside a test.
  • Chapter 24 (tracing): spans attach to futures, so log context survives .await and moves between worker threads with the task.
  • Chapters 25–26 (SQLx): the runtime-tokio feature, an async connection pool, and database transactions that stay open across .awaits.

Project step 21: async start-up and a shutdown signal

This step

Make main async with Tokio, read files without blocking, read two at once with join!, and wait for Ctrl+C or SIGTERM: the start-up and shutdown that Chapter 22's web server needs.

  • #[tokio::main] starts the runtime and runs the async main on it.
  • tokio::fs has the same functions as std::fs, but async: while a file is read, the thread can run other tasks. tokio::join! reads the two images concurrently and waits for both.
  • A borrow that has to live long enough. The futures borrow their paths until they finish. Writing load_image(&assets.join("volt.png")) inside join! fails to compile (error E0716) because the temporary PathBuf would be dropped while the future still uses it, so the paths are variables.
  • shutdown_signal completes on Ctrl+C (SIGINT) or SIGTERM, which is what podman stop and Kubernetes send. select! waits for whichever comes first. The next chapter hands this future to the web server for a graceful shutdown.
  • No lock across .await. The catalog is now a SharedCatalog, and the block that prints it drops the guard before main awaits the signal. A std::sync::Mutex guard held across an .await would block other tasks that need the lock.

Practice

  1. Port Appendix E's key-value server to Tokio: tokio::net::TcpListener, one task per connection, and the Store behind an Arc with a std::sync::RwLock that is never held across an .await. Then drop the thread pool and compare the code size.
    Solution

    Add Tokio with cargo add tokio --features full. The protocol and Store sections are copied unchanged. Store::execute stays a plain synchronous function, so every RwLock guard is dropped inside it, before serve_client reaches its next .await. The ThreadPool and the Server struct, with its AtomicBool flag and the dummy connection that wakes accept(), become one serve function that spawns a task per connection. Shutting down is JoinHandle::abort(). The client and the demo are the same with .await added.

    Both versions were run through rustfmt so the counts compare like for like (the compact listing in Appendix E has 268 lines). The Tokio version has 81 fewer lines, about 25%. The 50-line thread pool is gone, and the server section shrinks from 66 to 30 lines. Protocol, storage, client and demo stay the same size, because Tokio replaces the concurrency plumbing, not the logic. It's also no longer limited to 4 workers: an idle connection costs a parked task, not a thread.

  2. Simulate fetching 10 URLs (each a sleep of a different length) with at most 3 in flight at a time, using a tokio::task::JoinSet and a tokio::sync::Semaphore, and print each result as it completes.
    Solution

    All 10 tasks are spawned at once. Each one first waits for a permit from a Semaphore with 3 permits, so only 3 sleeps run at a time. Dropping _permit at the end of the task gives the permit back and lets the next waiter start. JoinSet::join_next returns results as they finish.

    There are never more than 3 pages between start and done, and the whole run takes about 760 ms instead of the 2100 ms the sleeps add up to. Waiters get permits first come, first served, but the start order isn't 1 to 10. On the multi-threaded runtime the spawned tasks first run in no fixed order, and that decides their place in the semaphore's queue. A new start can appear just before the matching done: the permit is released when the task ends, and main prints the result a moment later.

  3. Add graceful shutdown to the echo server: select! between listener.accept() and tokio::signal::ctrl_c(), stop accepting on Ctrl+C, and let open connections finish.
    Solution

    The accept loop becomes a select! with three branches: a new connection, a finished connection, and Ctrl+C. Connection tasks go into a JoinSet, so after the loop main can wait for the ones still open. Dropping the listener closes the port right away. A new client is refused instead of hanging in the kernel's backlog while the open connections finish.

    The slow client sent still here after the signal and still got its reply. Only then did the server exit. The join_next branch in the loop collects finished tasks as they end. Without it, the JoinSet would keep every finished task until shutdown, and connections.len() would count them too. One idle client can now delay shutdown forever. A real server puts a limit on the final wait, for example tokio::time::timeout(Duration::from_secs(10), ...), and calls connections.shutdown().await to abort whatever is left.

Next · Chapter 22A REST Microservice with axum
Chapter 22

A REST Microservice with axum

The shoe catalog becomes a web service: routes, extractors, JSON in and out, one error type mapped to status codes, image uploads as raw bytes, graceful shutdown, and tests that call the router without a network.

Project

From this chapter on, the main text builds the course project itself: every file shown carries the project badge and continues from project step 21. Chapters 22–24 keep the catalog in memory; Chapter 25 moves it to PostgreSQL by replacing one file, the repository, and the service methods that call it.

What we're building

A JSON API over the catalog. Products are created and replaced as a whole: the request body carries the product with its variants and versions, and versions refer to variants by SKU. Images are separate resources, uploaded and downloaded as raw bytes.

RequestSuccessErrors
GET /products?name=&brand=&minPrice=&maxPrice=200, a list (every parameter optional)400 unknown or malformed parameter
GET /products/{id}200, the product404
POST /products with a product as JSON201, the product with its ids400/415/422 bad JSON, 422 a broken rule, 409 name or SKU taken
PUT /products/{id} with a product as JSON200, the productthe same, plus 404
DELETE /products/{id}204, no body404
PUT /products/{id}/image with the file as the body204404, 413 too large, 415 not an image
GET /products/{id}/image200, the bytes with their Content-Type404 no product or no image
PUT and GET /products/{id}/variants/{sku}/imagethe same for one variantthe same

Every error body has the same shape, {"error": "product 7 not found"}, so a client can always show the message. Chapter 23 adds one more endpoint, GET /products/{id}/reviews, which calls another service.

Coming from Kotlin

axum fills the role of Ktor or Spring WebFlux. Routes map to handler functions as in Ktor's routing DSL or WebFlux's router functions. Handler parameters are typed "extractors", much like Spring's @PathVariable, @RequestParam and @RequestBody, but resolved at compile time by the types alone. There are no annotations, reflection or dependency-injection container: the objects a handler needs are values you pass to the router.

Add axum

axum is built on hyper (HTTP) and tower (middleware). The two dev-dependencies are only for the tests at the end of the chapter: tower's util feature provides oneshot, which sends one request to the router, and http-body-util reads a response body.

The structure: one feature module, four layers

Until now the library had one module per kind of code: model, validate, store. A service grows by features instead (products today; orders or customers later), so the code moves into a feature module, products/, with everything about products inside it:

The layers call each other in one direction only:

LayerKnows aboutDoes
routesHTTP, DTOs, the mapper, the servicetakes what the extractors parsed, maps requests to entities, calls the service, maps the result to a response
serviceentities, validation, the repositorythe use cases: validates, decides, calls the repository. Nothing about HTTP or JSON.
service::repoentities, the storagereads and writes; keeps names and SKUs unique, as a database's constraints would

Two rules come with it:

  • The API's JSON and the stored data are different types. model.rs holds the data transfer objects (DTOs), the contract with clients: they derive serde's traits and decide every field name. entity.rs holds what the service stores, with no serde at all. A stored field can be renamed, or added, without clients noticing, and the JSON can change without touching storage. mapper.rs is the one place that converts between them.
  • Only the service uses the repository, and the compiler enforces it. service.rs declares mod repo; without pub. A private module is visible only to its parent and to the parent's other child modules, and here the parent is service, so routes can't even name repo. In a Spring project, the same rule is a team convention.
Coming from Kotlin

This is the layered, package-by-feature structure of a typical Spring Boot service: routes ≈ a controller or router, service ≈ a @Service, repo ≈ a repository, model ≈ request and response DTOs, entity ≈ JPA entities, mapper ≈ a MapStruct mapper or hand-written extension functions. What differs is the wiring: main constructs the service and hands it to the router. There's no container, so there are no interfaces with a single implementation, and the repository is a struct, not an interface. (A trait would come in only with a second implementation, for example for tests.) Transactions are explicit too, as Chapter 25 shows.

Entities and DTOs

entity.rs is step 21's model.rs, moved and trimmed. The serde derives and the hand-written Serialize for Image are gone, because entities are never serialized. The product card's Display implementations and their helpers (variants_of, price_range, format_price) are gone too: the service shows products as JSON, so nothing calls them any more. NewProduct and its parts stay: they're what it takes to create or replace a product, without the ids the repository assigns.

model.rs holds the DTOs:

  • Requests derive Deserialize. ProductCreateRequest and ProductUpdateRequest have the same fields today, but they're separate types: what a client may send to create a product and what it may send to change one are separate decisions, and an update might later need, say, the version of the product the client last saw. deny_unknown_fields makes a misspelled field a 422 instead of a silently ignored value.
  • Responses derive Serialize. In ProductResponse an image is an ImageResponse, its type and size; the bytes have their own URL. What step 20 needed a hand-written Serialize for is now an ordinary struct.
  • ProductFilter, the query string of GET /products, derives Deserialize with camelCase names (minPrice). It's plain data without any JSON-specific shape, so the service takes it as it is instead of through the mapper.

The mapper

The conversions are From implementations, which is how Rust spells "a value of this type can be made from that one". Each one moves the fields across, and nested lists map element by element. Routes call them as request.into() and ProductResponse::from(product). A trait implementation is usable wherever both types are visible, so the module itself can stay private: mod mapper; in products/mod.rs.

None of the conversions can fail. A request that deserialized is a complete NewProduct, and whether it follows the rules is the service's question. A conversion that could fail would implement TryFrom and return a Result.

The repository and the service

validate.rs moves into the feature unchanged except for the paths in its use lines:

Changes since step 211 filesrc/products/validate.rs (moved)

The repository is step 21's Catalog, moved from store.rs. It keeps doing what a database's constraints will do in Chapter 25: hand out ids and keep names and SKUs unique. Two things leave it. Validation moves up to the service, which decides what a valid product is; the repository only stores. And ProductFilter::matches becomes a private function here, because filtering is how this storage answers a query, the in-memory version of a WHERE clause. The SharedCatalog alias goes: the service holds the Arc<Mutex<Catalog>> now.

Changes since step 211 filesrc/products/service/repo.rs (moved)

ProductService holds the shared catalog. Each method validates where needed, takes the lock, calls one repository method, and returns entities. A few details:

  • The lock is a std::sync::Mutex, not Tokio's async one. That's the right choice when the lock is held briefly and never across an .await: nothing between catalog() and the end of the statement awaits anything. Holding it while checking that a name is free and inserting the product makes those two steps atomic.
  • Copies out of the lock. The repository returns &Product, a borrow of the locked catalog, and the result must outlive the lock. Result::cloned() turns Result<&Product, _> into Result<Product, _>; this is what step 11's derived Clone was for.
  • The methods are async although nothing in them awaits yet. Their PostgreSQL versions in Chapter 25 will, and this way the routes won't change then.
  • #[derive(Clone, Default)]. A clone shares the same catalog, which is what axum needs: it clones the state for each request. ProductService::default() is a service with an empty catalog.

Routes and extractors

router() maps paths and methods to handlers:

  • Paths. {id} and {sku} capture a path segment. One .route() call can take several methods: get(get_product).put(update_product).delete(delete_product). A method that isn't listed gets 405 Method Not Allowed with an Allow header.
  • Layers. .layer(...) wraps the routes in middleware. DefaultBodyLimit::max caps request bodies at 1 MiB; axum's own default is 2 MB.
  • State. .with_state(service) gives every handler access to the service.

A handler is an ordinary async fn. Each parameter is an extractor: a type that knows how to take its value from the request. axum runs the extractors before calling the handler, and if one fails, the handler isn't called at all.

ExtractorTakesIf it fails
State(service): State<ProductService>the router's statecan't fail
Path(id): Path<i64>, Path((id, sku)): Path<(i64, String)>the captured path segments, parsed400: Cannot parse `abc` to a `i64`
Query(filter): Query<ProductFilter>the query string, deserialized with serde400, with serde's message
Json(request): Json<ProductCreateRequest>the body as JSON415 without Content-Type: application/json, 400 for invalid JSON, 422 for valid JSON of the wrong shape
body: Bytesthe raw body413 above the body limit

The body extractor (Json or Bytes) must be the last parameter, because it consumes the request. The others only read its head.

Handlers return anything that implements IntoResponse: Json<T> for a 200 with a JSON body, (StatusCode, Json<T>) to choose the status, a bare StatusCode for an empty body, and Result<T, E> where both T and E implement it. That last one is what lets handlers use ?.

Every handler has the same three lines: map the request (request.into()), call the service, map the result (product.into()). There's no parsing code: the extractors did it, with the DTOs' serde attributes as the specification.

products/mod.rs decides what the rest of the crate sees: the entity, model and validation modules, the router, and the service. mapper, routes and service stay private.

One error type, rendered as JSON

The service returns Result<_, CatalogError>, the error type from Chapter 9, so implementing IntoResponse for it decides every error response in one place. The match on the variant chooses the status, and the body carries the message with its causes: invalid product: the name is empty. Because the match has no _ arm, adding a variant later is a compile error here until it has a status.

VariantStatus
Invalid(_)422 Unprocessable Entity: well-formed but breaks a rule
NotFound, VariantNotFound, NoImage404 Not Found
DuplicateName, DuplicateSku409 Conflict: clashes with the current state
NotAnImage415 Unsupported Media Type

Extractor failures (malformed JSON, a bad path parameter) never reach the handler, so they don't go through CatalogError: axum answers them with a plain-text message. Practice task 2 changes that.

Images as raw bytes

An image is uploaded as the whole request body: curl -X PUT --data-binary @volt.png .../image. The Bytes extractor collects it, up to the body limit, and Image::from_bytes from step 8 decides the type from the magic number. The request's Content-Type header is ignored: a client can claim anything, the bytes can't lie. A download returns the stored bytes with the stored type in the Content-Type header, which a tuple of a header array and a body expresses: ([(header::CONTENT_TYPE, "image/png")], bytes).

Two other designs are common:

  • Base64 inside the JSON. One request creates everything, but the file grows by a third, every GET of the product carries the image, and both sides need extra code to encode and decode.
  • A multipart form (multipart/form-data), as a browser's file upload sends. It carries a file and other fields in one request, and needs axum's multipart feature and code to walk the parts.

A separate endpoint with a raw body is the simplest of the three, and keeps the product JSON small.

Start-up: serve, then shut down gracefully

lib.rs exports app(), the whole HTTP application: today, the product routes. With a second feature, its router would be merged in here, and middleware for every route is added here in Chapter 24.

main creates the service and loads the seed file through it. The file holds create requests, so they go through the same mapper and service as a POST /products. Then it binds a TcpListener to ADDR from step 19 and hands it to axum::serve with the app. with_graceful_shutdown(shutdown_signal()) uses the future from step 21: when it completes, the server stops accepting connections, lets requests in flight finish, and then serve returns.

Note

The default address is 127.0.0.1, so the service only accepts connections from the same machine. WSL 2 forwards localhost from Windows, so a browser on Windows reaches it too. In a container, set ADDR=0.0.0.0:3000 so connections from outside the container can reach it.

Run it

Two JSON files in the project directory hold request bodies for curl: a new product, and the same product changed (the white variant is gone, a size is added, and there's a second version).

Start the service in one terminal with SEED_FILE=seed.json cargo run -q, and send requests from a second one. python3 -m json.tool pretty-prints a JSON response (jq does the same if you've installed it); -i makes curl print the status line and headers.

Things to notice:

  • The second POST of the same product is a 409, and a zero price is a 422 that names the variant.
  • The text file is refused with 415 even though curl sent it like the image.
  • The downloaded image is byte for byte the uploaded one (cmp prints nothing for identical files, and && then runs echo).
  • After the PUT, RR-VOLT-42 still has id 8 and its image; RR-VOLT-43 is new.

Test it without a network

app() returns a plain Router, which is a tower Service: something that takes a request and returns a future of a response. oneshot calls it once, so tests send requests straight into the router without opening a port, and each test gets its own fresh service. #[tokio::test] runs each test on its own runtime. Two helpers keep the tests short: send returns the status, the Content-Type and the raw body, and call sends and parses JSON.

Step 18's tests/catalog.rs is gone: the repository is private now, so code outside the crate can't reach it. Its question, whether two concurrent creates of one name produce exactly one product, is now asked through the API, by sending both requests at once with tokio::join!. The unit tests inside the modules (repository, mapper, validation, DTOs) can still test private code.

What the compiler guarantees here

  • The layers stay layers. repo is private to service, so a handler that tries to use it doesn't compile.
  • Entities never leak into the JSON. They don't implement Serialize, so a handler can't return one by mistake; it has to go through the mapper.
  • Thread safety. Tokio runs handlers on a pool of worker threads, so axum requires the state to be Send + Sync and every handler's future to be Send. Arc<Mutex<Catalog>> satisfies that; with an Rc or a RefCell the router doesn't compile (Chapter 16).
  • No lock across .await. A std::sync guard held across an .await would make the handler's future non-Send, which is a compile error rather than a deadlock in production. Chapter 23 shows the error.
  • Every error has a status. The match in into_response has no catch-all arm, so a new CatalogError variant doesn't compile until it has a status.

Where to go next

  • Calling another service: Chapter 23 adds an endpoint that fetches reviews from another API with reqwest.
  • Logging: Chapter 24 adds structured logs, a span per request, and logged errors.
  • Persistence: Chapter 25 replaces the in-memory repository with PostgreSQL, and Chapter 26 changes its schema.
  • Authentication: Chapter 27 requires a bearer token on every request, checked by a middleware.
  • More middleware from tower-http: CORS, timeouts and compression, each added with .layer(...) like the body limit.
  • OpenAPI documentation generated from the DTOs, for example with utoipa.
  • Packaging: a multi-stage container build that compiles in a Rust image and copies the single binary into a small runtime image.

Practice

  1. Add a Location: /products/{id} header to the 201 response of POST /products. A handler can return a tuple (StatusCode, [(HeaderName, String); 1], Json<ProductResponse>). Extend create_then_get to check the header.
    Solution

    Only the handler changes. The header array goes between the status and the body: axum applies a tuple's parts in order, so a status first, then any number of header parts, then the body. The id comes from the stored product, so the header is built after the service call.

    The test helpers call and send don't return headers, so create_then_get sends its POST by hand with oneshot and reads the body itself. The GET half of the test is unchanged.

  2. Make extractor failures use the JSON error format: change create_product to take Result<Json<ProductCreateRequest>, JsonRejection>, and turn a rejection into a {"error": ...} body with the rejection's own status (rejection.status()) and message (rejection.body_text()).
    Solution

    Wrapping an extractor in Result makes it infallible: axum calls the handler either way and passes the failure in. A new CatalogError::BadBody variant carries axum's status and message, and From<JsonRejection> lets the handler write request?. The existing IntoResponse then renders it like every other error. The variant stores a StatusCode and a String rather than the JsonRejection, because CatalogError derives PartialEq and the rejection doesn't implement it.

    The test now checks the bodies too. send returns raw bytes, so a small call_raw helper parses the JSON answer to a body that isn't JSON.

    All three failures keep axum's status (422, 400, 415) and now have the {"error": ...} shape. update_product still answers in plain text. It needs the same two-line change.

  3. Add DELETE /products/{id}/image, which removes the image: 204 if there was one, 404 if not. Which layers need a new function, and which don't change?
    Solution

    Each of the three layers gets one function, top to bottom: a handler and a .delete(...) on the existing route, a service method, and a repository method. Like delete, the repository gives the removed image back. Option::take moves it out and leaves None, so "there was no image" falls out of ok_or.

    New functions: routes (delete_product_image), service (remove_product_image) and repository (Catalog::remove_product_image). Unchanged: model.rs and mapper.rs, because no JSON goes in or out; entity.rs, because image is already an Option; validate.rs; and error.rs, because NotFound and NoImage already become 404 with a message.

  4. Make the create and update requests differ: an update must include expectedName, and the service refuses it with 409 when the stored name is different. Only the DTO, the mapper, the service and the repository should change; the entity's NewProduct may gain a field.
    Solution

    The update DTO gets a required expectedName. NewProduct gets an expected_name: Option<String>: the update mapper sets Some and the create mapper sets None. That way the routes still call service.update(id, request.into()) and don't change.

    The service makes the decision. It keeps one guard for the check and the update, because two separate self.catalog() calls would let another request rename the product in between. None of the existing 409 variants says what went wrong (DuplicateName would claim that another product has the name), so CatalogError gets a NameChanged variant. The match in into_response has no catch-all arm, so the compiler asks for its status.

    The new field breaks every NewProduct { ... } literal. In the repository and in validate.rs, those are only the tests' helpers. The repository code itself doesn't change: the check needs the stored product, and the service already reads it with get. The curl request file used in the chapter needs the new field too.
