Chapter 23

Calling Other Services with reqwest

An HTTP client inside the service: fetch customer reviews from another API, deserialize its JSON into your own types, set timeouts, turn its failures into 502 Bad Gateway, and test against a local stand-in.

The use case: reviews from another service

Services rarely work alone: they call payment providers, other teams' services, and public APIs. This chapter gives the shoe service a dependency of that kind, a reviews service, and adds one endpoint:

RequestSuccessErrors
GET /products/{id}/reviews200, a list of reviews404 no such product, 502 the reviews service failed

The reviews come from JSONPlaceholder, a free fake REST API for exactly this kind of exercise. It has no reviews, but its comments have the right shape: each belongs to a post, has an author's e-mail, a title (name) and a body. The service treats a product id as a post id, so /comments?postId=1 is the list of reviews for product 1. Posts 1 to 100 have five comments each:

The service returns them in its own shape, {"author", "title", "body"}. Its clients don't need to know where reviews come from, and if the source changes, only the service changes.

Add reqwest

reqwest is the most widely used HTTP client in Rust. It's built on the same hyper and Tokio as axum, so its requests run on the service's runtime.

Changes since step 221 fileCargo.toml
  • json adds .json() to read a response body into any Deserialize type (and to send one).
  • query adds .query() to append URL parameters, encoded correctly. Since reqwest 0.13 it's an opt-in feature.
  • The default features include HTTPS through rustls, a TLS implementation written in Rust, so there's no OpenSSL to install.
Coming from Kotlin

reqwest::Client plays the role of Ktor's HttpClient, Spring's WebClient or OkHttp: one long-lived client with a connection pool, shared by the whole application, with .json() where Ktor has body<T>(). The calls are async, like Ktor's suspend functions.

A client for the reviews service

The new top-level reviews module wraps everything about the other service: its base URL, its query parameters and its JSON. It sits next to products rather than inside it, because it isn't a product feature: it's a gateway to another system, which any feature could use.

  • The other service's JSON stays here. Comment mirrors what JSONPlaceholder sends, and it's private. The rest of the program sees only Review, in this program's terms, and From<Comment> for Review converts at the boundary. That's the same separation as entities and DTOs, applied to the outgoing side. Fields that Comment doesn't declare (postId, id) are ignored.
  • One client, shared. A reqwest::Client keeps a pool of open connections, so later requests to the same host skip the TCP and TLS handshakes. It's an Arc inside, cheap to clone. Creating a new client per request would throw the pool away each time.
  • A timeout. Without one, a request to a server that never answers waits forever, and so does your client's request to you. timeout(5s) covers the whole request, from connecting to reading the last byte.
  • Each step can fail differently. send() fails when there's no connection or no answer in time. error_for_status() turns a 4xx or 5xx answer into an error; without it, a 500 page would go on to json(), and fail there with a confusing parse error. json() fails when the body isn't the expected JSON. All three return a reqwest::Error, so the function has one error type and uses ?.

The base URL is configurable, as REVIEWS_URL, so tests can point the client at a local stand-in.

Changes since step 222 filessrc/config.rs, src/lib.rs

The service gets a client

Fetching reviews is a product use case, so it's a method of ProductService, which now holds the client next to the catalog. Default no longer fits, because a service needs a client to be complete; ProductService::new(reviews) replaces it.

reviews() checks that the product exists, then calls the other service. The order matters twice:

  • An unknown product is a 404 without a network call.
  • The lock is released before the .await. self.catalog().get(id).is_some() is one statement, so the guard is a temporary dropped at its end.
Changes since step 221 filesrc/products/service.rs

Holding the guard across the .await instead, by writing let catalog = self.catalog(); and using catalog before the call, would block every other request that needs the catalog for as long as the reviews service takes to answer. The compiler doesn't let it get that far. A MutexGuard isn't Send, a future that holds one across an .await isn't Send either, and axum requires Send futures, because Tokio may move a task to another thread at any .await. The handler awaits reviews(), so the handler's future isn't Send. The default error only says that the handler function isn't a Handler. axum's #[axum::debug_handler] attribute (from its macros feature) on the handler explains why, and points into the service:

The response and the route

The API returns a ReviewResponse, a DTO like the others, and the mapper converts each Review into one. They have the same fields today, but Review is what the service works with and ReviewResponse is what clients rely on, so each can change on its own. The handler has the usual three steps.

Changes since step 223 filessrc/products/model.rs, src/products/mapper.rs, src/products/routes.rs

main creates the client once, at start-up, and passes it to the service:

Changes since step 221 filesrc/main.rs

Its failures: 502 Bad Gateway

When the reviews service fails, the request was fine and the shoe service is fine, but it can't answer. HTTP has a status for exactly that: 502 Bad Gateway, "a server I depend on gave me a bad answer, or none". CatalogError gets a Reviews variant that wraps the reqwest::Error, and From<reqwest::Error> lets the service use ?.

The error's message isn't sent to the client: it contains the other service's URL, an internal detail. The client sees the reviews service failed. Chapter 24 writes the full cause to the log.

reqwest::Error doesn't implement PartialEq, so CatalogError can't derive it any more. The repository's tests compared errors with assert_eq!; they now use matches! with a pattern, plus a guard where a field must have a certain value.

Changes since step 221 filesrc/products/service/repo.rs

Run it

Start the service as before (SEED_FILE=seed.json cargo run -q). The first request goes out to JSONPlaceholder. For the last one, the service was restarted with REVIEWS_URL pointing at a port where nothing listens:

Testing against a stand-in service

Tests that call the real JSONPlaceholder would fail without internet access, and they couldn't make it fail on purpose. Instead, the tests start a stand-in: a small axum app that answers /comments like JSONPlaceholder does. It listens on port 0, so the operating system picks a free port, and the test points the client at that address. tokio::spawn runs it in the background for the rest of the test. Separate tests start stand-ins that answer 500 or the wrong JSON, and one points at a port where nothing listens. All three must become 502.

Both test files now build the app the same way, so the helpers move to tests/common/mod.rs. Cargo compiles each file directly in tests/ as a separate test crate, but not files in subdirectories, so common is a module that each test file includes with mod common;. app() points the reviews client at port 9, where nothing listens, for tests that must never reach it.

Changes since step 221 filetests/api.rs

Crates such as wiremock offer the same idea with less code: they start a mock server, and you declare which requests it expects and what it answers. A twenty-line axum app is enough here, and it uses nothing new.

Production notes

  • Timeouts everywhere. Every outgoing call needs one, shorter than your own clients' timeout, or a slow dependency makes your service slow too. connect_timeout can be set separately from the overall timeout.
  • Retries, carefully. A GET can be retried after a connection error or a 503, with a growing delay between attempts. A POST generally can't, because the first attempt may have succeeded. Many services retrying at once can keep a struggling dependency down, so cap the attempts.
  • Calls in parallel. tokio::join!(a, b) runs two calls concurrently and waits for both; for a list of calls, futures::future::join_all or a tokio::task::JoinSet does the same. The total time is that of the slowest call, not the sum.
  • Degrade instead of failing. A product page could show the product without reviews when the reviews service is down. Here the endpoint returns 502 and the rest of the API is unaffected, which is the same idea at a smaller scale.
  • Caching. Reviews change slowly. Caching them for a minute in memory, keyed by product id, would remove most of the calls.

Practice

  1. Add a limit query parameter to GET /products/{id}/reviews (default 3) and return at most that many reviews. Does the limit belong in the request to JSONPlaceholder, in the service, or in the handler? Check whether JSONPlaceholder supports _limit.
    Solution

    A ReviewsQuery DTO reads limit from the query string. #[serde(default = "...")] names a function that supplies the 3, so the default is part of the API's contract, next to the other DTOs. The handler passes the number to the service, and the service passes it to the client, which sends it to jsonplaceholder as _limit.

    The new stand-in has five comments and honours _limit as jsonplaceholder does. The test therefore checks that the client really sends the parameter. The chapter's two-comment stand-in ignores the parameter, and its tests still pass.

    jsonplaceholder supports _limit: the same request returns 5 comments without it and 2 with _limit=2. So the limit belongs in the request. Fewer reviews are sent, parsed and converted. Reading the parameter and its default is still the handler's job, because the query string is HTTP. The service only passes the number on. The name _limit stays inside reviews.rs, the one module that knows jsonplaceholder. If a replacement service didn't support it, the client would truncate the list instead, and nothing above it would change. A malformed limit is a 400 from the Query extractor, like a bad filter on GET /products.

  2. Retry the reviews request once after 200 ms when it fails with a connection error (error.is_connect()) or a 5xx status. Write a stand-in that fails the first request and succeeds the second, and test that the endpoint returns 200.
    Solution

    The retry lives in ReviewsClient, because whether a failure is worth retrying depends on the other service. The service and the routes don't change. The old body of for_product becomes a private fetch. for_product calls it, and on a transient error sleeps 200 ms and returns the second attempt's result, whatever it is. That caps it at two attempts. error_for_status() keeps the status in the error, so error.status() tells a 503 from a 404. Timeouts and unparseable bodies are not retried.

    The stand-in counts its requests in an AtomicUsize, which it gets as router state. The test holds a second Arc to the counter, so afterwards it can check that there were exactly two requests.

    The chapter's 500 and unreachable-port tests still answer 502, but each now takes an extra 200 ms for its retry. That's why the reviews tests take 0.22 s instead of 0.02 s.

  3. Make the timeout configurable with REVIEWS_TIMEOUT_MS, then write a stand-in that sleeps longer than the timeout (tokio::time::sleep) and check that the endpoint returns 502 in roughly the timeout's time.
    Solution

    Config reads REVIEWS_TIMEOUT_MS the way it reads ADDR: a default when it's unset, and a ConfigError naming the variable when it doesn't parse. It stores a Duration, so the unit is settled where the number is read. ReviewsClient::new takes the timeout as a parameter, and main passes it in.

    The test helpers get app_with_reviews_timeout, and app_with_reviews keeps the 5 s. The stand-in sleeps 5 s and the client gives up after 300 ms. The test measures the call with Instant and accepts 300 ms to 1 s.

    The 502 comes 301 ms after the request, so the timeout, not the stand-in's sleep, decides how long a client waits. The stand-in's handler keeps sleeping after the client hangs up, but that doesn't delay the test: the runtime drops the task when the test ends.

  4. Add a rating to ReviewResponse, computed in the service from the length of the review's body (any rule will do). Which of Comment, Review and ReviewResponse change?
    Solution

    The rule is a small private function in the service: one star, plus one per 50 characters, capped at five. reviews() pairs each Review with its rating in a new RatedReview. The mapper flattens that into ReviewResponse, so the handler doesn't change: it still maps with ReviewResponse::from.

    Only ReviewResponse changes: it gains the field clients see. Comment doesn't, because jsonplaceholder's JSON is the same as before. Review doesn't either. It's what reviews.rs builds from a Comment, and that module knows nothing about ratings, so a rating field there would need a placeholder value until the service overwrote it. The service's own result type, RatedReview, carries the rating instead.

Next · Chapter 24Logging & Tracing for the axum Service
Chapter 24

Logging & Tracing for the axum Service

Structured logs for the shoe service with tracing, tracing-subscriber and tower-http: a span per request, events for every change, errors logged with their causes, RUST_LOG filtering and JSON output.

The service from Chapters 22–23 prints three lines at start-up and is otherwise silent. In production that means a 502 leaves no trace of what failed, and nobody can tell how long requests take. This chapter adds structured logging to the project, after a short tour of the API on its own.

log or tracing?

Rust logging has two layers, like SLF4J plus Logback on the JVM: a crate your code calls to emit messages, and a separate crate that decides where they go.

log tracing
Model levelled text messages events with structured fields, inside spans
Context none built in spans carry fields (request ID, user) to every event inside them
Async no notion of tasks spans attach to futures and survive .await and thread hops
Output a backend such as env_logger tracing-subscriber: human-readable or JSON, plus journald, OpenTelemetry and more
Typical use small CLIs, libraries services and async code; tokio, hyper and axum already use it

For a service, use tracing. Libraries that still use log aren't lost: tracing-subscriber installs a bridge by default, so their messages appear in the same output.

Coming from Kotlin

The JVM mapping: log ≈ the SLF4J API with a simple binding; tracing ≈ SLF4J, MDC and Micrometer Tracing spans in one API; tracing-subscriber ≈ Logback configuration, written in code instead of XML. RUST_LOG plays the role of logger levels in logback.xml.

The API in one example

  • Events are log lines: trace!, debug!, info!, warn!, error!. Fields come before the message: info!(user_id = 42, "login"). A bare variable name is shorthand for name = name, %x records with Display, and ?x with Debug.
  • Spans are periods of work with their own fields. Every event inside a span is tagged with it, nested spans included. #[instrument] wraps a function in a span named after it and records its arguments as fields.
  • The subscriber decides format and filtering. Install one, once, at the start of main.
Watch out

span.enter() is for synchronous code. Never hold an entered span's guard across an .await: the task may pause and another task on the same thread would inherit the wrong span. In async code use #[instrument] on the async fn, or future.instrument(span) from tracing::Instrument, which attach the span to the future itself.

Coming from Kotlin

This is where tracing beats MDC. MDC is thread-local, so Kotlin coroutines need MDCContext from kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j to carry it across suspension points. A tracing span travels with the future automatically, whichever worker thread polls it.

Add the crates

tracing is the API the code calls. tracing-subscriber formats and filters what it emits: env-filter reads RUST_LOG, and json adds the JSON format. tower-http's trace feature provides the middleware that logs every HTTP request.

Configure the subscriber

init_tracing runs first in main, so start-up itself is logged. It follows the usual conventions for services:

  • RUST_LOG chooses what to log. The syntax is a list of target=level entries, where a target is a module path: shoes=debug,tower_http=info shows debug events from the project and info events from the middleware. Without the variable, the default is info for both. Dependencies such as hyper and sqlx stay quiet unless you name them.
  • Logs go to stderr, the stream meant for diagnostics. Container platforms collect both stdout and stderr.
  • LOG_FORMAT=json switches from readable lines to one JSON object per line, which log collectors (Loki, Elasticsearch, a cloud provider's log service) parse without guessing. The two branches build subscribers of different types, but each ends with init(), which installs it as the global default, so the if doesn't need them to match.

The println! calls become events, with the seed file's details as fields.

A span per request

TraceLayer from tower-http wraps every request in a span named request with the method, URI and HTTP version as fields, and emits an event when the response is ready, with its status and latency. Both default to the DEBUG level; DefaultMakeSpan and DefaultOnResponse raise them to INFO, so every request appears in the default output. It's middleware for the whole application, so it goes into app() in lib.rs, around every feature's routes. Added after the product router's DefaultBodyLimit, it's the outer layer: it sees every request first, including those the body limit rejects.

The business events belong to the service, where the decisions are made: product created with its id and name, image stored with its type and size, and so on. They're logged inside the request's span, so each line also says which request it belongs to, without passing anything around. The seed products go through the same service, so they're logged too. %product.name records a field with its Display form; a field without a sigil, such as size, must be a number, a bool or a string.

Changes since step 231 filesrc/products/service.rs

Log the error path

into_response is the one place every error passes through, so that's where errors are logged:

  • Server errors (5xx) at error!. Something failed that isn't the client's fault, and someone should look. The 502 from a failed reviews call is one.
  • Client errors (4xx) at debug!. A 404 or a 422 is normal traffic, and TraceLayer already logs its status at info. The reason is useful while investigating, so it's there with RUST_LOG=shoes=debug.

The log gets the whole chain of causes, built by walking source(); the client still gets only the first part for a 502. The same chain string now serves as the client's message for the other errors, which replaces the earlier match on (self, self.source()).

Changes since step 231 filesrc/error.rs

See it run

The demo ran with RUST_LOG=shoes=debug,tower_http=info: it created a product twice, uploaded an image, then restarted the service with LOG_FORMAT=json and an unreachable REVIEWS_URL, and asked for reviews.

Things to notice:

  • The seed products are logged as they're created, before the server starts listening: there's no request, so there's no span.
  • Each line inside a request starts with request{method=... uri=...}: the span. In JSON it's the span object, which a log collector can filter on.
  • The 409 is explained by a debug event: a product named "Road Racer" exists.
  • The 502 is logged with the cause the client never sees: the URL, and Connection refused. TraceLayer also reports it as a failure (response failed), because it classifies every 5xx response as one.
  • Timestamps are in UTC. The latency is measured from the moment the request arrived until the response was ready.

Production notes

LevelUse it for
error!something failed and a human should look (5xx, lost data, a dependency down)
warn!unexpected but handled (retries, fallbacks, deprecated input)
info!business events and lifecycle (created, deleted, started, stopping)
debug!diagnostics you enable while investigating (rejected requests, decisions)
trace!very detailed flow, usually off even in development
  • Cost. A disabled event costs little more than one comparison, so leave debug! calls in. The tracing crate's max_level_* and release_max_level_* features can remove levels at compile time.
  • What not to log. Image bytes, passwords, tokens and personal data such as the reviewers' e-mail addresses. Log ids, sizes and types instead, as the handlers do.
  • Request IDs. When several services handle one user request, give it an id and log it everywhere. tower-http's request-id feature has layers that set an x-request-id header on each request (keeping one sent by a proxy) and copy it to the response; record it as a field of the request span with make_span_with, and pass it on to the reviews service as a header.
  • Tests. Logs from the code under test aren't shown by default. Add let _ = tracing_subscriber::fmt().with_test_writer().try_init(); at the start of a test to see them, captured per test by cargo test.
  • Where logs go. In containers, write to stdout or stderr, as here, and let the platform collect them. On a Linux host with systemd, the tracing-journald layer writes to the journal; on macOS you read the system log with log stream or Console.app. To export spans to a distributed-tracing backend such as Jaeger, Grafana Tempo or Honeycomb, add the tracing-opentelemetry layer with an OTLP exporter. The handlers' events stay the same; only init_tracing changes.

Practice

  1. Log the reviews call: an info! event with the product id, the number of reviews and the time the call took (std::time::Instant). Check that it appears inside the request's span.
    Solution

    The event goes in ProductService::reviews, next to the service's other business events. Instant::now() is taken just before the call, and elapsed = ?started.elapsed() records the Duration with Debug, which prints it with its unit (52.86411ms). When the call fails, ? returns before the event, and into_response logs the error as before.

    The new line starts with request{method=GET uri=/products/1/reviews ...}, like the finished processing request line after it, so it's inside the request's span. Nothing was passed to the service for that: the span is attached to the request's future, and the service runs inside it. Its elapsed is close to the request's latency, because almost all of the request's time goes to the other service. The 404 for product 9 has no reviews fetched event, because the service never called the reviews service.

  2. Put #[tracing::instrument(skip(self))] on ReviewsClient::for_product, so the call gets its own span with the product id as a field. Which events now carry two spans?
    Solution

    One attribute is enough. #[instrument] creates an INFO span named after the function, and records the arguments that aren't skipped as fields. self is skipped because ReviewsClient doesn't implement Debug, and it wouldn't be useful in a log anyway.

    Which events carry two spans? Only events emitted while for_product is running. The project has no events of its own in there, so with the default filter you see no difference. The events from reqwest and hyper-util (connecting, pooling) are inside the call, and once RUST_LOG enables them they show request{...}:for_product{product_id=1}. The 502's request failed event carries only the request span. into_response logs it after for_product has returned its error, and so do TraceLayer's response events. To get the error logged inside the call's span, write #[tracing::instrument(skip(self), err)].

  3. Add request IDs as described in the production notes: SetRequestIdLayer with MakeRequestUuid (the request-id feature), PropagateRequestIdLayer, and a make_span_with closure that records the id in the span. Write a test that sends x-request-id: test-123 and checks the response header.
    Solution

    Turn on the request-id feature. It pulls in uuid itself, so there's no other dependency to add. The span is built by a closure now, instead of DefaultMakeSpan. The closure reads the x-request-id header that SetRequestIdLayer has already set, so the layer order matters. With Router::layer, the last layer added is the outermost one: set the id, then open the span, then copy the id to the response. The HTTP version is left out of the span to keep the lines short.

    An id the client sends is kept (test-123), and a request without one gets a UUID. The 404 in the test shows that error responses carry the id too, because the layers wrap the whole router. The business event product created carries the request's id with no change to the service. To follow a request into the reviews service, the next step is to send the same header on the outgoing reqwest call.

  4. Add a LOG_LEVEL fallback: use RUST_LOG if it's set, else shoes={LOG_LEVEL},tower_http=info, else the current default. Where should an invalid LOG_LEVEL be reported, given that logging isn't set up yet?
    Solution

    filter_directives makes the decision, and it takes the two variables as arguments, so tests don't have to change the process environment. A level is parsed as a LevelFilter, which accepts off, error to trace in any case, or a number from 0 to 5. That also keeps LOG_LEVEL from smuggling in extra directives such as debug,hyper=trace. RUST_LOG is used as it is. If EnvFilter can't parse it, the default applies, as before.

    Where to report an invalid LOG_LEVEL? Not with warn! at the moment it's found, because there's no subscriber yet and the event would be dropped. You could eprintln! it, but that line wouldn't match the log's format, which matters with LOG_FORMAT=json. Here the problem is kept as a value, the subscriber is installed with the default filter, and the warning is logged right after, as the first line of the log. Refusing to start, as for a bad ADDR, would also work, but a wrong log level isn't worth an outage. In the third run RUST_LOG wins: LOG_LEVEL=debug is ignored, and since shoes isn't named, even listening isn't logged.

Next · Chapter 25Persisting the Catalog in PostgreSQL
Chapter 25

Persisting the Catalog in PostgreSQL

Replace the in-memory catalog with PostgreSQL 18 in a Podman container, using SQLx: a schema with one-to-many and many-to-many relations, compile-time-checked queries, transactions, binary columns, and a fresh database per test.

The catalog lives in memory, so a restart loses every product, and two instances of the service would each have their own catalog. This chapter moves it into PostgreSQL. The layers from Chapter 22 pay off here: the repository is rewritten, the service's methods get new bodies, and the routes, the DTOs and the mapper's request side don't change at all.

Which PostgreSQL version

The latest stable release is PostgreSQL 18. PostgreSQL 19 is in its release-candidate phase, with general availability planned for November 19, 2026. This chapter uses the postgres:18 image tag, which always points at the newest 18.x patch release. Moving to 19 later is a tag change plus a data migration, covered at the end.

Run PostgreSQL in Podman

Podman runs OCI containers without a background daemon, and by default rootless: the database runs as your own user, not root. Install it in your Ubuntu shell:

On macOS, containers need a Linux kernel, so Podman runs them inside a small Linux virtual machine that it manages for you. Create and start it once (and run podman machine start again after a reboot):

After that, every podman command in this chapter works unchanged: published ports such as 127.0.0.1:5432 are forwarded from the VM to your Mac, and named volumes live inside the VM.

Create a named volume for the data, then start the database:

Flag Why
-e POSTGRES_* the image creates this user (a superuser) and database on first start
-p 127.0.0.1:5432:5432 publish the port on localhost only, not on every network interface
-v catalog-pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql keep the data in the named volume, so it survives podman rm
--health-cmd lets podman ps and podman healthcheck run report when the server accepts connections
docker.io/library/postgres:18 a fully qualified image name, so Podman doesn't ask which registry to use
Note

Under WSL, rootless Podman may print "/" is not a shared mount, this could cause issues or missing mounts with rootless containers. It's harmless for this setup: the named volume and port publishing work normally.

Watch out

The volume path changed in PostgreSQL 18 images. Older guides mount the volume at /var/lib/postgresql/data. From 18 on, the official image stores its data in a version-specific directory (/var/lib/postgresql/18/docker) and expects the volume at /var/lib/postgresql. Using the old path with an 18 image either fails to start or silently writes to an unnamed volume that's lost when the container is removed.

Everyday commands:

Task Command
Is it up? podman ps (the STATUS column shows healthy) or podman healthcheck run catalog-db
See server logs podman logs -f catalog-db
Open a SQL shell podman exec -it catalog-db psql -U catalog -d catalog
Stop / start (data is kept) podman stop catalog-db, podman start catalog-db
Back up podman exec catalog-db pg_dump -U catalog catalog > backup.sql
Remove the container (data is kept) podman rm -f catalog-db
Delete the data too podman volume rm catalog-pgdata
Tip

Prefer a file to a long command? Save the same settings as a compose.yaml (service db, image docker.io/library/postgres:18, the three POSTGRES_* variables, port 127.0.0.1:5432:5432, volume catalog-pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql) and run podman compose up -d. That needs a compose provider, such as sudo apt install podman-compose.

Connect the project

The container's server can hold many databases. Create one for the project:

SQLx's tools read the connection string from DATABASE_URL: the query macros connect to the database while compiling, to check your SQL against the real tables, and the command-line tool and the tests use it too. Export it in your shell profile so the terminal, cargo and VS Code's rust-analyzer all see it. (The running service gets its database URL from its settings instead, as the section on settings shows.)

Add the crate with the features the project uses, and install the SQLx command-line tool, which creates and applies migrations:

The config crate reads the service's settings from YAML files, per environment; the section on settings below uses it.

runtime-tokio runs SQLx on Tokio, postgres is the driver, macros provides query!, migrate provides migrations, and chrono maps PostgreSQL's DATE and TIMESTAMPTZ to chrono's types.

Coming from Kotlin

The JVM equivalents: PgPool ≈ a HikariCP pool, SQLx migrations ≈ Flyway, the compile-time-checked macros ≈ SQLDelight, and #[sqlx::test] (later in this chapter) ≈ Testcontainers with a fresh database per test. Like jOOQ or Exposed, everything is typed, but you write plain SQL.

The schema, as a migration

A migration is a SQL file in migrations/, named with a version number and a description. cargo sqlx migrate add create_catalog creates an empty one, named with the current time. SQLx applies migrations in version order and records each one in a table called _sqlx_migrations, so it runs exactly once per database. Chapter 26 looks at that bookkeeping in detail.

The four tables hold the model from Chapter 7:

  • One-to-many: variants.product_id and versions.product_id are foreign keys to products. ON DELETE CASCADE deletes a product's variants and versions with it.
  • Many-to-many: version_variants has one row per (version, variant) pair. Its primary key is the pair, so a link can't be stored twice, and deleting either end deletes the link.
  • Ids: GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY is the standard replacement for SERIAL. PostgreSQL assigns the ids and rejects values supplied by clients. Each table has its own sequence, as the in-memory catalog had its own counters.
  • The rules the database can check itself: UNIQUE on product names and SKUs, and on (product_id, number) for versions; CHECK for positive prices and version numbers, the accepted image types, and "image and type both set, or neither". These hold even for a second service or a manual psql session that skips the Rust validation.
  • Indexes: PostgreSQL indexes primary keys and UNIQUE columns automatically, but not foreign keys. variants_product_id_idx makes "the variants of product 7" fast, and the index on version_variants.variant_id covers lookups from the variant side. Lookups from the version side use the primary key, which starts with version_id.
  • Images are BYTEA columns, PostgreSQL's type for binary data, next to a TEXT column with the media type. With the 1 MiB upload limit that's fine; the production notes discuss larger files.
  • Timestamps: created_at and updated_at are TIMESTAMPTZ, set by the database.

The timestamps reach the API in three small steps, one per layer: the entity gets the two fields (as chrono's DateTime<Utc>), the response DTO gets them too, and the mapper copies them across. JSON shows them as createdAt and updatedAt. The entity also loses find_variant and find_variant_mut, which only the in-memory repository used.

Changes since step 243 filessrc/products/entity.rs, src/products/model.rs, src/products/mapper.rs

Apply the migration, so that the tables exist when the query macros check against them:

The repository

service/repo.rs is rewritten: the in-memory Catalog gives way to async functions that run SQL. Each takes a &mut PgConnection and runs its queries on it. That connection may be a plain one from the pool or an open transaction: the repository doesn't know or care, which is what lets the service combine several calls into one transaction. There's no struct and no trait: functions are enough when there's one implementation.

The rest of this section walks through it.

Compile-time-checked queries

sqlx::query!("SELECT ... WHERE id = $1", id) sends the SQL to the database while compiling. PostgreSQL parses it and reports the parameter and column types, and the macro generates a struct with one field per column. A misspelled column, a wrong parameter type or a missing table is a compile error, and a nullable column becomes an Option: image is Option<Vec<u8>>, name is a plain String. query_scalar! does the same for a query with one column, returning its value directly. Each query runs on &mut *conn, a fresh reborrow of the connection, so the function can use it again for the next query.

Reading products: four queries, put together in Rust

load fetches products with their variants and versions, and turns the rows into entities. One SELECT joining all four tables would return a row for every combination: a product with 3 variants and 2 versions comes back as several rows, each repeating the product's columns, including its image. Instead, load runs four simple queries, one per table, each with WHERE product_id = ANY($1) (an array of ids), and groups the rows in HashMaps keyed by product id. That's four queries for one product or for a hundred.

The join in the fourth query is the many-to-many relation in action: it turns each link's variant_id into the variant's SKU, which is how versions refer to variants.

Turning rows into entities is the repository's job, as turning entities into JSON is the mapper's. Each layer converts at its own boundary.

Filtering in SQL

find_ids finds the matching ids with one query, using a common pattern for optional filters: $1::text IS NULL OR .... A None becomes NULL, which switches its condition off, so one query serves every combination. The ::text casts tell PostgreSQL the parameters' types, which it couldn't infer from IS NULL alone. strpos(lower(name), lower($1)) > 0 is a case-insensitive "contains". ILIKE '%' || $1 || '%' would also work, but it would treat a % or _ typed by a user as a wildcard. The price condition is an EXISTS subquery: "this product has a variant in the range".

Saving variants and versions

save_variants makes a product's variants match the new list in two statements' worth of work:

  1. Delete the product's variants whose SKU isn't in the list (sku <> ALL($2)).
  2. Insert or update the rest, keyed by SKU, with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE, an "upsert". An updated row keeps its id and its image, as the in-memory repository did. The WHERE variants.product_id = EXCLUDED.product_id clause skips the update when the SKU belongs to another product. The statement then returns no row, which becomes DuplicateSku.

replace_versions deletes the product's versions, which deletes their links too, by cascade, and inserts the new ones, each with its links from one INSERT ... SELECT.

An upsert takes a number from the identity sequence before it finds the conflict, so ids can have gaps. Ids are unique, not consecutive; don't rely on more.

Duplicates as errors

Uniqueness across products is checked by the database: a concurrent request can't slip in between a check and an insert, because the UNIQUE constraint is enforced inside the database. conflict() recognizes a unique violation (is_unique_violation(), SQLSTATE 23505) and turns it into DuplicateName; every other database error stays a Database error.

The service owns the transactions

Creating a product is several repository calls: the product row, its variants, its versions. They must succeed or fail together, so the service runs them in one transaction:

  • self.pool.begin() starts a transaction and returns a Transaction, which dereferences to a PgConnection. So &mut tx can be passed wherever the repository wants a &mut PgConnection.
  • tx.commit() makes all of the statements permanent at once.
  • If any call fails, ? returns early, the Transaction is dropped without a commit, and SQLx rolls it back: no half-created product is ever visible. One of the tests checks exactly that.
  • load_one runs on the transaction too, so it sees the rows just written, before the commit.

Reads and single-statement writes don't need a transaction: they borrow a connection from the pool with self.pool.acquire(), and it goes back to the pool when it's dropped.

This is the explicit version of Spring's @Transactional. There, the transaction is bound to the current thread, and every repository call made on that thread joins it. Rust has no such ambient state, and async tasks move between threads anyway, so the transaction is a value that you pass to each call that should join it. You can see which calls run in a transaction by reading the code.

The rest of the service is unchanged in shape: validate still runs first, the events are logged as before, and every method keeps its signature. ProductService::new takes the pool instead of creating an empty catalog.

Database errors as API errors

CatalogError gets its last variant, Database(sqlx::Error): the connection dropped, a timeout, or a bug in a query. That's a 500 Internal Server Error. The client gets only the database failed, because the underlying message can name tables, columns and hosts, while the log gets the whole chain at error! level (Chapter 24).

Changes since step 241 filesrc/error.rs

Settings in layers, per environment

The service now has settings that differ between environments: the database URL, the size of the pool, the address to listen on. Until now, Config::from_env from step 19 read a few environment variables with defaults in the code. This step replaces it with layered settings, the Rust counterpart of Spring Boot's application.yaml plus profile files:

  1. config/base.yaml holds the defaults for every environment.
  2. config/{APP_ENV}.yaml overrides them for the active environment. APP_ENV plays the part of spring.profiles.active; without it, the profile is local.
  3. Environment variables named APP_<SECTION>__<KEY> override both: APP_DATABASE__URL sets database.url, like SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL in Spring. The double underscore separates the levels, because keys such as max_connections contain single ones.

Secrets stay out of the files. The local database's password is a development convenience and can be committed; the production URL is never in a file, so production must set APP_DATABASE__URL, and a missing one stops the service at start-up.

settings.rs builds the layers with the config crate and deserializes the merged result into Settings, a plain struct deriving Deserialize. That struct is the counterpart of a @ConfigurationProperties class. Everything is checked when it's loaded: a missing key, a number that isn't one, an address that doesn't parse, or a profile without a file stops the start-up with an error naming the key or the file. The profile file is required on purpose: a misspelled APP_ENV would otherwise quietly run with the base settings only. The module is named settings rather than config so it doesn't shadow the crate of that name.

As in step 19, the tests don't change the process environment (that's unsafe in edition 2024). from_sources takes the variables as a map, and config's Environment::source reads that map instead of the real environment.

Coming from Kotlin

What differs from Spring is the last step. There's no container that injects a property into whichever bean asks for it with @Value. main loads Settings once and passes each value to the constructor that needs it: the pool size to PgPoolOptions, the timeout to ReviewsClient. No other code reads configuration, so a test can build any part of the service with whatever values it likes.

Start-up

routes.rs doesn't change: the service kept its methods and their signatures, so the handlers can't tell that the storage changed. main loads the settings and logs the ones worth knowing, connects with the configured pool size, applies pending migrations, gives the pool to the service, serves, and closes the pool after the server has stopped. A pool keeps a set of open connections; concurrent requests each borrow one, so their queries run in parallel. Like the reviews client, it's an Arc inside and cheap to clone. src/config.rs is deleted, and SEED_FILE is gone along with seed.json: the data now survives restarts, so there's nothing to load at start-up.

Changes since step 241 filesrc/lib.rs

The reviews client's timeout comes from the settings too, so ReviewsClient::new takes it as a parameter:

Changes since step 241 filesrc/reviews.rs

sqlx::migrate!() embeds the files in migrations/ into the binary at compile time, so the deployed binary carries its schema with it. run(&pool) applies the ones this database hasn't run yet; when there are none, it's a quick check.

Run it

Two misconfigured starts first: the production profile without a database URL, and a profile that has no file. Both stop before connecting to anything:

With the container running, cargo run -q starts the service with the local profile; no environment variables are needed. The demo started from an empty shoes database and restarted the service halfway. At the end, it restarted once more with the production profile, the way a deployment would run it:

Things to notice:

  • After the restart the product is still there, with its image and versions.
  • RR-VOLT-42 kept id 2 through the update, while the new RR-VOLT-43 got id 4, not 3: the upsert of RR-VOLT-42 took 3 from the sequence.
  • version_variants shows the many-to-many relation: RR-VOLT-42 is in both versions, and version 2 has two variants.
  • Deleting the product left no variants or links behind.
  • The log's first line shows the profile and the values that came out of the layers: 127.0.0.1:3000 and 10 connections locally, 0.0.0.0:3000 and 20 connections in production, with the URL from APP_DATABASE__URL.

Tests against a real database

#[sqlx::test] replaces #[tokio::test]. For each test, it creates a new, empty database on the server named by DATABASE_URL, applies the migrations, passes a pool connected to it as the test's argument, and drops the database after the test passes. A failing test's database is kept, so you can inspect it. Tests run in parallel without seeing each other's data, against the same PostgreSQL that production uses. The catalog user created by the container is a superuser, so it may create databases.

The existing tests change only in how they get their app: app(pool). The concurrency test from Chapter 22 now exercises the database: the second insert waits for the first transaction to commit, then fails on the UNIQUE constraint. New tests cover what's specific to the database: a SKU taken by another product rolls back the whole insert, deleting cascades to all three other tables, the database sets the timestamps, and an update keeps a variant's image. The cascade test counts rows with plain SQL. SQLx 0.9 accepts only string literals (&'static str) as SQL, a guard against building queries from user input, so each count is a literal.

Changes since step 241 filetests/common/mod.rs

Building without a database (CI)

The compile-time checks need a database, which a CI runner or a colleague's laptop may not have. cargo sqlx prepare saves the type information of every query into a .sqlx/ directory. Commit it, and builds that can't reach a database use it instead. When DATABASE_URL isn't set, SQLx uses .sqlx/ automatically; SQLX_OFFLINE=true forces it even when the variable is set.

Production notes

  • Pool size. PostgreSQL allows 100 connections by default, shared by every instance of every service. Ten per instance, as here, is a reasonable start. Size the pool from measurements, not guesses.
  • Credentials. The catalog/catalog password is for local development only. In production, the platform sets APP_DATABASE__URL from a secret store, and enable a TLS feature of sqlx (for example tls-rustls) when the database isn't on the same host.
  • Files in the database. BYTEA is simple and transactional: an image is deleted with its product, and backed up with everything else. It doesn't scale to large files or many of them: every listing here loads every image, and backups grow with the images. The usual next step is object storage (S3 or a compatible store such as MinIO), with only the object's key in the row, and listings that don't select the binary columns at all.
  • Settings. Only the files for environments you actually run belong in config/, and only values that aren't secret. Log the settings at start-up, as main does, but never the database URL: it contains the password.
  • Migrations in production are the subject of Chapter 26.
  • Upgrading to PostgreSQL 19 (generally available from November 19, 2026). Because the data directory is version-specific, a postgres:19 container on the same volume would initialize a new, empty cluster next to the old one. Instead, dump and restore:

pg_dumpall dumps every database on the server, shoes included, plus roles; pg_dump would dump only one.

Practice

  1. Make GET /products cheaper: write a query for listings that doesn't select the image columns, and use octet_length(image) to fill in the size. The response only needs the type and size, but the entity's Image always holds the bytes: which layer's types have to change?
    Solution

    The entity is what changes. Product.image and Variant.image become an ImageInfo (type and size) instead of an Image with its bytes. Image stays for uploads and downloads. load selects octet_length(image) AS image_size instead of image. No response from a loaded product ever needs the bytes, so GET /products/{id} and the responses to create and update get cheaper too, not only listings. The bytes are read only by product_image and variant_image.

    Which layer's types change? The entity layer's. The DTOs don't change: ImageResponse already has just contentType and size, so clients see the same JSON. The mapper converts from &ImageInfo instead of &Image, and the repository builds an ImageInfo from the size column. octet_length returns an integer, so SQLx hands it over as an Option<i32>. It's None when there's no image, because SQLx treats every computed column as nullable.

    Readers who changed a query must run cargo sqlx prepare -- --all-targets again to update .sqlx/ for offline builds.

  2. Add optimistic concurrency to PUT /products/{id}: the client sends the updatedAt it last saw in an If-Unmodified-Since-style header, and the UPDATE adds AND updated_at = $5. No row then means "not found" or "changed by someone else"; tell them apart and return 404 or 412 Precondition Failed.
    Solution

    The client sends back updatedAt exactly as the API returned it, for example If-Unmodified-Since: 2026-11-15T18:31:02.123456Z. The real header's format, an HTTP date, has only whole seconds, too coarse to compare with a timestamp that has microseconds. The header is optional: without it, $5 is NULL and switches the condition off, the same pattern find_ids uses. When no row was updated, the service checks whether the product exists, inside the same transaction. If it does, someone else changed it: 412. If not: 404. A header that doesn't parse is a 400.

    The check and the write are one statement, so two clients holding the same updatedAt can't both succeed. The second UPDATE waits for the first one's row lock, then finds a new updated_at and matches no row. The extra SELECT runs only on the failure path.

    Readers who changed a query must run cargo sqlx prepare -- --all-targets again to update .sqlx/ for offline builds.

  3. Add pagination to GET /products with LIMIT and OFFSET in list's query, and write a test with 25 products.
    Solution

    The page parameters go into the query-string type, ProductFilter, as limit and offset. They can't be a second Query struct, because both would reject each other's fields with deny_unknown_fields. They're u32, so ?limit=-1 is a 400 from axum, not a database error. The service picks the default page size (20) and the maximum (100), and the repository only adds LIMIT $5 OFFSET $6. The values are passed as i64, because PostgreSQL has no unsigned integers.

    Only find_ids needs paging: load then fetches just that page's products, variants and versions. Paging the ids is also what makes it correct. A LIMIT on a query that joins variants would count rows, not products. With OFFSET, PostgreSQL still reads and discards the rows it skips, so deep pages get slower. For large tables, keyset pagination (WHERE p.id > $last ORDER BY p.id LIMIT n) avoids that.

    Readers who changed a query must run cargo sqlx prepare -- --all-targets again to update .sqlx/ for offline builds.

  4. Make delete return the deleted product, as the in-memory version did: load it and delete it in one transaction in the service, or use DELETE ... RETURNING in the repository. Which is simpler here, and why does the first need a transaction?
    Solution

    This solution loads and deletes in one transaction in the service, reusing load_one and delete_product. Its first statement is SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, which locks the product's row. The route doesn't change: it still answers 204 and ignores the product. A test in service.rs checks that the returned product, variants included, is the one that was created.

    Which is simpler? The transaction, here. DELETE FROM products ... RETURNING * returns only the deleted products row. The variants, versions and links go by ON DELETE CASCADE, and their rows aren't returned. Getting the whole product that way would take more DELETE ... RETURNING statements in a CTE, plus new code to assemble the rows. Loading first reuses the code that already builds a Product.

    Why a transaction? Two separate statements leave a gap. Another request could update the product between the load and the delete, and the service would return a product that isn't the one it deleted. In a transaction, the two statements form a single unit, and the lock taken by FOR UPDATE lasts until the commit, so a concurrent update waits until the delete is done. The lock is needed too: at PostgreSQL's default isolation level, READ COMMITTED, a plain SELECT in a transaction doesn't stop other writers.

    Readers who changed a query must run cargo sqlx prepare -- --all-targets again to update .sqlx/ for offline builds.

  5. Add a test profile (config/test.yaml) with a smaller pool and a reviews timeout of 500 ms, and a settings test for it. Then add a log_format setting (text or json) that replaces the LOG_FORMAT variable from Chapter 24. What does init_tracing need, given that it runs before the settings are loaded?
    Solution

    The test profile overrides only what differs from base.yaml. Like production, it has no database URL: the CI job sets APP_DATABASE__URL. log_format is an enum, so serde rejects anything but text and json at start-up, naming the key. The base file says text, production says json, and APP_LOG_FORMAT overrides both, like any other key.

    What does init_tracing need? The format, as a parameter. And because the format now comes from the settings, main has to load the settings first and call init_tracing(settings.log_format) after. Nothing is lost by that. Loading the settings logs nothing, and if it fails, main returns the error and Rust prints it to stderr, as the last run shows. RUST_LOG stays an environment variable, because it's the convention every Rust tool follows.

Next · Chapter 26Changing the Schema
Chapter 26

Changing the Schema

Add a column to a table that already holds data: write and apply a migration, update the code the compiler points at, test the migration itself, and learn the rules that keep schema changes safe in production.

The shop wants to know how many pairs of each variant are in stock. That's a new column on a table that already holds data, in a database that the running service uses. This chapter makes the change the way it's done in practice: a new migration, code changes guided by the compiler, a test of the migration itself, and a deployment that doesn't break what's running.

How migrations work in this project

Everything in this chapter builds on the setup from Chapter 25:

  • Files. Each migration is a SQL file in migrations/, named <version>_<description>.sql. The version is a number, by default the creation time as YYYYMMDDhhmmss, and migrations run in version order.
  • Bookkeeping. Each database has a _sqlx_migrations table with one row per applied migration: its version, description, a checksum of the file, and whether it succeeded. Running migrations applies only the files without a row.
  • Checksums. If an applied file changes later, its checksum no longer matches, and SQLx refuses to run any migration, both from the command line and at the service's start-up. A migration is a record of what was done to every database, so editing it would leave databases that ran the old version different from new ones.
  • Transactions. Each migration runs in its own transaction, so one that fails halfway leaves nothing behind. PostgreSQL can roll back CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE too, which not every database can.
  • Two ways to apply. cargo sqlx migrate run applies pending migrations from the command line. The service calls sqlx::migrate!().run(&pool) at start-up, with the files embedded in the binary at compile time. Before migrating, SQLx takes a PostgreSQL advisory lock, so several instances starting at once don't apply the same migration twice.
  • Tests. #[sqlx::test] applies all migrations to each fresh test database, so every test run checks that the whole chain works from an empty database.
  • Compile-time checks. The query! macros check SQL against the database in DATABASE_URL, or against .sqlx/ offline. Both have to follow the schema.

The change: a stock count per variant

Create the migration with the command-line tool. It names the file with the current time:

The project's file is 20261115120000_add_variant_stock.sql; any version greater than the previous one works. It holds one statement:

The table already has rows, and a NOT NULL column must have a value in every one of them. DEFAULT 0 provides it: existing variants get 0, and an INSERT that doesn't mention stock gets 0 too. Since PostgreSQL 11, adding a column with a constant default doesn't rewrite the table: the default is stored once and filled in when rows are read. The CHECK keeps the count from going negative; adding it makes PostgreSQL read the existing rows once to verify them, which is quick for this table.

Without the default, the statement would fail on a table with rows: column "stock" of relation "variants" contains null values. That's the first rule of schema changes: think about the rows that are already there.

Apply it, then change the code

The order matters, because the queries are checked against the database while compiling. If the code mentions stock before the database has the column, the build fails, with the database's own message:

So apply the migration to the development database first:

Then change the code, layer by layer. A new field goes all the way through: schema, entity, repository, service rules, DTOs and mapper.

  • Entity. Variant and NewVariant get stock: i32, as PostgreSQL's INTEGER maps to i32.
  • Repository. The upsert writes stock, and load reads it. Forgetting the SELECT isn't possible: the compiler reports the missing field where Variant is built from the row.
  • Validation. A negative stock is a 422 with its own message, before the database's CHECK would turn it into a 500.
  • DTOs. VariantRequest gets the field with #[serde(default)], so a client that doesn't know about stock yet can still create and update products. A new field in a request should be optional, for the same reason the column has a default. VariantResponse gets it too.
  • Mapper. Two lines, one per direction. Because the entity and the DTOs are separate types, the compiler points at both: a struct literal that doesn't set every field doesn't compile.
Changes since step 255 filessrc/products/entity.rs, src/products/service/repo.rs, src/products/validate.rs, src/products/model.rs, src/products/mapper.rs

Finally, refresh the offline query data, so builds without a database (CI) know the new queries:

Test the migration with data

Ordinary tests start from an empty database with all migrations applied, so they never see a row that existed before the change. tests/migrations.rs does. #[sqlx::test(migrations = false)] gives it an empty database, and the test applies the migrations itself, in two steps. run_to applies them up to the old schema; the test inserts a variant with plain SQL; run applies the rest. The variant must come back with a stock of 0; the test reads it through ProductService, the crate's public way in, because the repository is private. A second test checks what _sqlx_migrations records, and that running the migrations again does nothing.

Changes since step 251 filetests/api.rs

Run it

The demo starts from a database in the state Chapter 25 left it in: the first migration applied, and a product with two variants inserted. migrate info lists each migration and whether this database has it. The second half edits the first, already applied migration (adding only a comment), to show what SQLx thinks of that, then restores the file:

With the migration applied, the service starts as usual. The existing variants have a stock of 0; a PUT sets real numbers, and a negative one is refused:

The workflow, step by step

  1. cargo sqlx migrate add <description>, then write the SQL. Consider the existing rows: defaults for new NOT NULL columns, and what happens to data that doesn't fit a new constraint.
  2. cargo sqlx migrate run against your development database.
  3. Change the code: types, queries, JSON, validation. The query macros point at every query that no longer matches the schema.
  4. cargo sqlx prepare -- --all-targets, so .sqlx/ matches the new queries.
  5. cargo test: every test database gets all migrations, from empty. For a change that touches existing data, add a test that migrates a database with data in it, as above.
  6. Commit the migration, the code and .sqlx/ together.
  7. Deploy. The new binary applies the migration when it starts, before it accepts requests, or a separate deployment step runs sqlx migrate run first (see the last section).

Rules that keep schema changes safe

  • Never edit an applied migration. Its checksum no longer matches, and every database that ran it refuses further migrations, as the demo showed. Write a new migration instead. The one exception is a migration that only exists on your machine: change it, and run cargo sqlx database reset to drop and recreate your local database.
  • Fix forward. cargo sqlx migrate add -r creates a pair of files, .up.sql and .down.sql, and cargo sqlx migrate revert runs the latest down migration. That's useful in development. In production, a down migration that drops a column also drops the data written since, so a mistake is usually corrected by another forward migration.
  • Old and new code run at the same time. During a rolling deployment, some instances still run the previous version while the migration has already been applied. Each migration must therefore work with the code before it and the code after it. That's why changes are split into expand and contract steps:
    • Expand: add things the old code doesn't notice, such as a new table, or a column that is nullable or has a default (like stock). Deploy.
    • Deploy code that uses them.
    • Contract: remove what the new code no longer uses, in a later release.
  • A rename takes several releases. ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN breaks every running instance that uses the old name. Instead: add the new column, write to both, copy the existing data, switch reads to the new column, stop writing the old one, and finally drop it.
  • Know which statements lock or scan. Many ALTER TABLE forms lock the table against reads and writes while they run. Adding a CHECK or FOREIGN KEY constraint to existing data scans the whole table; on a big table, add it as NOT VALID (which checks only new rows) and run ALTER TABLE ... VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a later migration, which scans without blocking writes. CREATE INDEX blocks writes while it builds; CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY doesn't, but it can't run inside a transaction, so its migration must start with the line -- no-transaction, which tells SQLx to run that file without one. SET lock_timeout = '5s'; at the top of a migration makes it fail fast instead of queueing behind a long-running query while every other query queues behind it.
  • Change data in batches. An UPDATE of millions of rows in one transaction holds its locks until it commits. Large backfills run in batches, often from a separate job rather than a migration.

Running migrations in deployment

At start-up (this project)A separate step before the rollout
Howsqlx::migrate!().run(&pool) in mainsqlx migrate run in a CI/CD job, a Kubernetes Job, or an init container
Goodnothing extra to deploy; schema and code can't get out of stepruns once; a failed migration stops the rollout before any new instance starts; the service's database user doesn't need the right to change the schema
Watch outa slow migration delays start-up and can trip health checks; every instance tries (the advisory lock makes the others wait)one more thing to deploy; the migration must still work with the old code, which keeps running until the rollout

Starting with migrations at start-up and moving them into a separate step once the service runs as several instances, or once migrations get slow, is a common path. Either way, the rules above apply.

Coming from Kotlin

This is Flyway's model: versioned SQL files, a history table with checksums, and "validate on migrate" that rejects edited migrations. sqlx migrate info corresponds to flyway info, and running migrate!().run() in main corresponds to Spring Boot running Flyway at start-up.

Practice

  1. Add a discontinued flag to products with a new migration (BOOLEAN NOT NULL DEFAULT false), accept it in the JSON, and make GET /products skip discontinued products unless ?includeDiscontinued=true is given. Write a migration test like existing_variants_get_a_stock_of_zero.
    Solution

    The flag goes all the way through, like stock did: a migration with a default for the existing rows, the entity, the repository's queries, the DTOs (optional in requests, always in responses) and the mapper. The list filter gets one more condition and one more query parameter.

    $5 is a plain bool, so ($5 OR NOT p.discontinued) is true for every row when the client asks for discontinued products, and keeps only the current ones otherwise. load doesn't filter, so GET /products/{id} still finds a discontinued product.

    The migration test follows existing_variants_get_a_stock_of_zero: migrate up to the version before the flag, insert a product with plain SQL, apply the rest, and read it back through ProductService. sqlx_records_every_applied_migration lists every version, so it gets the new one too. An API test covers the query parameter.

    A PUT replaces the whole product, so a client that leaves discontinued out of a PUT sets it back to false, the same as stock. That's consistent with the replace semantics; a client that wants to keep the flag sends it.

  2. Rename variants.description to variants.label the safe way, as a sequence of migrations and code changes, each of which could be deployed on its own while the previous version is still running. Write down which release contains which change.
    Solution

    Four releases. Each one is deployed only when the previous one runs everywhere, and each one works with the schema before its migration (the old instances still run) and after it:

    1. Release 1, expand. Migration: add label, nullable. Code: write the description to both columns; still read description.
    2. Release 2, backfill and switch reads. Migration: copy description into label, then make label NOT NULL DEFAULT ''. Code: read label; still write both.
    3. Release 3, stop writing the old column. No migration. Code: write only label.
    4. Release 4, contract. Migration: drop description. No code change.

    The JSON field stays description: the DTOs are a contract with clients, separate from the table, and only the mapper connects the two. Renaming the JSON field would be a separate change, with its own transition for clients.

    Release 1. The new column is invisible to release 0, which doesn't name it. Release 1 sends the same parameter, $3, to both columns.

    Release 2. Its migration runs when only release 1 instances are left, and they write both columns, so description is right in every row. label can be NULL (rows from before release 1) or stale (a release 0 instance updated a row while release 1 was rolling out), so the backfill copies every row where the two differ, not only the NULLs. After SET NOT NULL, SQLx types row.label as String instead of Option<String>, so the entity field can become label: String. The code still writes description, because release 1 instances read it until the rollout ends.

    Release 3. Only the upsert changes. Inserts that leave out description still work because the column has DEFAULT ''; without a default, this release would need a migration that drops its NOT NULL first.

    Release 4. Release 3 no longer names description, so dropping it breaks nothing that runs. No query changes, so .sqlx/ stays the same; only the list of versions in the test grows.

    Releases 1 to 3 change queries, so each one runs cargo sqlx migrate run and then cargo sqlx prepare -- --all-targets before it's committed. Each release passes cargo test, and the tests of each release's code also pass on the schema of the next release, which is the situation during a rollout. Skipping release 3 fails at once: release 2's code doesn't compile against the release 4 schema (column "description" of relation "variants" does not exist), and a running release 2 instance would fail every write the same way.

  3. Add an index on lower(products.brand) for the brand filter with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, in a migration that starts with -- no-transaction. Use EXPLAIN in psql to see whether the filter query uses it with a few thousand products.
    Solution

    The repository filters with lower(p.brand) = lower($2), so the index is on the expression lower(brand). -- no-transaction has to be the file's first line.

    No query changes, so .sqlx/ stays as it is. cargo test passes: #[sqlx::test] applies the no-transaction migration to every test database like the others. To look at plans, a scratch database gets the schema before the index and 5,000 products, 100 of them from Stride:

    SQLx sends find_ids as a prepared statement with parameters, so the fair test is the same: PREPARE the repository's exact SQL and EXPLAIN an EXECUTE of it, filtering by brand only.

    Before the migration, PostgreSQL reads all 5,000 rows and throws away 4,900. After it, a bitmap index scan on products_lower_brand_idx finds the 100 rows directly. That works for two reasons. The index expression lower(brand) is exactly the expression in the WHERE clause. And for this execution PostgreSQL makes a custom plan with the parameter values known: $2::text IS NULL is false, so the OR reduces to lower(brand) = 'stride', which the index can answer.

    The other side of both reasons:

    A generic plan, made without knowing the parameters, can't use the index: ($2 IS NULL OR lower(brand) = lower($2)) might be true for every row, so the condition becomes a filter on a full scan. PostgreSQL starts each prepared statement with custom plans and only switches to the generic plan if it isn't estimated to be more expensive. Here it's far more expensive (cost 47,849 against 57), so the custom plan stays: after seven EXECUTEs, EXPLAIN EXECUTE still showed the bitmap index scan. And brand = 'Stride' doesn't match the expression lower(brand), so that query doesn't use the index either.

  4. Make a migration fail on purpose (for example, add a CHECK (stock > 0) to a table that has zero stocks), run it, and look at _sqlx_migrations and the table afterwards. What did the transaction protect you from?
    Solution

    The migration has two statements, so a half-applied state is possible: the first adds a column, the second adds a constraint that the existing rows break. It runs on a scratch database that has the schema up to 0002 and two variants inserted before it, so both have a stock of 0.

    Nothing of the migration is left. _sqlx_migrations has no row for it (SQLx writes that row in the same transaction), reserved isn't in the table, the constraint isn't there, and the data is unchanged. migrate info still lists it as pending. A service that runs migrations at start-up would refuse to start with this binary, while the instances already running keep working on the unchanged schema.

    The transaction protected against a half-applied migration: a database with the reserved column but without the constraint and without a row in _sqlx_migrations. That state matches neither the old schema nor the new one. The next migrate run would fail on column "reserved" of relation "variants" already exists before it even got to the constraint, and someone would have to repair the database by hand. Because the migration was never applied anywhere, you're allowed to fix the file itself: fix the data first (or use NOT VALID), or delete the file.

    For comparison, the same file with -- no-transaction as its first line, on a second scratch database prepared the same way:

    The column wasn't left behind here either, because SQLx sends the file to PostgreSQL as one query string, and PostgreSQL runs a string of several statements as one implicit transaction. That's also why a -- no-transaction file should hold a single statement: with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY after another statement, the run failed with CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY cannot run inside a transaction block. So you can't count on the implicit transaction. Feeding the original file to psql, which sends one statement at a time with autocommit, does leave reserved behind, and a second run fails with column "reserved" of relation "variants" already exists.
