Chapter 27

Authentication with a Bearer Token

How axum handles authentication and authorization with middleware, extractors and request extensions, and a first check for the service: every request must carry a bearer token.

Anyone who can reach the service can change the catalog. This chapter makes every request say who sent it, in the form HTTP APIs use most: a bearer token in the Authorization header. The rule is deliberately simple. A token must be present and exactly 10 characters long, so the chapter can concentrate on where the check goes and how axum runs it. Replacing the rule with real token verification later changes one function.

Authentication and authorization

  • Authentication answers who is calling? A request without valid credentials gets 401 Unauthorized. Despite the name, 401 means "not authenticated". The response carries a WWW-Authenticate header naming the scheme the server expects.
  • Authorization answers may this caller do this? A known caller who isn't allowed gets 403 Forbidden; trying again with the same credentials won't help.

A bearer token (RFC 6750) grants access to whoever holds, or "bears", it. The client sends it as Authorization: Bearer <token>. The server doesn't care how the client got it: usually from an identity provider such as Keycloak, Auth0 or Microsoft Entra ID, as a signed JWT, and sometimes as an opaque API key. Because anyone who holds the token gets in, it only travels over HTTPS and never goes into logs.

How axum handles it

axum has no authentication module, no annotations and no security configuration. It has general building blocks, and authentication is built from them:

Building blockWhat it isGood for
Middleware, e.g. axum::middleware::from_fnan async fn that gets the request and Next; it either returns a response itself or calls next.run(request) to continue to the handlerone rule for many routes: "every request needs a valid token"
An extractor: a type that implements FromRequestPartsa handler argument, like Path or Json; if extraction fails, its rejection is the response and the handler doesn't runrequirements of one handler, documented by its signature: "this handler needs an admin"
Request extensionsa map from type to value attached to each request: request.extensions_mut().insert(caller), read in a handler with an Extension<Caller> argumenthanding the authenticated caller from the middleware to the handlers
Any tower layermiddleware from the tower ecosystem, such as tower-http's ValidateRequestHeaderLayerreusing existing middleware

A typical service combines them. Middleware authenticates every request and stores the caller in the extensions; handlers, or extractors that read the stored caller, authorize. Two variants are worth knowing: from_fn_with_state is for middleware that needs the application state, such as a key to verify signatures or a pool to look up API keys, and middleware::from_extractor::<T>() runs an extractor as middleware for a whole group of routes.

A router takes a middleware layer in one of two ways:

  • Router::layer wraps the whole router, including the fallback for unknown paths. An authentication middleware added this way answers GET /no-such-path with 401.
  • Router::route_layer wraps only the routes added so far, and runs only when one of them matches, so an unknown path is still 404. axum's documentation recommends it for middleware that returns early, such as authentication.

Layers wrap each other, so the one added last is the outermost and sees the request first. tower-http has a ready-made ValidateRequestHeaderLayer::bearer("..."), which compares the header with one fixed token, but it has been deprecated since tower-http 0.6.7 as "too basic to be useful in real applications". ValidateRequestHeaderLayer::custom takes your own check instead, which a from_fn middleware does with less ceremony.

Coming from Kotlin

In Spring Security, the servlet filters of a SecurityFilterChain authenticate before any controller runs: that's the middleware. @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on a method corresponds to an extractor in the handler's signature. SecurityContextHolder keeps the caller in a thread-local; axum puts it in the request's extensions instead, because an async request can move between threads, and the hand-over stays visible in the code.

Where the check goes

Authentication belongs to the HTTP layer, in front of the routes, not to ProductService: the service knows nothing about headers, and an unauthenticated request should never reach it. The check gets a module of its own next to products/, because it will apply to every feature the service gets. Its errors get their own type, AuthError, rather than new CatalogError variants, since the catalog never produces them.

Project step 27: require a bearer token

This step

Every request to a product route must carry Authorization: Bearer <token> with a 10-character token; anything else gets 401 with a JSON error. The handlers, the service and the repository don't change.

  • AuthError follows the pattern of CatalogError: an enum of reasons, Display for the message, and IntoResponse for the response, which is 401 with the WWW-Authenticate: Bearer challenge and the JSON error body the other endpoints use. Its debug event logs the reason, never the token.
  • bearer_token holds the whole rule, as a plain function from a header value to a token, so the unit tests check it without any HTTP. The scheme name is case-insensitive (RFC 9110), so bearer works too. HeaderValue::to_str accepts only visible ASCII, so here len(), which counts bytes, also counts characters.
  • require_bearer_token is the middleware. It takes the request and Next, the rest of the stack: any inner layers, then the handler. ? on the check returns the AuthError, which axum turns into the 401. Otherwise next.run(request).await passes the request on and returns the handler's response. The return type Result<Response, AuthError> works because both sides implement IntoResponse.

In app(), route_layer puts the middleware around the product routes, inside the trace layer. The trace layer is added after it, so it's the outermost, and refused requests still get a span and a status=401 event:

A request now passes through the trace layer, then the token check, then the handler. A request that fails the check never reaches the handler, so no extractor runs and no database connection is taken.

Watch out

A length check is not security: any 10 characters get in. It stands in for real verification, and the messages that say exactly why a token was refused are for development. A production service answers every bad token the same way, so the messages don't help an attacker. Real verification usually means checking a JWT's signature, issuer, audience and expiry, for example with the jsonwebtoken crate and the identity provider's public keys. That replaces the length check in bearer_token, and the keys reach the middleware through from_fn_with_state. If you compare a token with a stored secret, compare in constant time (the subtle crate), so the response time doesn't reveal how many leading characters matched.

Tests

The existing API tests all send their requests through common::send, so one header there keeps them passing; they now run as an authenticated client:

tests/auth.rs builds its requests by hand, with and without the header. It checks the three kinds of refusal, a request that gets through, and the 404 for an unknown path. The unit tests in auth.rs cover the rule itself.

Run it

Start the service with debug logging for the crate, so the log shows why each request was refused:

Each refused request leaves two events in the log: the debug event from AuthError with the reason, and the trace layer's event with status=401. The unknown path got its 404 without a token, because route_layer only runs the check for matching routes.

Practice

  1. Make reads public: only POST, PUT and DELETE need a token. Split the product routes into a public and a protected router and merge them, with route_layer only on the protected one. Why is this clearer than checking request.method() inside the middleware?
    Solution

    The products module now builds two routers: the public one with the GET routes, and the protected one with the writes and the route_layer. Where both have the same path, merge combines their method routers, so GET /products/1 runs without the middleware and DELETE /products/1 with it. app() keeps only the trace layer.

    In the tests, the 401 cases now send DELETE, because GET no longer needs a token. With a valid token, DELETE /products/1 reaches the handler, which answers 404. A new test reads without a token.

    The router already dispatches on method and path, so the split puts the rule where the routes are declared: routes.rs shows which endpoints are protected, and the middleware keeps one job, checking the token. A method check inside the middleware is a second copy of the routing. It knows nothing about paths: a public POST /products/search or a private GET would need path matching there too. It is also easy to get subtly wrong for HEAD, PATCH or OPTIONS. The price of the split: whoever adds a write route must put it in the protected router, while a method check would protect a new POST automatically.

  2. Add authorization: let the middleware store the caller in the request's extensions (struct Caller { token: String }), and allow DELETE /products/{id} only for tokens that start with admin-; any other caller gets 403 Forbidden with the usual JSON error. Which layer should make that decision, and why 403 rather than 401?
    Solution

    The middleware copies the token out of the header and inserts a Caller into the request's extensions. It has to copy: the &str borrows from the request, which is then moved into next.run. delete_product takes the caller with Extension<Caller>. For a non-admin, it returns the new CatalogError::Forbidden, which becomes 403 with the usual JSON body.

    The tests' TOKEN becomes an admin token, so the delete tests in tests/api.rs still pass. The new test sends a non-admin token by hand.

    Which layer: the handler (or the service), not the middleware. Authentication is the same for every route, so it fits a layer. Authorization depends on the operation, and later on the data (a seller may delete only their own products), and only the handler and the service know those. Here the handler checks before it calls the service, like @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") on a Spring controller method. If other entry points (a CLI, a queue consumer) could delete too, the check would move into ProductService::delete, which would then take the caller. If a route ever reached delete_product without the middleware, Extension<Caller> would reject the request with 500, because that is a server bug.

    403, not 401: 401 means the server doesn't know who you are. The WWW-Authenticate header says how to authenticate, and a retry with valid credentials can succeed. 403 means the server knows who you are and the answer is no. The same token will always be refused, so there's no challenge header.

  3. Replace the middleware with an extractor: implement FromRequestParts for Caller, reusing bearer_token, with AuthError as its rejection, and take it as an argument in create_product. What happens to a handler that forgets the argument, and when would you still choose an extractor?
    Solution

    Caller becomes an extractor. from_request_parts reads the header with bearer_token, and AuthError is the rejection, so a bad token still gets 401 with WWW-Authenticate and the JSON body. axum 0.8 uses native async fn in traits, so no #[async_trait] is needed. The middleware and its route_layer are gone. Caller must come before Json in the arguments anyway, because only the last extractor may consume the body. So a request without a token is rejected before its body is read.

    The 401 tests now send POST /products. The valid-token test creates a product through common::call, which sends TOKEN. The new test shows a handler without a Caller.

    A handler that forgets the argument still compiles, and it runs for everyone. Here every route except POST /products is now public, PUT and DELETE included. Protection becomes opt-in for each handler, and forgetting it fails silently. With the middleware, the decision is made once, for a whole router.

    Choose an extractor when the handler needs the caller anyway, for example to record who created a product or to check ownership. It also fits when only a few endpoints need authentication, or for a requirement on one handler, such as an Admin extractor that rejects with 403. Like @PreAuthorize, it makes the requirement visible in the signature. A common mix is middleware that authenticates every route and stores the Caller in the extensions, plus handlers that take it as an argument when they need it.

Next · Appendix ASingle-Threaded Shared Ownership: Rc, Weak, Cell & RefCell
AppendicesRarely Needed in Services
Appendix A

Single-Threaded Shared Ownership: Rc, Weak, Cell & RefCell

Shared ownership and mutation through shared references, without threads. Useful for graphs, interpreters and GUI code; a multithreaded service uses Arc and Mutex instead (Chapter 16), because Rc is neither Send nor Sync and RefCell isn't Sync.

Rc<T> and Weak<T>: shared ownership

Rc<T> (reference counted) lets several owners share one immutable value; it's freed when the last Rc is dropped. Rc::clone only bumps a counter. Cycles of Rc would never be freed, so back-pointers use Weak<T>, which doesn't keep the value alive and must be upgrade()d to an Option<Rc<T>> before use. Rc is single-threaded; its atomic sibling is Arc (Chapter 16).

Interior mutability: Cell and RefCell

Sometimes a value must be mutated through a shared reference: a cache inside a &self method, a counter shared by several owners. Interior mutability types move the borrow check from compile time to run time:

  • Cell<T>: get/set/replace by value. No references into it are ever handed out, so it's always safe and has zero overhead. Best for small Copy types.
  • RefCell<T>: borrow() and borrow_mut() return guards and enforce the aliasing rule at run time: violating it panics (or returns Err with try_borrow_mut).

Neither is thread-safe (!Sync); the multi-threaded equivalents are atomics, Mutex and RwLock.

Rc<RefCell<T>>: shared, mutable state

Combining them gives several owners that can all mutate one value: the single-threaded version of Arc<Mutex<T>>. It's the natural fit for callbacks and observer-style designs.

Design note

Rc<RefCell<T>> everywhere is a smell: it recreates a garbage-collected object graph with runtime borrow panics. Prefer clear ownership (a tree owns its nodes, an arena or Vec holds them and you pass indices) and reach for shared mutability only at the edges.

Practice

  1. Build a doubly linked list with Rc<RefCell<Node>> forward links and Weak back links, with push_back and a to_vec() that walks forward. Notice how much harder this is than in C, and why.
    Solution

    Each node is an Rc<RefCell<Node>>: Rc because two places point at it (the previous node's next and, for the last node, the list's tail), RefCell because we must change its links through those shared pointers. The back link is Weak, so a pair of neighbours doesn't keep each other alive.

    Why it's harder than in C. In C a node is two raw pointers and you rewire them freely; nothing checks that prev still points to a live node, or that a node is freed exactly once. Rust's single-owner model has no place for a node that is pointed to from both sides, so you have to spell out the ownership: Rc for the shared forward links, Weak for the back links (two strong links would form a cycle and leak), and RefCell to mutate through them, with borrow(), borrow_mut() and upgrade() on every access. The C version is shorter but trusts you; this one can't dangle or double-free, and pays for that with reference counts and runtime borrow checks. (std::collections::LinkedList uses raw pointers and unsafe inside for exactly this reason.)

  2. Write a memoized Fibonacci struct whose fn get(&self, n: u64) -> u64 stores results in a RefCell<HashMap<u64, u64>>.
    Solution

    get takes &self, so the cache is behind a RefCell. The one trap: the borrow() for the lookup must end before the recursive calls, because they call borrow_mut() to insert. Holding it across the recursion compiles, then panics with RefCell already borrowed.

Next · Appendix BMore Concurrency: Scoped Threads, Channels & Condition Variables
Appendix B

More Concurrency: Scoped Threads, Channels & Condition Variables

Threads that borrow, message passing with std channels, and a blocking queue. In a Tokio service, tasks and tokio::sync channels do these jobs (Chapter 21); the std versions matter for CPU-parallel batch work and libraries.

Scoped threads

thread::scope guarantees that every thread spawned inside it is joined before the scope returns, so those threads may borrow local data, including disjoint &mut slices. This is the simplest way to parallelize work over a local buffer.

Channels

mpsc::channel() creates an unbounded multi-producer, single-consumer queue; clone the Sender for each producer. Iterating the Receiver ends when every sender has been dropped. mpsc::sync_channel(n) is bounded: send blocks while the buffer is full, which gives you backpressure.

Condition variables: a blocking bounded queue

Condvar lets a thread sleep until another thread signals that a condition may have changed. wait_while re-checks the predicate in a loop, which handles spurious wakeups. Here's the classic producer/consumer buffer from an operating systems course, with the lock owning the queue:

Note

Also in std::sync: Barrier (wait until N threads arrive), OnceLock (initialize once, from any thread), and thread::available_parallelism() to size a worker pool. Appendix E builds a complete thread pool.

Practice

  1. Count word frequencies of a large text in parallel without copying it: split it into N chunks with thread::scope, let each thread borrow its chunk and build its own HashMap, and merge the maps at the end (no Mutex needed).
    Solution

    split_chunks cuts the text into &str slices at whitespace, so no word is split and nothing is copied. Each scoped thread borrows its slice and returns its own HashMap<&str, usize>, whose keys also borrow from the text. The maps are merged on the main thread after the scope has joined every thread, so no thread ever shares a map and there's no Mutex.

  2. Add fn pop_timeout(&self, d: Duration) -> Option<T> to the bounded queue using Condvar::wait_timeout_while, and test it with a producer that is slower than the timeout.
    Solution

    pop_timeout is pop with wait_timeout_while in place of wait_while. It returns the guard plus a WaitTimeoutResult. We don't need the result: if the queue is still empty, we timed out, and pop_front()? returns None. The producer pushes every 150 ms and the consumer waits 100 ms at a time, so every item comes after one timeout.

Next · Appendix CAsync Rust, From the Standard Library Up
Appendix C

Async Rust, From the Standard Library Up

Futures are lazy state machines driven by an executor. The standard library defines the protocol but ships no runtime, so we build a small one to see every moving part. You don't need this to use Tokio (Chapter 21): it explains what happens underneath.

The model

  • An async fn doesn't run when called. It returns a value implementing Future<Output = T>: a compiler-generated state machine holding the function's locals across .await points.
  • An executor drives a future by calling poll. poll returns Poll::Ready(value) or Poll::Pending.
  • When a future returns Pending, it first stores the Waker from the Context. When the awaited thing (a socket, a timer) becomes ready, someone calls waker.wake(), and the executor polls again.
  • .await inside an async function means "poll this inner future; if it's pending, return Pending myself".

The standard library provides Future, Poll, Context, Waker, the Wake trait, Pin, pin!, poll_fn and the async/await syntax. It does not provide an executor, async I/O or timers: those come from runtimes such as Tokio (Chapter 21). Building a tiny executor with std alone is the best way to understand what those runtimes do.

Coming from Kotlin

Rust's model is closest to Kotlin coroutines: async fn ≈ suspend fun, both compile to state machines, and both need a library to actually run them (kotlinx.coroutines there, a runtime crate such as Tokio here). One difference: kotlinx.coroutines' async { } builder starts running right away by default, while a Rust future does nothing until it is awaited or polled.

A minimal executor

block_on polls a future on the current thread. When it gets Pending, it parks the thread; the waker unparks it.

Why Pin?

The state machine for an async fn may hold a reference to one of its own locals across an .await. If the future moved in memory after being polled, that internal pointer would dangle. Pin<&mut F> is a promise that the value won't move again (unless the type is Unpin, meaning it doesn't care). pin! pins on the stack; Box::pin pins on the heap. You mostly meet Pin when writing executors or hand-written futures, as here.

A real Pending: a timer future and concurrent joins

To return Pending honestly, a future needs some external event to call its waker. This Sleep future spawns a helper thread that sleeps and then wakes the task. (Real runtimes use one timer wheel plus the operating system's event queue instead of a thread per timer: epoll or io_uring on Linux, kqueue on macOS.)

join2 then runs two futures concurrently on one thread by polling both whenever either is woken. That interleaving is what "async" buys you.

Design note

Async pays off when you have many tasks that mostly wait (thousands of sockets). For CPU-bound parallelism, threads (Chapter 16) are simpler and faster. In production you'd use a runtime crate; the concepts above (poll, Waker, Pin, executors) are exactly what you'll be debugging when you do.

Practice

  1. Write a YieldNow future that returns Pending once (calling cx.waker().wake_by_ref() first) and Ready the second time. Use it to show two tasks in join2 taking turns.
    Solution

    block_on and join2 are the appendix's, unchanged. YieldNow calls wake_by_ref() before it returns Pending. That unparks the executor thread at once, so join2 is polled again and polls the other task. Each yield_now().await hands the turn to the other worker.

    Without yield_now, worker A would print all three steps before B started, because a future only gives up control at an .await that returns Pending. Without the wake_by_ref() call, nobody would wake the executor: the program prints A step 1, B step 1 and then parks forever.

  2. Extend the executor into a tiny scheduler: a VecDeque of Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = ()>>> tasks, polled round-robin until all are complete.
    Solution

    run replaces block_on. Each round pops every task from the front of the queue, polls it once, and pushes it back if it is still Pending. After a round it parks the thread. If a waker fired during the round (as YieldNow's does), park returns at once. If every task is waiting on something like Sleep, the thread sleeps until the timer thread calls wake, so the scheduler doesn't spin. Sleep is the appendix's.

Next · Appendix DUnsafe Rust & FFI
Appendix D

Unsafe Rust & FFI

unsafe doesn't switch the checker off. It unlocks five operations whose safety you vouch for, so you can build safe abstractions on top of them and talk to C. Services rarely need it: it's for wrapping C libraries and writing low-level data structures.

What unsafe allows

Inside an unsafe { } block, and only there, you may:

  1. dereference a raw pointer (*const T, *mut T)
  2. call an unsafe fn, including foreign (C) functions
  3. read or write a mutable or extern static
  4. read a field of a union

The fifth unlocked operation isn't written in a block at all: unsafe impl implements an unsafe trait (such as Send or Sync), and the unsafe keyword goes on the impl itself. Putting a plain impl Send for X {} inside an unsafe { } block is rejected with E0200.

Everything else, including the borrow checker, type checking and lifetimes, still applies:

The contract: an unsafe block is a promise that the code inside upholds Rust's rules (no dangling or misaligned pointers, no data races, no aliasing &mut, only valid values). Breaking it is undefined behavior, exactly as in C. The idiom is to keep unsafe blocks tiny, wrap them in a safe API whose checks make misuse impossible, and justify each block with a // SAFETY: comment.

Tip

Run tests under Miri (cargo +nightly miri test), an interpreter that detects undefined behavior in unsafe code: out-of-bounds accesses, use-after-free, invalid aliasing and data races.

Building a safe abstraction

The standard library's split_at_mut can't be written in safe Rust: the borrow checker can't prove that two &mut slices into one array don't overlap. With raw pointers and one bounds check, we can uphold that invariant ourselves and expose a 100% safe function:

unsafe fn and statics in edition 2024

  • An unsafe fn declares a precondition the caller must satisfy (document it under # Safety). In edition 2024 its body is not treated as an unsafe block: the unsafe_op_in_unsafe_fn lint (warn by default) flags every unsafe operation that isn't wrapped in its own unsafe { }, so each one gets its own justification.
  • static mut is almost never what you want. Edition 2024 denies taking references to it; use an atomic, a Mutex or OnceLock instead, which are safe.

Calling C, and being called from C

Rust speaks the C ABI directly, with no wrapper generator required for small interfaces:

  • declare foreign functions in an unsafe extern "C" { } block (required in edition 2024). Items you know are always safe to call can be marked safe fn.
  • CString makes an owned, NUL-terminated string to pass to C; CStr borrows one that C returned.
  • #[repr(C)] gives a struct C's field layout.
  • #[unsafe(no_mangle)] pub extern "C" fn exports a Rust function under a plain C symbol name. The attribute is spelled unsafe(...) because a symbol clash could cause undefined behavior.
Coming from C

The mental shift: in C every line is implicitly "unsafe". In Rust the unsafe surface is grep-able and usually tiny, so a security review starts with grep -rn unsafe rather than reading the entire codebase. As of Rust 1.99 you can even define C-style variadic functions (... parameters) in Rust.

Shipping a Rust library to C on Linux

To let existing C code call Rust, compile the crate as a cdylib: a normal ELF shared object with C symbols whose only runtime dependencies are libc and libgcc_s (used for stack unwinding), as ldd libpoint.so shows. In a Cargo project set [lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"] (output: target/release/libpoint.so); for a single file, rustc does the same:

Use crate-type = ["staticlib"] to produce libpoint.a for static linking instead. Going the other way, Rust links a system C library with #[link(name = "...")] on the extern block (or a build.rs printing cargo:rustc-link-lib=...); glibc itself is linked automatically.

On macOS the shared library is a .dylib, exported symbols get a leading underscore, and its only runtime dependency is libSystem (check with otool -L libpoint.dylib). Linking with an rpath of @executable_path lets ./main find the library next to it:

Practice

  1. Implement a fixed-capacity RawStack<T> on top of std::alloc::{alloc, dealloc, Layout} with push, pop and a Drop impl that drops the remaining elements. Write the // SAFETY: comment for every unsafe block.
    Solution

    The invariant the unsafe code relies on: slots 0..len are initialized and len..cap are not. push uses ptr::write because plain assignment would drop the garbage in the slot first. pop uses ptr::read to move the value out. Drop drops only the live elements, then frees the block with the same Layout it was allocated with. Zero-sized allocations are rejected, because alloc with a zero-size layout is undefined behaviour.

  2. Call qsort from the C library through FFI to sort a [i32; 8], passing an extern "C" fn comparator.
    Solution

    qsort sees the array as untyped bytes. We pass a *mut c_void to the first element, the element count, the element size, and a comparator with the C signature. The comparator is an unsafe extern "C" fn: it dereferences raw pointers, so it's only safe to call with pointers to valid i32s, which is what qsort guarantees.

Next · Appendix EA Multithreaded Key-Value Server
Appendix E

A Multithreaded Key-Value Server

A Redis-like TCP server in about 270 lines of std-only Rust, combining enums, errors, traits, a thread pool, locks, atomics and RAII shutdown. Chapter 21 builds servers the async way; this appendix shows how a thread-pool server works underneath.

What we're building

A line-based TCP server that stores strings, with a client to drive it, all in one program:

How the pieces map to the chapters

Component Technique Chapter
Command + ParseError enums with data, FromStr, custom Display 8, 9, 11
Store RwLock<HashMap> for data, AtomicU64 for stats 16
ThreadPool channel of boxed FnOnce jobs shared via Arc<Mutex<Receiver>>; Drop joins workers 13, 15, 16, B
Server TcpListener, Arc shared state, AtomicBool shutdown flag 16, 19
Client BufReader over TcpStream, io::Result and ? 9, 19

Two details worth studying in the code:

  • Lock scope in the worker loop. let job = rx.lock().unwrap().recv(); drops the MutexGuard at the end of the statement, so the lock is released before the job runs. Holding it while running the job would serialize the whole pool.
  • INCR is atomic because the read, the parse and the write happen under one write lock. Taking a read lock to get the value and a separate write lock to store it would be a classic lost-update race, which Rust does not prevent (it isn't a data race).

Talk to it from a terminal

Run it as a long-lived server in one WSL terminal and connect from another with netcat (sudo apt install netcat-openbsd if nc is missing). From Windows, localhost:7878 reaches it too.

Inspect it while it runs: ss -tlnp | grep 7878 shows the listening socket, and ps -T -p $(pgrep kv_server) shows six threads: the main thread (blocked in Server::wait), the acceptor thread and the four workers (assuming your Cargo package is named kv_server). On macOS, use lsof -nP -iTCP:7878 -sTCP:LISTEN and ps -M -p $(pgrep kv_server) instead.

The GET hits reply of 200 in the demo is the proof of correctness: eight clients on four threads raced to increment one key, and no update was lost. Notice also what wasn't needed: no unsafe, no manual memory management, no close() calls, and the compiler checked every cross-thread access.

Design note

This design dedicates a worker thread to each connection for its whole lifetime, so with 4 workers the 5th to 8th clients wait in the queue until earlier clients disconnect. That's the scalability limit async runtimes remove: one thread can multiplex thousands of mostly-idle connections (Appendix C).

Extension ideas

  1. Add EXPIRE key seconds using Instant deadlines checked lazily on GET, plus a background thread that sweeps expired keys every second.
  2. Add persistence: append every mutating command to a log file through a BufWriter, and replay the log on startup.
  3. Replace RwLock<HashMap> with 16 shards (Vec<RwLock<HashMap>>, shard chosen by key hash) and measure the throughput difference with 32 clients.
  4. Add #[cfg(test)] unit tests for Command::from_str covering every ParseError variant.
Next · Appendix FIdiomatic Design Patterns
Appendix F

Idiomatic Design Patterns

Which GoF patterns survive the move to Rust, which ones the type system absorbs, and the Rust-native patterns that replace the rest. The service in this course needs none of this machinery: it's here for reading and designing larger codebases.

The GoF catalogue, translated

Pattern Rust idiom
Strategy a trait object, a generic parameter, or simply a closure
Command an enum of commands + match; or Box<dyn FnOnce()>
Visitor match over an enum (closed set of types); a trait with visit_* methods for open sets
Observer callbacks (Vec<Box<dyn Fn(&Event)>>) or channels between threads
Iterator the Iterator trait
Builder a builder struct with chained methods consuming self
Factory method an associated function (Shape::circle(r), like a companion-object factory) or a trait with fn create() -> Self
Singleton a static with LazyLock/OnceLock where Kotlin uses object, but usually: pass the dependency explicitly
Decorator / Adapter a wrapper struct implementing the same trait; iterator adapters are the canonical example
State an enum state machine (Chapter 8) or the typestate pattern below
Template method a trait with default methods calling required ones
RAII / scoped resource Drop, used everywhere

Newtype: make illegal values unrepresentable

Wrap a primitive in a single-field struct to give it a distinct type and an invariant. Validate once, at construction ("parse, don't validate"), and every function that takes the newtype gets the guarantee for free. Zero runtime cost.

Builder

Rust has no overloading and no default arguments, so types with many optional settings use a builder. Methods take self by value and return it, which allows chaining; build() validates and returns a Result.

Coming from Kotlin

In Kotlin you'd rarely write a builder: named and default arguments (Request(url = "...", retries = 3)) or apply { } cover it. Rust has neither, so builders are idiomatic here, and build() is the natural place to validate.

Typestate: invalid transitions don't compile

Encode an object's state as a type parameter. Each state gets its own impl block, and a transition consumes self and returns the object in the next state. Calling publish() on a draft isn't a runtime error; the method doesn't exist for that type. The state markers are zero-sized, so this is free at run time.

RAII guards

Any "undo on early exit" logic belongs in a Drop impl. The guard runs on return, on ? and during panic unwinding, so there's no finally and no forgotten cleanup path.

Strategy, three ways

Command with undo

An enum of commands is data: you can store it, log it, send it over a channel, or compute its inverse. Here each command returns its own inverse, which makes undo a stack pop.

Anti-patterns to unlearn

  • .clone() to silence the borrow checker. Sometimes right, often a sign the ownership design is off. Ask who should own the data first.
  • Rc<RefCell<T>> object graphs. Recreating a GC heap gives you runtime panics instead of compile errors. Prefer tree ownership, or store nodes in a Vec and refer to them by index.
  • Deref for inheritance. Implementing Deref<Target = Base> so a struct "inherits" methods confuses readers and trait resolution. Delegate explicitly or use traits.
  • Stringly-typed APIs. fn set_mode(mode: &str) should take an enum Mode.
  • unwrap() in library code. Return Result; let the application decide what's fatal.
  • One giant struct borrowed as a whole. Borrowing &mut self for a method that only touches one field blocks everything else. Split into smaller structs, or borrow fields separately.

Practice

  1. Add a Rejected state to the typestate example, reachable only from Review, that can be revised back into a Draft.
    Solution

    Two changes to the example: a Rejected marker type, and two methods. reject exists only on Post<Review> and revise only on Post<Rejected>, so a rejection can only follow a review, and the only way out of Rejected is back to Draft. revise resets the approvals, so the revised post has to be approved again. The commented-out lines fail to compile with the errors shown.

  2. Rewrite the Strategy example so Checkout holds a Box<dyn Fn(f64) -> f64> (a closure trait object) instead of a Box<dyn Pricing>, and compare the two designs for testability.
    Solution

    The Pricing trait and its two structs are gone: a strategy is now any Fn(f64) -> f64, and regular and sale are functions that build one. Note the call syntax (self.pricing)(b): without the parentheses Rust would look for a method named pricing.

    Testability. With closures, a test double is a single line (Box::new(|_| 1.0)), and a spy is a closure that captures an Rc<RefCell<Vec>>; the trait version needs a struct and an impl for every fake. In return, the trait's strategies are named types: you can derive Debug and PartialEq on them, assert which strategy a Checkout holds, and add more methods (say, a label for the receipt) that every fake must implement too. A boxed closure is opaque: you can only call it. Use a closure when the strategy is one function, and a trait when it has state worth inspecting or more than one operation.

Every example was compiled and run with Rust 1.100.0 (edition 2024) on Ubuntu 26.04 in WSL 2, and the output panels show the captured output; the only differences you should see are thread IDs, file paths, timings and test order. Shell commands are bash. Chapters 1–19 use the standard library only. Chapters 20–27 use third-party crates (serde, serde_json, chrono, tokio, axum, tower, tower-http, reqwest, tracing, tracing-subscriber, sqlx). The serde and Tokio examples were built and run, and every step of the shoes project was built with Cargo from the files shown, passed cargo fmt --check, cargo clippy -- -D warnings and its tests, and had its terminal output, HTTP sessions, logs and psql output captured from real runs, Chapters 25–27 against PostgreSQL 18.7 in Podman. Chapter 23's reviews come from the live JSONPlaceholder API. The Playground runs the single-file examples in Chapters 20, 21 and 24; the project runs with Cargo.
